Assessing RTNET Solution Status

     • INVALID SOLUTION
              − Did not converge, i.e. Voltage difference at least one bus > tolerance
              − Voltage Magnitude and Angle Converged, but Error could not be
                reduced below threshold
     • SOLVED WITH EXCESS MISMATCH
              − Solved but a validity check failed
                 • Bus Mismatch > acceptable mismatch
                 • Solution quality check failed
     • VALID SOLUTION
              − All convergence, error processing, and validity criteria are met


Network Analysis | RTNET Miscellaneous Topics | 87


                                         Proprietary – See Copyright Page                3-87
                                           RTNET Miscellaneous Topics


<!-- salto de página -->

                                                     Network Analysis


Assessing RTNET Solution Quality


    • Obtaining a VALID SOLUTION from RTNET’s perspective does
      not always mean that the solution is operationally useful.
    • Criteria for an operationally acceptable solution
             − RTCA runs to completion
             − STNET case initialized from RTNET solves
             − The flows and voltages in and near the area that you want to study
               are reasonable.
             − Largest bus mismatch < 20
             − Voltage magnitudes are reasonable (look on Abnormal Voltage
               Summary display)

Basic RTNET Troubleshooting

• Check that ICCP data links are up
• For INVALID SOLUTION, look at the Real-Time Network Solution Analysis
  display
   − If ERRORMX
                  • Try running RTNET again or few times in sequence
         − If ITERMX
                  • Look at the listed worst bus angle and magnitude updates and then navigate
                    to the related buses on the Buses display for possible issues like switch in
                    wrong state
                  • Look on Log display for external units repeatedly placed on then off AVR
                    control (disable AVR for unit)
• For SOLVED WITH EXCESS MISMATCH, look at the Bus Mismatch display
   − Look on the Buses display at and near the worst mismatch stations for
                  • Bad topology status or unreasonable unit/load MW and MVAR

• Tracks measures of solution quality through time, geographically
  by station and company

  and geographically, so they can be correlated with changes in
  solution quality

  and includes links from each problem area to more detailed
  views.

DC Estimator Iterations

Support for DC estimator iterations
       − Primary use is as a pre-solver following a flat start, before the full
         ‘AC’ iterations
       − ‘DC’ iterations are essential to solving models with large phase-
         shifter angles

   Lab: Load Data Parameter Adaption - Load
                          Schedule Update
Objectives
     The following section tests RTNET's capability to update the schedule
     values associated with load areas that are measurement observable.


Setup
     The test in the previous section is the setup for this test.


Procedure
     1. Call up the process parameters tab in Real-Time Network Parameters
        display and set the Terms Constant/Load Schedule Error Filter value to
        a small number such as two. Also make sure the Load Model
        Observability Factor is close to one, for example 0.95.
     2. Call up the RTNET Load Area view of the Network Load Summary
        display, and Set the Enable LDAREA Update flag. This flag enables or
        disables the updating of load area schedules. There is a flag in
        schedule/loss details tab in network parameters display, what's the
        relationship?
     3. Call up the RTNET Load Area view of the Network Load Summary
        display and locate a non-top load area that has its MOBED
        (measurement observable) flag set. This indicates that the
        measurement observable percentage of the total load within that load
        area is at least equal to the Load Model Observability Factor. If there
        are no such non-top load areas that are measurement observable, skip
        the remainder of this section.
     4. Select the schedule update field (Update SKED) so that a check
        appears for the chosen MOBED load area.
     5. Call up the Load Areas view (the first tab), and note the schedule that
        is assigned to the selected load area. Also note the current PARENT
        FRAC MW value and the ACTUAL MW value for the chosen load area.
     6. Call up the Load Area view of the Network Schedules display, and find
        the load area schedule noted in the previous step. Locate the
        PARENT FRAC MW values in the schedule corresponding to the
        current study time.

                          Proprietary – See Copyright Page                   3-100
                            RTNET Miscellaneous Topics


<!-- salto de página -->

                               Network Analysis


     7. Significantly modify the related PARENT FRAC MW values to
        introduce a discrepancy between the evaluated model loads and the
        existing measurement based estimate for the chosen load area. If the
        chosen load area has a step schedule (STEP flag is set), raise the
        PARENT FRAC MW value by 10% for the time point at or just ahead of
        the current time. If it has a non-step schedule (STEP flag is blank),
        raise the PARENT FRAC MW value by 10% for the nearest time point,
        which is just ahead of or behind the current time, with respect to the
        current time.
     8. Call up Real-Time Network Debug display; select the EVALUATE
        SCHEDULES poke point to evaluate the time-dependent schedules,
        then run the state estimator.
Verification
     1. Go to Load Area Summary view of the Network Load Summary display
        and confirm that the new PARENT FRAC MW and the resulting
        MODELED MW values reflect the altered schedule value. Also confirm
        that the ACTUAL MW values are still essentially the same as before
        the schedule change. The difference between the two will be the basis
        for the schedule value update.
     2. Observe the altered schedule value on Load Area view of the Network
        Schedules display and confirm that it is being moved back towards its
        original value.
     3. Select the RUN STATE ESTIMATOR poke point on Real-Time
        Network Debug display few times.
     4. Observe that the altered schedule value on Load Area view of the
        Network Schedules display continues to approach the original value.
        Note that this updated schedule value may not equal the original value,
        but it should become a constant value after several State Estimator
        executions.
     5. Updates of individual load point model data will be tested in the
        following steps. On the Loads view of the Network Load Summary
        display, locate a load point which is measured and belongs to a load
        area that currently has schedule updating enabled. Make a note of
        Fraction MW value for this load point. The global schedule update flag
        for load area schedules must also still be set on Load Area view of the
        Network Load Summary display.
     6. Locate the selected load point's measurement on the All Analog
        Measurements view of the Telemetered Network Data display and add
        a bias of 10% to the MW value.
     7. Run the state estimator a few times.
     8. Observe that the Fraction MW value of the selected measured load
        point on Loads view of the Network Load Summary display has been

                        Proprietary – See Copyright Page                  3-101
                          RTNET Miscellaneous Topics


<!-- salto de página -->

                               Network Analysis


      changed such that the Model MW value is approaching the Estimated
      value.
Cleanup
          None, as this test is the setup for the next section.

       SCT Overview - Activation

                  Short circuit analysis program is activated in :

                            − Study environment: STSCT application
                                     • on operator request

                                                   Network Analysis


                                 SCT Main Features


        Flexible fault definition :
                 −     selection of any live node of the network as fault location
                 −     fault type : three phase, double phase (grounded or not), single phase
                 −     possibility to define the fault impedance
                 −     possibility to associate with a fault simultaneous component outage(s)
                 −     possibility to perform sequential line outages around the fault location
                 −     filtered output : neighborhood, minimum current level, tolerance
        Use of efficient methods :
                 − compensation = THEVENIN = WOODBURY
                 − sparse matrix techniques
        Only user-selected faults are processed
        Broad set of result reporting displays
        Result filtering to limit / expand output

 SCT : Options
Pre-fault state selection
        −     Magnitude (in p.u.) of the pre-fault voltage to be used
              during the solution. 1.0 means nominal voltages

Generator modeling
        −     Define the generator reactance (transient / sub-
              transient) to be used when building the positive
              sequence matrix

Load modeling
        −     Indicate whether loads are to be modeled in the fault
              study
        −     Note that only a solved voltage solution should be used
              when load modeling is done

Detailed output selection
        −     ID of a fault for which an entire network solution will
              be output on the Network Bus Summary display

CB rating threshold:
        −     Factor in % for CB rating violation report
        −     90% indicates that the flows exceeding 0.9*rating will
              be reported as warning

        Lab 1: Starting Short Circuit Analysis in
                                     Study Mode
Objectives
     Upon completion of this lab, you will be able to:
        •    Initialize STSCT with data
        •    Start the process
        •    Request a short circuit analysis execution
        •    Examine the basic short-circuit results


Task 1: Initialize STSCT with Data
     1. Call up the Short Circuit Analysis Study display. Start Process.
        Use the Data Retrieval, Savecase Directory buttons to see the
        application savecases.
     2. Retrieve the following savecases into STSCT:
        NETAPP : ESCA_EMP_DEFAULTS
        ENTIRE : TRAIN_NET_FEATURES


Task 2: Determine Active Faults and Examine Fault Definitions
     1. Call up the Short circuit Fault Definition and Activation display
     2. Click on the Directory symbol
     3. Observe that most faults are active
        (active faults are shown in red color)
     4. Click on any fault identifier, for instance GOLDEN619
     5. Examine the fault definition in the lower part of the display
        Notice the fault type : Phase to Ground with “regular” analysis (no
        lineout)
        Notice the AUTO in the fault descriptive text to remind you that this
        fault was created by the automatic option
     6. Examine also the fault GOLDEN619Y
        Notice the “Y” referring to a symmetrical fault.


                          Proprietary – See Copyright Page                      5-33
                                Short Circuit Analysis


<!-- salto de página -->

                                Network Analysis


Task 3: Execute a Short Circuit Analysis
     1. Call up the Short Circuit Analysis Study display
     2. Run Short Circuit Analysis.


Task 4: Observe the Results
     1. Verify that the Process status box changes from Sleep to Active during
        solution processing and goes back to Sleep status after completion.
     2. Observe that the Time of Last Execution is updated (to the DTS time in
        the DTS environment)
     3. Observe the text written in the Last Result box :
        “Normal” indicates that there is no breaker violation.
        “CB rating violations” indicates that at least one violation exists.
        “Abnormal” indicates abnormal conditions (for example that no active
        fault exists).
     4. Review the Network Message Log display
     5. Use the Related Displays to access various SCT result displays.
        Call up the Directory sub-view of the Solution Results Details display
        and click on the appropriate buttons to review the results at the faulted
        bus and adjacent components.

Lab 2: Defining Faults to be Analyzed by SCT
     In this lab, you will define your own faults. You will update and delete
     existing faults and you will create a savecase of the faults.


Objectives
     Upon completion of this lab, you will be able to:
        •    Define faults, with the capability to specify :
             − The type of fault
             − The fault location
             − The fault impedance
             − Whether some branch(es) should be simultaneously outaged
               with the fault.
             − Whether the fault analysis should be repeated with each of the
               branches connected to the faulted node sequentially outaged.
             − The extent of the fault neighborhood in which bus and branch
               output should be produced
             − The minimum fault current level to be included in the output
        •    Update an existing fault
        •    Delete an existing fault
        •    Create a savecase of the STSCT fault list.


Task 1: Define a New Fault
     You will define a 3-phase fault at some node in the KINCARD station.
     Proceed as follows :
     1. Call up the Fault Definition and Activation display.
     2. Enter a fault identifier ( LAB_F3 for example) in the ID field provided in
        the Fault Definition Update Area box.
     3. Select the     Define New Fault       button.
     4. Wait until you see the Process Status turn to “DEF FLTS DONE”
     5. Click on the Select Outage Devices button to select the node to be
        faulted.

                           Proprietary – See Copyright Page                     5-35
                                 Short Circuit Analysis


<!-- salto de página -->

                                           Network Analysis


     6. Select the node you want to be faulted (for instance, node 26 at
        KINCARD).
     7. Enter the fault parameters in the rectangle shown on top of the display.
     8. Select OK to return to the Fault Definition and Activation display.
     9.    Validate your definitions
     10. Select the         Save Selections and Changes button.
     11. The fault definition is brought up in the lower part of the display.
         Enter data into the Description field.
     12. Ensure that the fault activation status is DEFAULT.
     13. Validate again your definitions
          Notice that your fault has been recorded in the directory, but it is not
          active because ........................................................................................
          ......................................................................................................


Task 2: Define a New Fault with Line-Out Option
     1. Call up the Fault Definition and Activation display.
     2. Enter another fault identifier ( SEQ_OUTAGE for example) in the ID
        field provided.
     3. Define the fault as before (same location) but also click the Line_Out
        radio button.
     4. Validate / save the new fault.
     5. The fault definition is brought up.
        The branches directly connected to bus containing the faulted node are
        listed under the fault location for sequential outage.


Task 3: Define a New Fault with Simultaneous Outages
     1. Enter another fault identifier ( SIM_OUTAGES for example) in the ID
        field provided.
     2. Define the fault as before (no line out option), but when going to the
        Outage Selection view, set the Select flag of some branches that you
        want to be simultaneously outaged with the fault.
        Click on the Done button.
     3. Validate / save the new fault.
     4. The fault definition is brought up.
        The branches selected to be simultaneously outaged are listed under
        the fault location.


                                 Proprietary – See Copyright Page                                          5-36
                                       Short Circuit Analysis

Task 4: Execute a Short Circuit Analysis, Observe the Results
     1. Call up the Short Circuit Analysis Study display
     2. Run Short Circuit Analysis.
     3. Use the Related Displays to access various SCT result displays.
        Call up the Directory sub-view of the Solution Results Details display
        and click on the appropriate buttons to review for each previously
        defined faults the results at the faulted bus and adjacent components.


Task 5: Create a Savecase with Your Fault Definitions
     1. Call up the Short Circuit Analysis Study display.
     2. Enter a complementary descriptive text for your faults in the Fault
        Definition Description field.
     3. Select the Data Retrieval button
     4. Go to the savecase directory display thanks to the shortcut button and
        save your faults savecase (faults case type).
     5. Check in the savecase directory that your savecase has been properly
        created.


Task 6: Update an Existing Fault Definition
     1. Call up the Fault Definition and Activation view
     2. View the current definition of the LAB_F3 fault by clicking its ID on the
        Directory view.
     3. To modify this fault definition, use the Fault Definition Update Area
        box to enter the ID (LAB_F3) of the fault to be updated, and click on
        the Modify Existing Fault button.
        (You could also have used the Load Into Update Area          button in
        the fault description.)
     4. A Delete button appears on the left of the fault location at the
        bottom of the display. To modify the fault location, click on this button
        and use the Blue navigation “Select Outage devices” to select
        another node (for instance, node 19 at HEARN).
     5. Change the fault type from 3-phase to double-phase-to-ground.
     6. Change the fault impedance to 2 + j 1
     7. Click the Save Selection and Changes          button. Verify that the fault
        description is well updated.

     8. Validate your definitions.


Task 7: Delete an Existing Fault Definition
     1. Call up the Fault Definition and Activation display
     2. Create a TEST fault (for instance, a 3-phase fault at HEARN 18)
     3. Check its proper creation in the fault directory
     4. Enter its id (TEST) in the field provided
     5. Click on the Delete Fault button.
     6. A pop-up appears on screen to confirm the deletion.
        Click to confirm.
     7. Verify in the directory that the fault has been deleted.

                           Lab 3: Building Faults Groups
     In this lab, you will build fault groups and you will assign fault to fault group
     so as to control their activation status by group.
     You will also use the facility to create at once a set of faults at all
     energized buses in a company.


Objectives
     Upon completion of this lab, you will be able to:
        •    Build fault groups
        •    Validate the faults
        •    Request an automatic creation of faults


Task 1: Building Fault Groups
     1. Call up the Fault Definition and Activation display
     2. Define 3 more faults (named 2PH1, 2PH2, 2PH3), all involving phase-
        to-phase faults at different locations. Set their fault activation status to
        Default.
     3. Check in the directory that the 3 faults are well created.
     4. Call up the Group view of the Fault Definition and Activation display.
     5. To insert a group, click the [+/-] button on the left of any group
        record. A pulldown menu appears. Choose the Insert Group Record
        item.
     6. Enter the following ID for this new group : 2PHS and a group
        description : “two phase to ground faults”.
     7. Insert the 3 faults records under this group and enter the fault IDs :
        2PH1, 2PH2, 2PH3
     8. Click on the Active radio button for the 2PHS group to be active.
     9. Click on the Validate button.
     10. Verify in the fault directory that the fault activation status for the 3
         faults is now Active.
     11. Set the activation flag of the 2PH2 fault to Ineligible. Validate.
     12. Verify that fault 2PH2 is now inactive.

                          Proprietary – See Copyright Page                          5-39
                                Short Circuit Analysis


<!-- salto de página -->

                                  Network Analysis


     13. Notice the group 2PHS is declared Partially Active and shows green
         in the directory.


Task 2: Create Faults at Each Bus Automatically
     1. Retrieve the fault savecase titled “EMPTY”.
     2. Observe that the fault list is empty.
     3. Call up the Short Circuit Solution Options analyst display.
     4. In the Busbar Group Definition box, specify the mode as “Automatic”.
     5. Enter the characteristics that will be attributed to each fault : fault level
        threshold = 0 and neighborhood = 0.
     6. Enter the ID of the company in which all buses will be fault location in
        turn (for instance : ECAR).
     7. Enter the name of the fault group in which you want the automatic
        faults to be inserted (for instance : ZZZZ).
     8. The fault type identifier is not used : the worst case will be examined
        at all buses : 3-phase and single phase-to-ground faults.
     9. Run a short circuit analysis while watching the fault list. Notice the fault
        list is being created, initially inactive, but will become active on
        completion.
     10. Also, have a look at the fault group list. Notice that the ZZZZ group is
         created containing the desired faults : 3-phase to grounds followed by
         1 phase to ground at all the buses.
     11. Look at the SCT results.


Summary
     In this lab, you learned how to build faults groups and how to use them for
     controlling the fault activation.
     You also learned how to automatically place faults at all energized buses
     of a company.
     In the next lab, you will study how to filter the fault analysis results.

             Lab 4: Filtering Short Circuit Analysis
                                             Results

Objectives
     Upon completion of this lab, you will be able to obtain the desired level of
     output information from the short circuit analysis results.


Task 1: Filter by the Neighborhood Output Selection
     1. Stop the STSCT process
     2. Retrieve the TRAIN_NET_FEATURES savecase
     3. Start STSCT
     4. Set all fault groups to inactive
     5. Define a single-phase-to-ground fault at DOUGLAS, node 11. Identify
        this fault as “DISTANCE”.
     6. Set neighborhood = 1 to specify the electrical distance from the
        faulted bus in which you want to see the detailed bus and branch
        results.
     7. Set the fault activation status to “Must Run”
     8. Validate / save this fault definition.
     9. Create a second fault with the same definition and call it “TWIN”.
     10. Run Short Circuit Analysis.
     11. View the results for the fault DISTANCE. One neighborhood of buses
         and the branches connected to them should be displayed.
     12. Update fault DISTANCE so that the neighborhood level is now 3,
         validate and save.
     13. Run the short circuit analysis and verify that now 3 neighborhoods of
         buses are displayed for the fault DISTANCE.
     14. Notice that many fault currents are below 1.0 kA.


                          Proprietary – See Copyright Page                    5-41
                                Short Circuit Analysis


<!-- salto de página -->

                                  Network Analysis


Task 2: Filter by the Minimum Fault Current
     1. Modify fault DISTANCE by entering a minimum fault current level =
        1.0 kA to filter the output.
     2. Validate / save.
     3. Run Short Circuit Analysis
     4. Check that the output is much shorter and that all the listed flows
        exceed the minimum fault level specified.


Task 3: Request a Detailed Output for a Given Fault
     1. Call up the Short Circuit Solution Options display
     2. Enter the ID of an active fault for which a detailed fault output is
        desired (DISTANCE for example)
     3. Enable the detailed output option by clicking the button.
     4. Run Short Circuit Analysis
     5. Call up the Network Bus Summary display (in the SC_BUSES
        display) and locate the bus where the fault occurred.
     6. In another viewport, look at the results for fault TWIN. The flows
        should agree with those shown on the Bus Summary display.
     7. Notice that the fault DISTANCE is not listed anymore in the directory
        of the Results Details display.


Task 4 (Optional): Filter the List of Breaker Violations
     Among the SCT Solution Options, the CB rating threshold ( referred to as
     Ponderation Factor for CB rating violation [%] ) represents a multiplier of
     the CB rating below which the violation will not appear in the list.
     1. Stop the STSCT process.
     2. Retrieve the NETMOM savecase titled HIGH_CB_RATING
     3. Retrieve your fault savecase
     4. Start STSCT
     5. Set the ponderation factor to 100 and run the analysis
     6. Observe that there is no short circuit warnings
     7. Observe that a number of violation percentages are below 200%
     8. Change the value of the CB rating threshold to 200%
     9. Run the short circuit analysis
     10. Verify that only the short circuit violations exceeding 200% are listed.

                           Proprietary – See Copyright Page                    5-42
                                 Short Circuit Analysis


<!-- salto de página -->

                                  Network Analysis


     11. Now, set the ponderation factor to 60 and run the analysis.
     12. Verify that all fault currents between 60 and 100% of the CB ratings
         are listed as warnings.


Task 5 (Optional): Analyze a Fault with Sequential Line Outages
     1. Define a fault with line out option set.
     2. Set it to MUSTRUN
     3. Run a short circuit analysis
     4. Call up the short Circuit Results Summary display or the Directory
        view of the Solution Results display. The fault appears several times.
        For a bus connected to n branches, (n+1) solutions are determined :
        one for the fault without outage, and one for each branch outage.


Summary
     In this lab, you learned how to filter the output results of a short-circuit
     analysis.

                                            Network Analysis


Summary of Network Analysis (1 of 3)

The network analysis applications are used to simulate the electric
  power grid for given times and conditions.
Network Analysis can be performed in the real-time or study
  environment.
The output from these applications provides:
       − an assessment of the current network state, including:
                • Flows and Voltages
                • Device Outages
                • Split Buses
                • Islanding
       − an indication of overloads
       − an indication of high/low voltage
       − the likely effect of pre-defined contingencies on the given network

Network Analysis | Conclusion | P3


                                     Proprietary – See Copyright Page          7-3
                                                Conclusion


<!-- salto de página -->

                                            Network Analysis


Summary of Network Analysis (2 of 3)


The network database, NETMOM, contains all of the information
  necessary for the applications to calculate a power flow as best
  they can and to report anomalies to the user.
Included in the database is the definition data as well as all output
   data from the system analysis:
       − Topology – how each device is connected into the system
       − Device Parameters – impedances, MW/MVAr limits, tap data, etc.
       − Limits – Operating limits for branches, interfaces, node voltage
       − Schedules – CB Status, Voltage Regulation, Load Area
       − Monitoring Criteria – what is an overload and when should it be
         reported
       − All output data – Bus Voltages, MW/MVAR flows, loads,
         generation, tap positions, violations, etc.
Network Analysis | Conclusion | P4


                                     Proprietary – See Copyright Page   7-4
                                                Conclusion


<!-- salto de página -->

                                            Network Analysis


Summary of Network Analysis (3 of 3)


The contingency database, CTGS, contains all of the information
  necessary to define a contingent network for use during analysis.
The CTGS database also contains all of the processing parameters
  for the contingency analysis software.
Included in the database are:
       − The contingency definitions – component outages, processing type,
         activation, processing flags, etc.
       − Conditional Components – a monitored element and its associated
         component outages
       − Processing Tolerances and Parameters – values specifying solution
         tolerances and processing parameters. These are used in
         determining how many contingencies are processed during full
         processing and what should be reported as a violation.

                                                Conclusion

Summary of Real-Time Network Analysis
(1 of 3)

The most commonly executed Real-Time Network Analysis Tasks
  include:
       − RTNET: A State Estimator which calculates the real-time network
         state for the given set of input (both real-time SCADA and model
         data).
       − RTCA: Real-Time Contingency Analysis calculates the contingent
         network state for selected contingencies using real-time data from
         RTNET.
Online Network Sequence (OLNETSEQ) coordinates the execution
  of the real-time network analysis tasks.
In the real-time environment, there is only one instance of each
   application (clone), which means that all users are viewing the
   same set of data.
Network Analysis | Conclusion | P6


                                     Proprietary – See Copyright Page     7-6
                                                Conclusion


<!-- salto de página -->

                                                 Network Analysis


     Summary of Real-Time Network Analysis
     (2 of 3)


     RTNET simulates the current state of the system using
            − Real-time data from SCADA
            − Model data
     RTNET uses pseudo- measurements to fill in areas where SCADA
       data is not available in order to increase observability.
     The RTNET solution satisfies, as best it can, Kirchoff’s Law – the
       sum of the flows at each bus must be zero.


     Network Analysis | Conclusion | P7


To determine the quality of SCADA measurements, i.e. bad data detection,
you must have redundant measurements.


                                          Proprietary – See Copyright Page   7-7
                                                     Conclusion


<!-- salto de página -->

                                                 Network Analysis


     Summary of Real-Time Network Analysis
     (3 of 3)


     The RTNET solution matches, as best it can, the SCADA values for
       all flows and voltages.
     RTNET processing uses only ‘good’ data from SCADA and is able to
       identify anomalous or “bad” measurement data.
     A valid RTNET solution can be used as a basecase by downstream
        applications.


     Network Analysis | Conclusion | P8


To determine the quality of SCADA measurements, i.e. bad data detection,
you must have redundant measurements.


                                          Proprietary – See Copyright Page   7-8
                                                     Conclusion


<!-- salto de página -->

                                            Network Analysis


Summary of Study Network Analysis
(1 of 2)

The most commonly executed Study Network Analysis Tasks
  include:
       − PWRFOW: Study Power Flow simulation calculates the network
         state for a specific time and set of conditions as defined by the
         user.
       − STCA: Study Contingency Analysis calculates the contingent
         network state for selected contingencies for a specific time and set
         of conditions as defined by the user.
The Study Network Analysis application (STNET) can include any or
  all of the study tasks and is used to coordinate their execution.
In the study environment, there can be multiple instances (clones)
   of the same application (i.e.: STNET), so each user can work
   independently without impacting anyone else.

Network Analysis | Conclusion | P9


                                     Proprietary – See Copyright Page       7-9
                                                Conclusion


<!-- salto de página -->

                                             Network Analysis


Summary of Study Network Analysis
(2 of 2)


PWRFLOW simulates the state of the system for a specific time and
  set of conditions as defined by the user.
PWRFLOW’s solution depends on the basecase from which it was
  initialized and model data.
A basecase can be retrieved from:
       − RTNET (real-time data initialization).
       − a savecase (savecase directory).
       − another user’s study (network copy)
PWRFLOW is typically used to study:
       − Outages (Planned and Unplanned)
       − Peak and Low Load Periods
       − Change in Transactions
Network Analysis | Conclusion | P10


                                      Proprietary – See Copyright Page   7-10
                                                 Conclusion


<!-- salto de página -->

                                                  Network Analysis


     Summary of Contingency Analysis
     (1 of 2)

     Contingency Analysis can be executed within the real-time and
       study environments:
            − RTCA: Real-Time Contingency Analysis is executed in sequence
              with RTNET by OLNETSEQ.
            − STCA: Study Contingency Analysis is executed in sequence with
              PWRFLOW by STNET.
     Contingency Analysis assesses the impact of user defined
       contingencies upon the basecase network.
     The basecase for RTCA is copied automatically from RTNET during
       the real-time sequence.
     The basecase for STCA is contained within STNET. Once STNET
       has been initialized, no further initialization is needed for STCA.

     Network Analysis | Conclusion | P11


You design and define contingencies for CA.


                                           Proprietary – See Copyright Page   7-11
                                                      Conclusion


<!-- salto de página -->

                                             Network Analysis


Summary of Contingency Analysis
(2 of 2)

Contingency Analysis processing consists of several steps:
       − DPF – A decoupled powerflow is run on the initial basecase
       − Screening – A quick analysis is run on all active contingencies
         looking for potential violations
       − Selection – The screening results are ranked and the worst are
         selected for full processing.
       − Full Processing – A complete powerflow analysis is done on each
         of the selected contingencies.
Contingency Analysis reports violations based on the defined
  monitoring criteria. Violations include:
       − Branch overloads
       − High/Low voltage
       − Interface Flow
       − Phase Angle Difference
       − Loss of Load/Loss of Generation
Network Analysis | Conclusion | P12


                                      Proprietary – See Copyright Page   7-12
                                                 Conclusion


<!-- salto de página -->

                                             Network Analysis


Conclusion


The network analysis applications provide the tools necessary for
  operators to evaluate the current state of the system.
The network analysis applications also allow the user to study
  various scenarios like upcoming outages or peak load periods.
These tools can be used to assist in the planning of outages as well
  as scheduling generation and/or interchange.
The network analysis applications can alert the user of current or
  potential overloads.
The applications can also be used to track down problems with
  SCADA data.


Network Analysis | Conclusion | P13


                                      Proprietary – See Copyright Page   7-13
                                                 Conclusion

<!-- salto de página -->

                                            Network Analysis


Network Analysis Terms

Basecase: Any valid and solved model of the power system.
Mismatch: The difference between the amount of flow into a bus and the
   amount of flow out of a bus.
Contingent Network: Networks resulting from user-specified component outages
   and switching operations
Cost: A metric for the fit or level of consistency between the measured or
   modeled value and the estimated value.
Degree of Freedom: The difference between the number of equations and the
   number of variables.
Factor: Type of RTNET iteration. A factor iteration does a complete rebuild of
   the Jacobian matrix.
Flatstart: Processing initialization. It sets all bus voltages that are not regulated
    to 1.0 pu and 0 degrees. Those that are regulated will be set to their
    scheduled target regulation value.
Network Analysis | Appendix A | P5


                                   Proprietary – See Copyright Page                 8-5
                              Appendix A: Glossary of Terms and Definitions


<!-- salto de página -->

                                            Network Analysis


Network Analysis Terms


Full Processing: Part of contingency analysis, full processing runs a full
    powerflow solution on the selected contingencies.
Measurement-Observable: Portions of the network where RTNET can estimate
  the state using measured data.
Observable: Portions of the network where RTNET estimates the state using
   available measurements, but primarily modeled data.
Preferred Tap: A tap that is estimated by RTNET based on voltage and flow
   measurements.
Pseudo-measurement: Value generated from model data or ICCP data to fill in
   gaps where measurement (SCADA) data is not available.
Refactor: Type of RTNET iteration. A refactor will update the matrix with any
   changes that have occurred since the last iteration.

Network Analysis | Appendix A | P6


                                   Proprietary – See Copyright Page             8-6
                              Appendix A: Glossary of Terms and Definitions


<!-- salto de página -->

                                            Network Analysis


Network Analysis Terms


Repeat: Type of RTNET iteration. A repeat iteration uses the matrix as it was in
   the last iteration.
Savecase: A database or set of databases saved for future study.
Screening: Part of contingency analysis processing, screening does a quick
   evaluation of the contingent network, looking for potential violations.
Selection: Part of the contingency analysis processing, selection occurs after
   screening. It ranks the contingencies found by screening and sends the
   highest ranked contingencies to full processing. The number of contingencies
   sent to full processing by the selection process is based on the contingency
   selection parameters.


Network Analysis | Appendix A | P7


                                   Proprietary – See Copyright Page            8-7
                              Appendix A: Glossary of Terms and Definitions

              Security Enhancement looks for control changes in order to improve the security

                       − For the basecase network state (current or postulated)

                                                  Network Optimization


       Terminology : Limits and constraints


 Minimize J = J ( x, u )                                           J = cost-objective function
          − u = control variable ( decision variable )
          − x = resulting vector of state variables
 Subject to the following constraints:
          − h(x,u) = 0                                                      equality constraints
          − y_min < y = y (x)                              <   y_max        inequality constraints


          − Constraints define the ‘‘ feasible operating subspace ‘‘
          − A solution which violates some constraint(s) is ‘‘ not feasible ‘‘
            ( the solution shows constraint violations )
          − Binding constraints :     y = y_min      or    y = y_max

                      Lab: Enhancing Network Security
                                       Using STSENH
       In this lab, you will use the STSENH application to evaluate/ improve a
       network state before contingencies (basecase) and after contingencies.


Objectives
       Upon completion of this lab, you will be able to :
          •   Initialize STSENH with data
          •   Run a network security enhancement study and view the results
          •   Use Security Enhancement to determine control actions to relieve
              violations in the basecase and in contingency cases
          •   Modify the SENH optimization problem definition
          •   Create a savecase of the STSENH results.
       Except when otherwise stated, all the displays used in this lab belong to
       the STSENH application.


Task 1: Initialize STSENH with Data
       You have to retrieve savecases of the following databases : NETAPP,
       SENHAPP, NETMOM, CTLMOM, CTGS, DPF.
          •   First, retrieve the NETAPP and SENHAPP savecases containing
              default application characteristics.
          •   For this lab, an ENTIRE savecase has been prepared which
              contains all the other databases.
          •   Retrieve the ENTIRE savecase titled TRAIN_NET_FEATURES.
       Note: You can also navigate to the savecase list via the Menu Bar :
       HABITAT Applications / Savecase Manager / Savecase Manager master
       and there, select the desired application.

Task 6: Restrict one Control Variable
       In this part of the lab, you will reduce the move magnitude available to one
       of the control variables. The result should be a more expensive solution.
       1. Find a generator that was significantly moved by the cost minimization
          run, for instance the generator at WVILLE.
          Note the initial generation: …….….……….. MW
          and the generation recommendation: ………………… MW
       2. Call up the View Controls tab of the Define Controls display.
       3. You will reduce the magnitude of the allowable move in the direction
          the MW generation was initially moved (make the limit enterable and
          modify the adequate limit, so as to prevent the unit to move as far as
          it moved in the previous run).
          For instance, change the max generation at WVILLE from 1000 to 400 MW.
          (Do not change a limit to a value that would make the current
          generation unfeasible. In this case, SENH would not attempt to move
          that control anymore).
       4. Run STSENH (base case).
       5. Notice that the unit was moved just to the new limit.
       6. Note the cost C3 of this new solution ............... $/h.
          Notice that normally C3 > C2 because the problem’s degree of
          freedom has also been reduced (one variable can not be moved as
          much to improve the solution).
       7. Restore the full range of MW generation for the selected unit. It is
          enough to reset the limits to not enterable : SENH will restore the initial
          limit at the next execution.
       8. Run STSENH (base case) to restore the full range solution.
       9. Check that the cost is back to C2.

        Terminology : Limits and constraints


      Minimize J = J ( x, u )                                       J = cost-objective function
               − u = control variable ( decision variable )
               − x = resulting vector of state variables
      Subject to the following constraints:
               − h(x,u) = 0                                           equality constraints
               − y_min < y = y (x)                             <   y_max       inequality constraints


               − Constraints define the ‘‘feasible operating subspace”
               − A solution which violates some constraint(s) is ‘‘ not feasible‘‘
                 ( the solution shows constraint violations )
               − Binding constraints : y = y_min or            y = y_max


Network Optimization | Basic Features of OPF and VVD | 2


                                         Proprietary – See Copyright Page                         2-2
                                         Basic Features of OPF and VVD


<!-- salto de página -->

                                                    Network Optimization


   Definition of OPF

        OPF scope: any problem that involves the determination of the
          optimal steady-state operation of an Electric Power Generation-
          Transmission system
        Optimal Power Flow (OPF) = Power Flow
                                                           + Objective
                                                           + Controls
                                                           + Constraints

        Objective : value to be minimized, such as fuel cost or MW losses
        Controls : unit MW, unit MVAR, capacitors and reactors, LTC and
              phase shifter taps, and area interchanges
        Constraints : high and low voltage limits, branch flows, interface
              flow limits, and node pair limits

     Optimization versus regulation in OPF

   • LTC taps of a transformer will be moved by OPF to
     optimize the objective if the device is selected as a
     control variable.
   • Otherwise, LTC taps of a transformer will be moved by
     OPF to locally regulate a bus voltage, if the device is
     specified as on AVR, and XF tap regulation is globally
     enabled.

        Lab 2: Optimal Power Flow Background
     This section contains a short text that summarizes the basic concepts
     involved in optimization problems, and how these concepts apply to the
     optimal power flow problem. This text will also drive you to some of the
     OPF displays to show where the concepts apply.
     Students who are not familiar with optimization problems will benefit from
     reading this text before proceeding to the subsequent lab.
     Students who are already familiar with these concepts can jump directly to
     the next lab (using OPF).

1.1 Optimization Problems
     Any optimization problem is defined in terms of :
        • An   objective function to optimize (usually a cost to minimize).
        •   Control variables that are allowed to be moved by OPF to correct
            constraint violations and/or improve the objective function.
        •   Constraints that put high and low limits on the feasible range for
            state variables and control variables - these are known as
            inequality constraints. OPF also enforces equality constraints,
            which impose relationships (such as Kirchoff’s laws) between the
            variables.
     The Engineer/Analyst sets up these various elements of the problem in
     the OPF databases. The procedure to setup these problem elements will
     be the object of a subsequent module. In the present module the user
     only activates or deactivates these elements to modify the problem
     definition.

1.2 The Optimal Power Flow (OPF) Problem

1.2.1 OPF Objective Function
     OPF allows you to select an objective function from a defined set, using
     the Objective view of the Define Controls display .
     Your task: Have a look at this view of this display. Do not modify any
     data. Typically there would be an objective function defined with unit
     incremental cost curves (ICCs).


                         Proprietary – See Copyright Page                     2-23
                         Basic Features of OPF and VVD


<!-- salto de página -->

                               Network Optimization


1.2.2 OPF Controls
     OPF allows you to activate / deactivate control variables by group or
     individually using 2 views of the Define Controls display :
        •    “View Controls“ allows you to enable / disable individual controls
            and modify their limits
        •   “Define Groups” allows you to activate / deactivate control groups
     Your task: Have a look at these 2 views. Do not modify any data.
        1. Notice in the “Define Groups” view the names of the control group
           types, and their association with either OPF or the various control
           groups dedicated to SENH (xPREVIOL, WPRECOST, xPSTVIOL)
            -   x = W for real power
            -   x = R for reactive power
        2. Notice also that the corresponding control groups further identify
           the control type : UN, XF, CP.
        3. Page down in the “View Controls“ tab and observe that most
           controls are enabled.

1.2.3 OPF Constraints

1.2.3.1 Equality Constraints and Regulations
     In the OPF problem, the equality constraints are the power flow equations,
     including area MW interchange constraints (if applicable).
     The powerflow equations can also include more complex relations to
     represent regulations that can exist in the power system. For instance,
     voltage regulation can exist at various places by various network
     components (generating units, transformers, shunt reactances). These
     constraints model the physical or operational characteristics of the power
     system behavior.
     For controls that are activated to participate in optimization, the local
     regulation is disabled, because the goal is to determine the optimal target
     for regulation. Thus, their existing regulation target is ignored by OPF in
     order to determine the optimal regulation target.
     For controls not activated to participate in optimization, local regulation (if
     defined) will be maintained during the optimization. This applies to devices
     that are physically located in the external model, or that are not needed or
     not available for optimization.
     OPF will impose the local regulation target if:
        •   the regulating device is not activated as a control


                          Proprietary – See Copyright Page                      2-24
                          Basic Features of OPF and VVD


<!-- salto de página -->

                               Network Optimization


        •   and the regulating variable is specified as ON-regulation (ON-AVR
            or ON-AWR) in the corresponding network component summary
            display,
        •   and if the global regulation flag is enabled
     Your task : See these global regulation mode flags on the OPF Options
     display. Do not modify any data.

1.2.3.2 Inequality Constraints
     Inequality constraints represent high and low operating limits on the power
     system elements.

1.2.3.2.1 Monitored Constraints
     EMP network applications can monitor the following inequality
     constraints:
        •   Voltage : Upper and lower limits on the voltage magnitude
        •   Branch : Upper limits on the flow across lines and transformers
        •   Interface : Upper and lower limits on the total net MW and/or MVAr
            flow across specified sets of branches
        •   Node pair : Upper limits on the difference in the voltage angle
            between the 2 specified nodes
        •   Reserve Group : Min MW reserve
     In OPF, you activate/deactivate the monitoring of constraints individually,
     or by group, or by constraint type.

1.2.3.2.2 Enforced Constraints
     When solving with OPF, you may wish that OPF enforces only a subset of
     the monitored constraints.
     Two views of the Optimization Constraint Definition display --- similar to
     those used to specify the monitored elements --- allow you to specify the
     constraints to be enforced by OPF.
     Your task : Find these 2 views (Equipment and Group). Do not modify
     any data.
     The enforcement definition is the same as the logic used to control the
     monitored elements. Thus, in the Group view of the display, you can
     enforce constraints by enforcement group, and in each enforcement group
     by constraint type, but you can also disable individual constraint from
     being enforced ( Equipment view ).
     In addition to this facility, the OPF options also allow you to globally
     activate or deactivate the constraint enforcement by type.


                          Proprietary – See Copyright Page                      2-25
                          Basic Features of OPF and VVD


<!-- salto de página -->

                               Network Optimization


     Your task : See these global enforcement flags on the OPF Options
     display. Do not modify any data.

     constraints to be enforced.
     Your task :

        Definition Summary

        to what is specified in the Control Definition display.

        corresponds to what is specified in the Optimization Constraint
        Definition display.
     4. Disable enforcement of the voltage constraints in the area WEST
     5. Check the result in the Problem Definition Summary
     6. Restore the voltage constraint for enforcement; check again.

                   Lab 3: Using Optimal Power Flow
    In this lab, you will gain experience with OPF by solving a few common
    problems.
    Upon completion of this lab, you will be able to:
       •   Run a simple power flow using OPF
       •   Solve a MW loss minimization problem

Task 1: Solve a Simple Powerflow Problem Using OPF
    1. Call up the Define Controls display, Define Groups view.
    2. Deactivate all OPF controls by making sure that all Active buttons are
       off.
       Without controls, OPF defaults to a standard powerflow solution.
       Since no controls are active, the objective function setup is ignored by
       OPF; without controls, there cannot be any optimization.
    3. From the Optimal Power Flow Study display, call up the Options
       display and check the options. Review the option settings, to see if
       they make sense for a simple powerflow solution. You can turn options
       on/off by clicking on the appropriate buttons.
       •   Select the Flat Start option to provide reasonable starting values for
           all variables to be solved.
       •   When no controls are available, OPF is unable to enforce
           constraints, so do not expect OPF to eliminate violations in this
           case. There is no need to turn off enforcement of constraints,
           because in this mode OPF will ignore them.
    4. Select OK when done (or use the Previous Display arrow).
    5. Select the Run Optimal Power Flow button.
    6. Check the Last Result to see if a valid (= converged) solution was
       obtained
    7. If OPF did not converge, see the convergence trace on the analyst
       displays : Optimal Power Flow Performance display :
       •   Bus Mismatch view, for the largest bus mismatches present on
           each iteration of the solution process.

     1. Call up the Objective view of the Define Controls display.

              Lab 4: Using Voltage-Var Dispatch
Note: Objective Function Verification VVD's software design is such that it
is a shell around OPF software. VVD relies on OPF software to calculate
a solution that optimizes the active objective function, while meeting
constraints. Strict verification of VVD's supported objective functions is
considered beyond the scope of this lab.
Setup: The proper data initialization (NETAPP case, OPFMOM case,
and CTLMOM case) of VVD clone should be done. VVD should be
running properly as part of online network sequence.
Procedure: Student will perform the following steps in sequence:
1. On the Network Online Sequence (Real-Time Network Analysis)
   display, bring up the triggers popup, and DISABLE all triggers except
   MANUAL triggers.
2. Voltage violations in the SE solution will be required. If no appropriate
   violations are already present, change voltage limits in RTNET to get
   voltage violations. If possible, locate the violation(s) where VVD's
   controls can have an impact. In other words, pick voltage violations
   that VVD should be able to correct given its active controls. All voltage
   violations that you cause should be confined to one operating area.
3. Manually trigger the network sequence.
4. Check the Network Basecase Violations under application VVD to see
   if VVD was able to correct the violation. Check the Optimal Power
   Flow Control Summary display to see what controls VVD recommends
   moving.
   Results:
   •   VVD should have recommended control movements to correct or
       improve the voltage violation(s). VVD should have corrected the
       violation if possible.
   •   VVD should have recommended control movements only in the
       operating area where the voltage violation(s) occurred.
5. Change voltage limits if necessary in RTNET to avoid any voltage
   violations in the state estimator.
6. Manually trigger the network sequence.
7. Check the Network Basecase Violations under application VVD to
   make sure that VVD did not create any new violations.


                    Proprietary – See Copyright Page                    2-31
                    Basic Features of OPF and VVD


<!-- salto de página -->

                        Network Optimization


8. Check the Optimal Power Flow Control Summary display to see what
   controls VVD recommends moving. Check the losses in the RTNET
   solution on the Network Area and Company Summary display in
   RTNET. Compare with the losses in the VVD solution on the Network
   Area and Company Summary display in VVD.
   Results: If VVD had sufficient controls to reduce losses, then total
   system losses should be reduced in the VVD solution as compared
   with the RTNET solution. Normally, loss reduction occurs primarily in
   the operating areas where the active controls are located.

                          Lab 1: OPF Problem Summary

Objective
     Upon completion of these labs, you will be able to define and activate:
        • Controls
        • Control    Groups
     This lab contains a short summary on how to define the elements of the
     OPF problem. It introduces the multi-purpose mapping facility which is
     used in the problem definition. It also drives you to the main displays used
     to define the OPF problem elements.
     This lab is followed by a second lab to familiarize the student with how to
     create or modify the OPF problem definition.
     For these labs, you will use a specific savecase of the OPF application
     titled TRAIN_OPF_PROBLEM_DEFINITION.


Task: Retrieve the OPF savecase titled
TRAIN_OPF_PROBLEM_DEFINITION


1.1 OPF Problem Definition Logic
     Defining the OPF problem means defining:
        • an   objective function
        •   controls that can be adjusted to reach the objective
        •   constraints to be observed by the solution
     OPF provides a lot of flexibility in defining these elements of the OPF
     problem. Flexibility involves some complexity. The following is a
     summary of the logic and displays provided in EMP’s OPF to define these
     3 elements and their links. Two main displays are used :
        •   Optimization Constraint Definition
        •   Define Controls
     These two displays each have several views which allow you to perform
     specific tasks related to the optimization problem definition.
                         Proprietary – See Copyright Page                      3-16
                             OPF Advanced Features


<!-- salto de página -->

                              Network Optimization


1.1.1 Controls

1.1.1.1 Control Availability
     You define available controls by selecting them from the Insert Controls
     analyst display (available from the Analyst menu). This display shows, by
     station, a list of all devices in the network model (NETMOM database) that
     are potential OPF controls. You make a control available to OPF by
     clicking on the [+/-] button on the left of each control, which causes a
     control record to be inserted into the OPF control database (CTLMOM) for
     that device. (If you select the same device multiple times, the logic is
     smart enough to avoid duplicate controls.)
     You see the result of that selection in three views of the Define Controls
     display (which show data in the CTLMOM database):
        •   Controls are listed by station in the View Controls tab
        •   Controls are also listed by station in the Assign Controls tab, but
            with their group and cost curve assignments
        •   Controls assigned to one or more control groups are listed under
            their assigned group(s) on the Assign Groups tab

1.1.1.2 Control assignment to Control Group(s)
     Controls can be assigned to Control Groups. Control Groups belong
     hierarchically to Control Group Types. See the summary figure in section
     1.2.
     You define Control Group Types and Control Groups by inserting them
     [+/-] in the Define Groups view of the Define Controls display.
     You assign controls to control groups using the multi-purpose mapping
     facility (introduced later).
     Note: Any control can be assigned to multiple control groups.

1.1.2 Cost Curves

1.1.2.1 Defining Cost Curves in Cost Curve Groups
     Cost curves are defined independently so as to allow several controls to
     use the same cost curve, if needed. However, only control variables can
     be assigned to have a cost curve, not the state variables.
     Cost curves belong hierarchically to cost curve groups. See again the
     summary figure in section 1.2.
     You create cost curve groups by inserting them [+/-] in the Cost view of
     the Define Controls display.


                         Proprietary – See Copyright Page                     3-17
                             OPF Advanced Features


<!-- salto de página -->

                              Network Optimization


     You create cost curves by inserting them [+/-] under the desired cost
     curve group.
     You create incremental cost curve points (x, slope(x)) by inserting them
     [+/-] under the desired cost curve in the same Cost view of the of the
     Define Controls display.
     It should be mentioned that the use of cost curves is being de-emphasized
     in the latest version of OPF. The selection of minimum control changes to
     correct violations, previously handled using cost curves, is now done using
     the latest Control Selection logic. If is very easy to use cost curves to
     define problems that are difficult or impossible to solve, so cost curves
     should be used only when necessary to accurately model the problem
     definition.

1.1.2.2 Assigning Cost Curves to Controls
     You associate cost curves and controls by using the multi-purpose
     mapping facility.
     Note 1 : Several cost curves can be assigned to a control.
     Note 2 : A multiplier (SCALE) can be specified for each curve when
     assigning it to a control
     Note 3 : If a control has more than one cost curve assigned to it, the cost
     of moving that control will be defined by the composite sum of all assigned
     cost curves.

1.1.3 Objective Functions
     You create objective functions by inserting them [+/-] in the Objective
     view of the Define Controls display.
     You define a particular objective function by assigning to it a curve group
     using the multi-purpose mapping facility.
     Note 1: Several cost curve groups can be assigned to an objective
     function.
     Note 2: The resulting objective function will be the sum of all the costs
     derived from all the cost curves contained in the curve group(s).


                         Proprietary – See Copyright Page                        3-18
                             OPF Advanced Features


<!-- salto de página -->

                            Network Optimization

       Elements

1.3 OPF: Mapping Problem Definition Elements
   Mapping associates one of the elements of the problem definition (control,
   cost curve, objective) to one of the others.
   There are 3 possible bi-directional associations between mapping
   partners:
      •   Objective Function           ÅÆ             Cost Curve Group
      • Control                        ÅÆ             Control Group
      • Control                        ÅÆ             Cost Curve
   In the displays that show these mappable entities, a specific mapping
   button is provided. Clicking on that button initiates a mapping operation
   and shows --- in the mapping line on top of the display --- the possible
   partner(s) of that mapping operation. Direct navigation to the display(s)
                       Proprietary – See Copyright Page                    3-19
                           OPF Advanced Features


<!-- salto de página -->

                          Network Optimization


listing the possible partners is provided. After finding the desired partner,
the user can click on the partner’s mapping button to create the
association.
Note 1 : When referring to a control, the control parent (station) is shown
as a reminder and for unique identification (controls in different stations
can have the same name). The control type is also shown for
convenience.
Note 2 : When referring to a curve, the owning curve group is also shown
as a reminder and for unique identification.

        control group name should appear in the mapping window, and a blue
        navigation text to the Controls. Click on Controls to go to the list of
        controls.
     3. On the Assign Controls view, locate the DOUGLAS station, and
        select the Map CTL button for each of the two MW controls in turn.
        A [+/-] button with the assigned control group will be inserted under
        each control in the Control Assignment Definition view.
     4. Also, the 2 controls should appear under the control group on the
        Assign Groups view of the Define Controls display.
     5. If not done by default, enable the two controls.
     6. Validate your definitions.
     Similarly, define a new control group type QG_DOUGLAS, and a new
     control group DOUG_MR; then, map the 2 MVAr controls at DOUGLAS to
     this new control group. Validate again.


Task 3: Define New Cost Curves for the New Controls
     Reminder : Cost curves belong to cost curve groups.
     1. Call up the Costs view of the Define Controls display.
     2. INSERT a curve group by selecting a [+/-] button and choosing the
        Insert Curve Group option. The new curve group you just inserted is


                          Proprietary – See Copyright Page                  3-22
                              OPF Advanced Features


<!-- salto de página -->

                               Network Optimization


        presented for entry of its parameters. Give it the name DOUG_PG.
        Toggle the curve group type to “Absolute”.
     3. At the curve group, select the [+/-] button to insert a curve record.
        Give the curve the name DOUGLAS_MW_GENERATION.
     4. At the curve, select the [+/-] button to insert three curve points. Use the
        TAB to access quickly each entry field successively, and enter X
        values of 0, 200, and 600 MW, with slope values of 8, 12, and 16
        respectively.
     5. Click on the Map Curve button corresponding to the curve you just
        entered in order to initiate its mapping to the 2 MW controls at
        DOUGLAS.
     6. Use the automatic navigation to Controls, and select the      Map CTL
        button for each of the 2 MW controls. This tells OPF that each of these
        controls will use the cost curve you inserted. Notice the insertions
        caused by your actions.
     7. Validate your definitions.
     8. Call up the Costs view.
     9. Check the display. All the controls you linked to the curve should be
        listed under it. Ignore the Reference value which is only used for
        relative cost curves.
     The slopes that you have just defined are incremental costs ( =
     derivatives of the hourly cost curve). They will be interpolated linearly
     between the specified values. Thus, the cost curve obtained by
     integrating these slopes starting from Y_Base as y-intercept (no-load
     cost)--- will be a piecewise quadratic cost function.


Task 4: Define a New Objective Function
     Reminder : Objective functions are made up of control cost curve groups.
     1. Call up the Objective view of the Define Controls display, and select a
        [+/-] button. On the pop-up, select to Insert OBJF to insert a new
        objective function. Give it the name DOUGCOST.
     2. Click on the Map Function button next to the new objective function.
        This will prepare navigation to the curve groups in the COSTS view of
        the Define Controls display.
     3. Locate your cost curve group (DOUG_PG),
        click on the Map Object Function button next to the curve group so
        as to establish the link with the new objective function.
     4. Verify in the Objective view that the selected curve group is now
        associated with the new objective function.
                         Proprietary – See Copyright Page                        3-23
                             OPF Advanced Features


<!-- salto de página -->

                            Network Optimization


   5. If applicable, repeat this mapping operation with the reactive
      generation cost curve group
   6. Notice the 2 curve groups associated with the new objective function.
   7. Click on the Active button to activate the new objective function.
   8. Go back to the appropriate views of the Define Controls display, to
      ensure that the MW and MVAr generation controls at DOUGLAS will
      be active.
   9. Validate your problem definition.
   10. Run OPF
   11. If OPF converged, check the cost values in the Result popup
      Initial cost : ………………………
      Final cost: ………………………
      Cost change : ………………………
      Also note the losses : …………………….. MW
   Look at the OPF Control Summary display to see the recommended
   controls.
   Notice also that the solution may not be feasible because it is not possible
   to eliminate the violations with just the allowed controls.
   Stop the OPF process


Summary
   In this lab, you learned how to define and activate OPF Controls, Cost
   Curves, and Objective Functions.

                           OPF Advanced Features
