9. e-terratransmission Modeling Tasks
               This chapter provides information about the specifications that determine
               the operating limits of core transmission equipment and determine the
               operating parameters of a company’s transmission network security
               analysis system.

9.1 Building Operating Schedules for Network Entities
               Schedules allow other static elements of the network topology to change
               with time. Network entities such as loads, generating units, transformers,
               circuit breakers, and capacitor banks are constructed to change their
               operating characteristics over time.
               Network applications, including RTNET, PWRFLOW, Contingency
               Analysis, Optimal Powerflow, and Security Enhancement, use schedules
               to drive the model in order to evaluate and analyze the security and
               efficiency of the power grid.
               Records that make up the Network Schedules data structure:
               •   SKEDTY (Schedule Type) records distinguish between types of
                   schedules: load area forecast schedules (LDAREA), forecast breaker
                   schedules (CBFCST), and regulation schedules (REGSK).
               •   TYMSET (Timeset Definition) records represent the time models that
                   are built underneath them. Each record has a name, as well as a field
                   specifying the type of model represented: either a weekly cycle
                   CYCLE) or a linear time trend (TREND).
                   CYCLE TYMSET schedules repeat each week; that is,
                   CYCLETYMSET time models contain a set of time points (times when
                   component values change) that repeat week after week, except for
                   defined abnormal dates (ABDATEs) that interrupt the weekly cycle.
                   TREND TYMSET schedules are linear time models made up of trend
                   points (TRND records), which are selected dates arranged in calendar
                   order. This type of TYMSET is used in the modeling of linear functions
                   over long time periods.
               •   WKSEG (Week Segment) records are children of CYCLE TYMSETs.
                   They break the week up into groups of consistent daily schedules.
                   WKSEGs are used to specify when a new daily schedule becomes
                   effective. You add another WKSEG to a TYMSET only when the times
                   at which you want the component’s value to change are different from
                   those of the previous day.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page            199             e-terratransmission Modeling Tasks
                                                                  EMS Schema Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

                                   Figure 75: WKSEG Definition
                   Each WKSEG record contains the day of the week, the time of day the
                   WKSEG becomes effective, and the name of the DAYSEG that is used
                   in the WKSEG.
                   WKSEGs must be in chronological order, from the earliest day and
                   time to the latest. The convention is that the week begins on Sunday at
                   00:00. The first WKSEG record under a TYMSET may refer to a later
                   day and time, such as Monday at 00:00, but if a Sunday WKSEG
                   record is defined later in the sequence, it is ignored. Validation warns
                   you of non-chronological entries.
               •   DAYSEG (Day Segment) records define a “day’s schedule”. Each
                   record contains a name for the DAYSEG (which must be unique within
                   the TYMSET) and a set of sequential time points (TYMPTs) specifying
                   when the values (defined on CBFORSK, LDFORSK, REGSK, or
                   LDVARSK) are scheduled to change.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page              200           e-terratransmission Modeling Tasks
                                                                  EMS Schema Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

                               Figure 76: DAYSEG Definition
                   A “day’s schedule” refers to a time period from 00:00 hours to
                   23:59 hours. It is a fixed day, unrelated to when a WKSEG becomes
                   effective.
                   The daily schedule defined by the DAYSEG repeats each day until the
                   WKSEG that called it is superseded by a new WKSEG.
                   DAYSEG records belong to TYMSET records rather than to WKSEG
                   records. This is important when defining abnormal dates, because it
                   enables a TYMSET to contain DAYSEGs that are not called by a
                   WKSEG. Only the TYMSETs that contain the name of the DAYSEG
                   called by an ABDATE are affected by the ABDATE. This flexibility lets
                   you control which TYMSETs are affected by the ABDATE. For
                   example, if the ABDATE FOURTHOFJULY called a DAYSEG named
                   “JULY4”, then only those TYMSETs with a DAYSEG called “JULY4”
                   would be affected by the ABDATE.
                   The requirement that DAYSEG names need only be unique within a
                   particular TYMSET lets you set up a standard naming convention for
                   the DAYSEGs. For example, you might have a DAYSEG named
                   “FRIDAY” because it begins on Friday in each of 10 different
                   TYMSETs. Each “FRIDAY” DAYSEG could have a different set of

Proprietary – See Copyright Page            201            e-terratransmission Modeling Tasks
                                                                 EMS Schema Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

                   TYMPTs. Similarly, in the example of the DAYSEG called by the
                   ABDATE, the TYMPTs for each of the DAYSEGs called “JULY4” could
                   be different. The point here is that the data structure encourages you
                   to use a consistent DAYSEG naming convention that makes it easier
                   to design and track your schedules.
               •   TYMPT (Time Point) records are the time points, which specify the
                   times when the component’s value changes. The acceptable values for
                   TYMPTs lie between 00:00 and 23:59. They are children of DAYSEGs,
                   and they must be entered in chronological order, from the earliest time
                   to the latest. The first TYMPT in a DAYSEG that violates chronological
                   sequence is ignored, along with all the other TYMPTs that follow it.
                   Validation warns you of non-chronological entries.
               •   TRND (Trend) records represent calendar dates. They are children of
                   TREND TYMSETs, and they must be entered in chronological order.
                   As with TYMPTs, the first TRND record that violates chronological
                   order is ignored, along with all the TRND records that follow it.
               •   ABDATE\* records specify “abnormal” dates or holidays that have
                   abnormal patterns. They are used to “override” a day, or a portion of a
                   day, in a CYCLE TYMSET.
                   Each ABDATE record contains an identifier or name, the abnormal
                   date, the time span (TSTART and TSTOP) that is overwritten on that
                   date, and the name of the DAYSEG to be used on that date in place of
                   the one normally used. ABDATE records also have an
                   UPDATE/NOUPDATE flag, which is used to indicate whether or not
                   the model should be updated with real-time data during the abnormal
                   period specified.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page            202             e-terratransmission Modeling Tasks
                                                                  EMS Schema Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

                       Figure 77: Load-Based Regulation Schedule
9.2 Defining and Building a Station Group Load Schedule
               Load area schedules are a set of time-varying distribution factors used to
               break down values of total system load into individual substation (busbar)
               loads.
               The modeler can define two kinds of schedules: constant schedules and
               time-dependent schedules. Constant schedules assume that the
               LDAREA’s load shape conforms to the load shape of its parent LDAREA.
               However, time-dependent schedules allow the modeler to represent
               “non-conforming” loads. Time-dependent schedules follow the load shape
               of the LDAREA, and do not conform to the load shape of the parent
               LDAREA.
               These are the options:
               •   If a constant schedule applies, a LDAREA is modeled as a constant
                   fraction, in proportion to its parent LDAREA’s MW load.
               •   If a time-dependent schedule is required, the LDAREA’s MW load is
                   modeled as a time-dependent fraction of its parent LDAREA’s MW
                   load.

Proprietary – See Copyright Page           203             e-terratransmission Modeling Tasks
                                                                 EMS Schema Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

               To build a constant load area schedule, complete these steps:
               1. Select the Schedules option on the View menu.
                   The Auxiliary Tables view appears.
               2. Open the Schedules folder to reveal the LOAD_AREA_SCHEDULES
                  item.
               3. Open the LOAD_AREA_SCHEDULES branch and open the Timeset
                  Definitions folder.
               4. Position the cursor on the Timeset Definitions folder icon and click the
                  right mouse button.
               5. Select the Add TYMSET option in the pop-up menu.
                   The Timeset Definition form appears in the right pane.
               6. Name the timeset, specify the Cycle assignment, and save the record.
               7. Select the Day Segment tab and add a DAYSEG record in the Day
                  Segment table.
               8. Name the record and save the entry.
                   ModelerUI will prompt users if they start other entry work before saving
                   the previous entry.
               9. Add TYMPT records in the Time Break Points table.
               10. Select the Week Segments tab and insert the WKSEG record.
               11. Position the cursor on the Schedules folder icon and click the right
                   mouse button.
               12. Select the Add SKED option in the pop-up menu.
                   The Network Schedules form appears in the right pane.
               13. Name this new schedule, and specify which timeset the schedule will
                   follow.
               14. Click the Build Schedules button. When the Validation window
                   appears, click the Start button in the Validation window menu bar.
               15. When the Forecast Scheduling process completes, review the results
                   for errors that indicate the schedule you created might be faulty, then
                   dismiss the Validation window.
                   The Forecast Scheduling process provides one schedule value
                   (VALUE) record with each forecast schedule created.
                   Note: The screen refresh to display this item may take a few moments.

Proprietary – See Copyright Page            204              e-terratransmission Modeling Tasks
                                                                   EMS Schema Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

               16. Save your work.

9.3 DC Circuits
               A DC circuit is an interconnected collection of DC nodes, DC lines, and
               DC converters. Multiple DC circuits within the entire network model are
               supported.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page           205             e-terratransmission Modeling Tasks
                                                                 EMS Schema Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

        Pac                                                      +
                     +       Idc                                 Vdc     +
                                                                 _

        Pac
                                                                  +
                     +       Idc                                 Vdc     +
                +                                                 _


                                        Pdc = Pac
                                        Pdc = Vdc + Idc


                                   Figure 79: DC Network
9.3.1.1 Definitions
               •    DC Controller: Refers to a strategy for distributing a single power
                    regulation setpoint to one or more poles, or to a device for
                    implementing the strategy.
               •    DC Pole: A user-defined collection of one or more interconnected
                    converters. A pole exists between two nodes, and it is connected to
                    DC lines and other poles only at those two nodes.
               •    DC Converter: An AC-DC conversion device, consisting of one or
                    more bridges that are connected to the AC network by a single
                    modeled transformer.
9.3.1.2 DC Topology
               DC ground returns must be modeled explicitly using the DC line model.
               DC line records representing ground return are flagged as such.
               Circuit breakers and switches in the DC network are not supported,
               although DC Poles, DC Converters, and DC lines can be individually
               removed from service. Poles and converters removed from service can be
               either blocked (open-circuit) or bypassed (short-circuit).


Proprietary – See Copyright Page             206             e-terratransmission Modeling Tasks
                                                                   EMS Schema Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

9.3.1.3 DC Controllers
               DC controllers deal in power setpoints only. They get their power setpoints
               either from manual entry, from the definition of a contingency being
               analyzed, or from an assigned power schedule.
9.3.1.4 DC Poles
               A DC pole has two connections in the DC network: a single neutral
               connection, and a single “top” or “bottom” connection to one or more DC
               lines. Between its neutral connection and its DC line connection, a DC
               pole is modeled as a collection of DC converters in parallel, in series, or in
               both configurations. Within a pole, all series and parallel converter
               topological configurations are supported, including combinations of series
               and parallel converters. Topology changes can be made online by
               changing component node assignments.
               Unbalanced operation of bipoles is supported. There are no distinctions
               made in the model between “top” and “bottom” poles in a bipole, nor are
               there any restrictions against monopolar operation.
               Each pole regulates current, voltage, power, or firing/extinction angle,
               depending on its regulation mode. Poles regulate to their individual
               setpoint, which may be derived from a pole measurement (State Estimator
               only), from a schedule, or from its share of the DC controller’s setpoint. In
               the network model, each pole that is regulating power or current is
               assigned to one, and only one, DC controller.
               All poles in constant power mode must get their power setpoint from pole
               power measurement (state estimator only), from their assigned DC
               controller, from their assigned MW schedule, or (optionally) from a
               user-entered override setpoint on the pole. If from a DC controller, the
               pole will be assigned a portion of the DC controller’s power setpoint,
               based on the pole’s participation factor.
               Within the DC network solution software, all actual regulation is done at
               the pole level. Individual converters within a pole do not need to be
               assigned their own regulation setpoints or regulation modes, either by the
               user or internally by the software. At the solution, each converter’s solved
               voltage and current values are derived from its pole’s solved voltage and
               current values, distributed to converters based on converter topology
               within the pole.
9.3.1.5 Rules for the Selection of Pole Regulation Modes
               To avoid unsolvable or unrealistic problems, the following rules must be
               followed regarding the selection of regulation modes for DC poles:


Proprietary – See Copyright Page             207             e-terratransmission Modeling Tasks
                                                                   EMS Schema Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

               •   In every DC circuit, there must be at least one pole that is regulating
                   voltage or angle. However, multiple poles regulating voltage or angle
                   cannot be connected in parallel (that is, to the same nodes).
               •   Each pole that is regulating current or power must be a part of at least
                   one loop in the DC circuit containing no other poles in that mode (a
                   loop can include ground return).
               •   In any pole that is regulating angle, and whose taps are discretely
                   regulating voltage, all converter transformers in the pole must use the
                   same tap model. That is, they must have the same nominal tap setting,
                   the same tap step size, etc., since taps in this pole will move together.
                   This requirement applies only to poles regulating both angle and
                   voltage.
9.3.1.6 DC Converters
               DC converters are modeled as station components. Each converter
               consists of one or more bridges. The number of bridges in a converter can
               be changed online and will impact the nominal voltage of the converter.
               Converter nominal voltage per bridge is entered during the modeling
               phase.
               Converters cannot control independently. The concept of regulation
               modes for individual converters does not apply. Regulation modes are
               applied to poles during the solution process, and solved pole voltage and
               current levels are distributed to converters within the pole.
               No distinctions are made in the modeling or the software between
               inverters and rectifiers, except when determining angle limits. Different
               limits are supported for firing angle and extinction angle.
               The DC converter transformer model supports both two-winding
               transformers and a three-winding transformer model, with a synchronous
               condenser at the tertiary. For each converter, a single two- or
               three-winding transformer will connect it to the AC network.
               Three-winding converter transformers are modeled as three two-winding
               transformers in a Y configuration, with only the primary tap being movable.
               This configuration also supports a synchronous condenser connected to
               the tertiary.
               Movable taps on converter transformers cannot be used to regulate any
               AC bus voltages, but they can be used to regulate DC voltage, current, or
               MW by controlling the AC voltage input to the converter.
               Violations of DC converter current ratings will cause warning messages to
               be logged on the application message log. Only one set of converter
               current ratings is supported.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page             208             e-terratransmission Modeling Tasks
                                                                   EMS Schema Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

9.3.1.7 Distributing Solution Values from Pole to Converter
               Although converters are individually modeled in the network model, they
               are not represented individually in the internal DC network solution, where
               only poles and DC lines are represented. A solution is obtained for the DC
               network by considering only the DC lines and poles, with the poles
               modeled as pure sources (of current, voltage, etc.). Once the pole voltage
               and current values are solved for, they will be distributed to the converters
               in the pole using the following rules:
               •   Voltage: A pole voltage will be split among the series configuration
                   converters in proportion to the converter’s nominal voltages. A
                   bypassed converter, and any converters in parallel with a bypassed
                   converter, will always be assigned zero voltage.
               •   Current: A pole current will be split among parallel configuration
                   converters in proportion to the converter’s current ratings.
9.3.1.8 Defining DC Converters
               To model DC converters for a substation, complete the following steps:
               1. Click the Equipment toolbar button.

                   a. Navigate to the Equipment Groups folder for the appropriate

                   b. Model voltage level information.

                   b. Expand the DC Converters folder to expose its contents.
                       i. To add a new DC converter record, place the cursor on the DC
                          Converters folder, click the right mouse button, and select the
                          Add DCConverter option.
                       ii. To update an existing DC converter record, select its icon.
                   c. Model DC converter information in the DC Converter form.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page             209             e-terratransmission Modeling Tasks
                                                                   EMS Schema Modeling Guide

                   d. Model topology as described in Configuring Nodes and Connecting
                      Terminals.


                             Figure 80: DC Converter Definition
9.3.1.9 DC Lines
               A DC line is used to transfer DC power from one location to another
               location, just like the AC line does. A DC line must be specified by its
               “from” and “to” DC nodes, and their characteristic resistance. The name of
               the DC node is 8 characters long, and it must be unique across DC nodes.
               The resistance of a DC line is specified in ohms, while the resistance of
               every other network element (including converter transformers) is
               specified in percent on a 100-MVA base.
               DC lines cannot be tie-lines and they cannot cross area boundaries. You
               can model all DC lines within one area, and create pseudo-substations
               that contain the DC converters. These pseudo-substations can then be
               connected to the real stations across area boundaries with zero
               impedance branch (ZBR) tie-lines.
9.3.1.10 Defining DC Lines
               To model DC lines for a substation, complete the following steps:
               1. Click the Line toolbar button.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page            210            e-terratransmission Modeling Tasks
                                                                 EMS Schema Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

               2. Navigate to the appropriate substation in the Transmission Lines
                  folder, and expand it.
               3. Expand the HVDC Transmission Lines folder to expose its contents.
                   a. To add a new DC line record, place the cursor on the HVDC
                      Transmission Lines folder, click the right mouse button, and select
                      the Add DC Line option.
                   b. To update an existing DC line record, select its icon.
               4. Model DC line information in the HVDC Transmission Line form.
9.3.1.11 Defining Other DC Components
               DC Controllers, Control Blocks, Control Functions, and DC Poles are
               modeled using the DC Components tree of the Related Tables view.
               To model a DC Controller, open the DC Components tree to reveal the DC
               Controllers folder and complete these steps:
               1. Place the cursor on the DC Controller folder, click the right mouse
                  button, and select the Add DCTL option.
               2. Model the controller ramp rate and MW schedule (if any) using the DC
                  Controller form.
               To model a DC Control Block, open the DC Components tree to reveal the
               DC Control Blocks folder and complete these steps:
               1. Place the cursor on the DC Control Blocks folder, click the right mouse
                  button, and select the Add DCTLBL option.

               To model a DC Control Function, open the DC Components tree to reveal

9.5 Installation Information
               To define network subsystem installation information, specify integration
               and configuration details using the fields provided on the Installation
               Information tab as follows:
               •   Functions Installed
                   − SCADA Map? When selected, this check box specifies that
                     SCADA node mapping is enabled.
                   − Generation Map? When selected, this check box specifies that
                     Generation mapping is enabled.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page            212             e-terratransmission Modeling Tasks
                                                                  EMS Schema Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

                   − Short Circuit? When selected, this check box specifies that the
                     Short Circuit application is enabled.
                   − Contingency Analysis? When selected, this check box specifies
                     that the Contingency Analysis application is enabled.
                   − State Estimator? When selected, this check box specifies that the
                     State Estimator is enabled.
                   − Powerflow? When selected, this check box specifies that the
                     powerflow application is enabled.
                   − Security Constrained Dispatch? When selected, this check box

                   − Map Board: When selected, this check box enables mapboard

                       ∗    Note: This feature is not currently supported in e-terraplatform.
                   − Optimum Powerflow: When selected, this check box enables the
                     Optimal Powerflow application.
                   − Operator Guides: When selected, this check box enables the
                     Operator Guides function.
               •   General Options
                   − Enter Voltage Regulation in kV: When selected, this check box
                     specifies that the option for voltage regulation input data is in
                     Kilovolts.
                   − Exclude Auxiliary Loads in Load Summary Calculations: When
                     selected, this check box specifies that auxiliary loads will not be
                     included in the sum total of company and division load calculations.
                   − Enter Line Limit in Amps: A check mark indicates that entries on
                     the Line Limit form will be accepted as Amps, not MVA.
                   − Branch End Naming Option: The branch end naming convention.
                     Valid entries are:
                        1       Means ID_LN2 = ID_LINE
                        2       Means ID_LN2 = ID_LINE//_//ID_LN
                        3       Means ID_LN2 = concatenation of From and To
                                station names
                        4       Concatenates LINE_ID and LN_ID with no “ ” for
                                ID_LN2
                        5       Uses a custom naming convention

                   − Suppress Equipment with Voltage Below this Level: The
                     voltage level used to suppress unwanted output on the BUSES

                     below this voltage level will not be displayed.
                   − Enter Transformer Limit in Amps: A check mark indicates that

9.8 Debug Parameters
               System administrators and integrators set mapping and initialization
               parameters for the Network model using the fields provided on the Debug
               Parameters tab as follows:
               •   Mapping Parameters
                   − Number of Station Characters: The number of characters in the
                     substation ID that will be used for mapping.
                   − Map Temperature Rating Info from SCADA: When selected, this
                     check box specifies that the temperature-dependent rating
                     information is from SCADA.
                   − Map System Voltage Reduction Info from SCADA: When
                     selected, this check box specifies that the system voltage reduction
                     information is from SCADA.
               •   Transaction Direction
                   − Sale: Sales transactions can be designated “D” for Deliver, “S” for
                     Sale, or “-”.
                   − Purchase: Purchase transactions can be designated “R” for
                     Receive, “P” for Purchase, or “+”.

9.9 PSSE, IEEE, and CIM/XML Data Sets
               PSSE Power Flow Data format and IEEE Common Data format are two of
               the most widely used industry-standard data formats. e-terramodeler

Proprietary – See Copyright Page            216             e-terratransmission Modeling Tasks
                                                                  EMS Schema Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

               provides a utility called “PSAImport” that imports these data into the
               PowerModel database and HABITAT modeling clones. This utility
               interfaces with the Batch Loader tool that creates and implements the
               import transactions using the ADE Controls API.
               The PSSE and IEEE data formats evolved over time as the standard for
               the exchange of power flow data among power system utilities and
               vendors.
               An industry-leading implementation of the Common Information Model
               (CIM) is delivered with each release of the e-terramodeler modeling
               system. The CIM XML Import/Export is used both for creating the export
               XML files and for importing CIM XML files into e-terramodeler.

                                                                 EMS Schema Modeling Guide

10. Network Data Import
               This chapter provides details about PSSE and IEEE data block
               architecture, and the data propagation paths that move the PSSE and
               IEEE data from the e-terramodeler PowerModel database into the
               subsystem HABITAT databases.

10.1 PSSE-26™ Data Blocks
               The PSSE-26 data structure consists of 16 sections of records, with each
               section containing a particular type of data required in power flow work. A
               comma or a blank separates the data items. Each section of data, except
               the case identification data, is terminated by a record value of zero.
               The 16 data blocks must maintain this order:
               • Generators
               • Branches
               • Transformer Adjustment
               • Area Interchange
               • Two-Terminal DC Lines
               • Switched Shunt
               • Transformer Impedance Correction Tables
               • Multi-Terminal DC Lines
               • Multi-Sectional Line Groupings
               • Zone
               • Inter-Area Transfer
               • Owner
               • FACTS Control Device
               Each section of record data begins with a section header.
               The mapping tables below indicate the intermediate mappings that are
               required to translate the Bus model of the PSSE to the PowerModel
               database.

10.2 IEEE Data Blocks
               The IEEE data structure consists of six sections. Each section is
               terminated by a record of value zero.
               The six data blocks must maintain this order:
               • Title
               • Busses
               • Branches
               • Loss Zone
               • Interchange

Proprietary – See Copyright Page            218                         Network Data Import
                                                                 EMS Schema Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

               •   Tie-Lines
               Each section of record data begins with a section header.

10.5 CIM XML Import
               By representing the common features and attributes of a power grid in
               XML format, modeling engineers can exchange system operations data
               with other CIM-compliant sites.
               The CIM is a vendor-neutral information model for representing data
               maintained in an EMS. The CIM defines the meaning or semantics of
               data, not the data’s physical representation.
               The NERC CIM XML format defines a text file representation of data in a
               CIM-inspired schema, based on XML and the Resource Description
               Framework (RDF).
               The import process is a two-step procedure and is managed through a
               Perl script, “ADECimImport.pl”. The import script (ADECimImport.pl)
               initially calls a converter program (ADECimXml.exe) that translates the
               CIM/XML data into a format compatible with the e-terramodeler Batch
               Loader. The import script then runs the Batch Loader to import the data
               into the e-terrahabitat databases via the e-terramodeler PowerModel
               database (see Table 3 below for the propagation pattern that the batch
               loading software uses when importing and distributing data to the
               e-terraplatform subsystem HABITAT databases).
               The export process is managed via the ADEUtility.exe command-line
               application, which queries the CIM server and generates a translation of
               the model in CIM/XML format.
               All of the configuration files used by CIM XML Import/Export are located in
               the Model Server/bin directory of the ADE binary distribution. The Model
               Server/bin directory will be referred to as “%ADE_ROOTDIR%” throughout
               this description.
               During the execution of the CIM Import process, two log files are
               generated that detail the progress: errors and warnings. The first of these
               files is generated by the converter program, and it will be referenced as
               “%CONV_LOG%”. The second log file is generated by the Batch Loader
               program, and it will be designated as “%BL_LOG%”. When the converter
               program is run, it creates several CSV files in addition to the log file. The
               path of this directory can be specified and will be designated as
               “%CSVDIR%”.
               All of these environment variables can be designated for creation at
               system startup, or specified interactively during run time.
               To run the CIM Import from the command line into the “%IMPORTURL%”
               context, issue the following command:


Proprietary – See Copyright Page             234                         Network Data Import
                                                                  EMS Schema Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

                           perl ADECimImport.pl -x %CIMURL% -f %CIMXML -n %CIMNS% -c
                           %IMPORTURL% -o %CSVDIR%

11. e-terrageneration Modeling Tasks
               This chapter provides information about the modeling tasks that specify
               the operating parameters of the e-terrageneration subsystem functions
               such as Automatic Generation Control (AGC), Operating Area Frequency
               control, and NERC reporting, and that delimit the operating ranges and
               modes of the plant equipment.

11.1 Modeling an Automatic Generation Control (AGC) Area
               An “operating area” is defined in the EMS as an Automatic Generation
               Control (AGC) area. Operating areas are at the top of a hierarchical tree
               that is usually associated with the central business unit, the utility.
               At least one operating area must be designated as the EMS operating
               area. All other operating areas must be designated as non-EMS (external)
               areas.
               Note: Consider AGC area ordering carefully. While random order is
               allowed, it is more desirable to insert internal operating areas ahead of
               external operating areas in the e-terrageneration subsystem schema.
               Once the operating area order has been built, it cannot be changed
               without losing the structures built under each area definition.
               Whenever you define an operating area, you need to define at least one
               generating unit, so that power exchanges can be represented and
               calculated properly by the e-terrageneration and e-terratransmission
               applications, which account for power transactions by adjusting unit
               output. In addition, you must define an area frequency measurement for
               the EMS operating area.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page            237               e-terrageneration Modeling Tasks
                                                                  EMS Schema Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

                        Figure 82: Operating Area Definition Form
11.1.1 ACE Deadband and Control Regions
               Figure 83 shows how the Area Control Error (ACE) deadband and the
               various AGC control regions are defined. The deadband and control
               regions (regulation region indicator, RRI) are a function of the relative
               values of ACE and the integral of ACE. In addition, the ACE deadband is
               dynamic, being a function of time.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page           238              e-terrageneration Modeling Tasks
                                                                EMS Schema Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

                  Figure 83: ACE Deadband and AGC Control Regions
               The dynamic attribute of the ACE deadband is used to adjust the effective
               deadband for AGC controls. As soon as ACE comes within the static
               deadband range, the dynamic deadband is increased to its maximum
               value, known as the “ACE emergency assist limit”. As long as ACE stays
               within the static deadband range, the dynamic deadband equals the
               emergency assist level. If ACE comes out of the static deadband range
               and stays out, the dynamic deadband will gradually decay from the
               emergency assist level to the static deadband level. The rate of decay is a


Proprietary – See Copyright Page            239              e-terrageneration Modeling Tasks
                                                                 EMS Schema Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

               function of the analyst-entered dynamic deadband time constant, as
               Figure 84 illustrates:


                   Figure 84: ACE Deadbands and ACE Region Limits
               The dynamic ACE deadband is defined as follows:
                   DACEDB = ACEDB + (DT/DTMAX) * (ACEEMN – ACEDB)
               where:
               • DACEDB is the dynamic ACE deadband.
               • ACEDB is the static ACE deadband defined in the database.
               • DT is DTMAX minus the time (in seconds) for which ACE has
                 remained outside DACEDB (limited between zero and DTMAX).
               • DTMAX is the maximum time limit (in seconds) defined in the
                 database.
               • ACEEMN is the emergency-assist ACE level defined in the database.
               Also:
               If the magnitude of ACE < ACEDB
               then:
               Set DT = DTMAX, or DACEDB = ACEEMN

Proprietary – See Copyright Page          240              e-terrageneration Modeling Tasks
                                                               EMS Schema Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

               The integral of ACE is internally limited to a maximum value, whereas
               ACE itself is not.

11.1.2 Variable Frequency Bias Calculation
               Variable frequency bias (VFBIAS) predicts how much the MW output of an
               operating area will change for every 0.1 HZ of frequency variation that
               occurs in one AGC cycle. Valid values of VFBIAS reside between the
               variable frequency bias low limit (VFBMIN) and the high limit (VFBMAX).
               Variable frequency bias is calculated as follows:
                   VFBIAS = FBLOAD + FBGEN
               where:
               •   FBLOAD represents the Load Contribution and is calculated as
                   follows:
                   FBLOAD = LDBIAS /1000 * SLOAD
                   where LDBIAS represents the Area Load Bias, and SLOAD represents
                   the System Load.
               •   FBGEN represents the Generation Contribution and is calculated as
                   follows:
                   FBGEN = DBV * DSK * SGVRES
                   where DBV represents the Deadband Variable. DBV represents how
                   the unit governors respond to the frequency deviation exceeding a
                   threshold.
                   DBV values reside between the unit contribution minimum (DBVMIN)
                   and maximum (DBVMAX).
                   The term “DSK” represents the Droop Scalar constant. This constant
                   specifies how much of the generation frequency bias will be applied to
                   the area frequency bias.
                   DSK is used to globally adjust the droop characteristics of all
                   generators. DSK also models how the area’s unit governors will
                   respond to frequency deviations.
                   SGVRES represents the sum of all responses from generators that are
                   online and can respond in the direction of the frequency error without
                   violating the unit regulation limit.
               In the calculation of FBGEN, the value of DBV changes with transitions of
               the absolute Actual Frequency Deviation value (AFD) into the VFBIAS
               deadband region. The change in the DBV value is determined by the
               transition scalar, PINC. This scalar specifies the change in governor


Proprietary – See Copyright Page            241               e-terrageneration Modeling Tasks
                                                                  EMS Schema Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

               response as the frequency deviation continues to be greater than the
               threshold.
               PINC affects DBV values as follows:
               When absolute AFD exceeds the VFBIAS deadband minimum (VFBDB1),
               then:
                   DBV = min (DBVMIN, (DBV – PINC))
               When absolute AFD drops below the VFBIAS deadband maximum
               (VFBDB2), then:
                   DBV = max (DBVMAX, (DBV + PINC))

11.2 e-terrageneration Alarms
               Generation alarms can be issued by various tasks, as specified in the data
               structure set up by a programmer or engineer.
               When defining Generation alarms, the following three components must
               be considered:
               •   Alarm characteristic definition in GENMODEL
               •   Alarm specification in the ALARM database
               •   Alarm format picture definitions in RTGEN.ALMMSG
               The request to issue an alarm originates in RTGEN, using the data
               defined in GENMODEL. The Alarm application uses ALARM database
               data to process the application and display the corresponding message
               defined in RTGEN.ALMMSG.
               How a Generation alarm is set up depends on whether the alarm needs to
               be acknowledged individually, acknowledged as part of a group, or simply
               shown on the System Activity Log (SYSACT).
               •   Alarms that need to be acknowledged individually must be set up with
                   a one-to-one relationship between the GENMODEL definition and the
                   ALARM database definition.
               •   Alarms that need to be acknowledged as a group, but not individually,
                   must be set up using one of the following methods:
                   − Grouping alarm exceptions under an OBJDEF record in the ALARM
                     database defined for group acknowledgement. Normally, this is the
                     preferred approach.
                   − Assigning the same alarm exception ID (from the ALARM
                     database) to more than one Generation alarm.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page            242              e-terrageneration Modeling Tasks
                                                                 EMS Schema Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

               •   Operator entry logging alarms are simply logged in SYSACT.
               For detailed information about ALARM database definitions and
               procedures, see the Alarm Programmer’s Guide.

11.2.1 Modeling Generation Alarms
               To model generation alarms, complete the following steps:
               1. Select the e-terrageneration Alarms option from the View menu.
                   The Generation Alarms view displays.
               2. Expand the Alarm Definitions folder (in the Generation Alarms View
                  folder) to expose its contents.
               3. Place the cursor on the Alarm Definitions folder, click the right mouse
                  button, and select the Add ALMTSK option.
               4. Model generation alarms information in the fields provided.

11.4 Combined Cycle Unit Definition
               The Combined Cycle Unit definition describes the deployment of one or
               more combustion turbines with one generic steam turbine in a Combined
               Cycle group. This deployment is defined by specifying combined cycle
               turbine types in the Generating Unit definition, by specifying the Steam
               Turbine control scheme and by denoting which Plant Controller(s) the
               turbines are assigned to.

11.5 Defining a Combined Cycle Group
               The database builder defines Combined Cycle groups (combustion and
               steam turbine deployment) in the Power Equipment view of ModelerUI.
               To define a Combined Cycle Group, complete these steps:
               1. Open the Generating Unit folder of the substation (plant) where the
                  units reside.
               2. Specify which PLCs are deployed at the plant.
               3. Establish the Combined Cycle Group by inserting one Generating Unit
                  record for each unit in the group, and by assigning the combustion
                  turbine and steam turbine Plant Controllers.
               4. Specify which generating units are deployed as combustion turbines in
                  the group using the Turbine Type dropdown menu on the Types tab.
               5. Specify which unit is the steam turbine using the Turbine Type
                  dropdown menu on the Generating Unit Types tab.

Proprietary – See Copyright Page            244               e-terrageneration Modeling Tasks
                                                                  EMS Schema Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

               6. Save the Combined Cycle Group definition.
               Note: The Combined Cycle Unit model plays a significant role in the
               Dispatcher Training Simulation (DTS), and it is stored in the
               e-terrasimulator database’s CCYC record structure. This
               simulation-specific structure is built using the Combined Cycle Modeling
               view of ModelerUI, and it stores setpoint and MW output information for
               the combustion turbines. Refer to the chapter e-terrasimulator Modeling
               Tasks for details about the CCYC record structure.

11.6 Defining the Steam Turbine Incremental Heat Rate Curve
               The output of the steam turbine in a Combined Cycle group will be a
               function of the combined combustion turbine outputs. The steam turbine
               will follow its assigned incremental heat rate curve in order to meet its
               output requirement.
               Incremental heat rate curves (IHRCs) are constructed as a series of points
               that specify the incremental heat units per MWH required to maintain
               output at an MW level.
               •   Accuracy increases if numerous rate points (RATEPT) are modeled,
                   especially in portions of the curve where the slope changes rapidly.
               •   The amount of heat required to maintain synchronous generation must
                   be defined at the first point of the curve.
               •   The first rate point MW must be 0. Each rate point must have an MW
                   value.
               •   Incremental heat rates must increase for successive points between
                   the MW level of the economic dispatch minimum and the maximum
                   capacity.
               •   Set the boiler efficiency to 100 for each unit that is not economically
                   dispatchable.
                   A unit is “economically dispatchable” if an IHRC can be defined for it
                   and assigned to it, and if the generation type is specified as
                   economically dispatchable.
               To specify the incremental heat rate curve for the steam turbine in the
               Combined Cycle group, complete these steps:
               1. Find the group’s steam turbine in the Power Equipment view, and open
                  the Incremental Rate Curves tab.
               2. Specify the steam turbine MW output based upon the combined CT
                  output (see sample tables below).
               3. Save the Incremental Heat Rate Curve definition.

Proprietary – See Copyright Page             245               e-terrageneration Modeling Tasks
                                                                   EMS Schema Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

               The values in the translation tables below show how the steam turbine
               MW output will “follow” the combined combustion turbine MW output of the
               Combined Cycle Unit group. The MW Level entries specify the CT MW
               output. The Incremental Heat Rate entries specify the ST MW output
               corresponding to the combined CT MWs.


                           MW Level                 Incremental Heat Rate (MBTU)
                              0                                  0
                              30                                 0
                              40                                 40
                             100                                 40
               Note: In the table above, the ST maximum output is reached before the
               maximum combined output of the group’s CTs. This is a common
               condition.


                           MW Level                 Incremental Heat Rate (MBTU)
                              0                                  0
                             100                                 45
               Note: The PLC regulates steam turbine output by interpolating between
               the modeled ST MW output values when the combined MW output of the
               CTs resides between the modeled MW levels.

11.7 Defining the Steam Turbine Control Scheme
               Units in a combined cycle group may all be under the same PLC, or under
               individual PLCs. If each unit has its own PLC, two possibilities for control
               exist:
               •   Issue control to the CTs if they are in “simple-cycle mode” (not
                   contributing heat to the steam turbine), but redirect control to the ST if
                   any CT is in “combined-cycle mode”.
               •   Always issue control to the CTs to move them to their desired MW
                   level (“boiler-following mode”).
               To specify whether a steam turbine controls the Combined Cycle Unit
               group, complete these steps:
               1. Find the steam turbine in the Power Equipment view and open the
                  Types tab.
               2. Locate the Combine Cycle Unit information.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page             246                e-terrageneration Modeling Tasks
                                                                    EMS Schema Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

               3. Select the Steam Turbine option from the Turbine Type dropdown
                  menu.
                   Notice that radio buttons in the Group Control panel are now active.
               4. Click the button for the desired control scheme:
                   − Issued from ST PLC: Toggle this button ON to specify that control
                     for the group will come from the Plant Controller that issues
                     controls to the steam turbine.
                   − Issued from CT PLCs: Toggle this button ON to specify that
                     control for the group will come from the Plant Controller(s) that
                     issues controls to the combustion turbines.

11.8 Role of the Telemetered Status of the Heat Recovery
    Valve (HRV)
               Each CT in the Combined Cycle Unit group has a heat recovery valve that
               directs the flow-through heat of the gas turbine to the boiler of the steam
               turbine. In combined-cycle mode, where the CT contributes heat to the
               ST, the CT’s HRV is open (telemetered status = OPEN). In simple-cycle
               mode, the CT’s HRV is closed (telemetered status = CLOSED). Refer to
               the section Generation Telemetry Model in this chapter to determine how
               generation telemetry for CT HRV status is modeled.
               In brief, the principal steps for modeling HRV telemetry are as follows:
               1. Copy a Measurement Group record that contains a Status Input
                  definition for the Heat Recovery Valve (HRV) status to each of the
                  Combustion Turbine records.
               2. Specify the card and storage location (physical address) of the HRV
                  status value using the Substation Telemetry definition.
               3. Map the telemetry for the HRV status value from SCADA to
                  e-terrageneration using the Generation Telemetry table.
               Note: Having the Heat Recovery Valve status telemetered is not an AGC
               requirement. Frequently, the HRV status is changed manually by the
               operator on the AGC displays.

11.9 Connecting Area Tie Corridors and Tie-Lines
               The model builder defines the EMS tie corridor topology by inserting Tie
               Corridor (TIE) records on the Connecting Area Tie Corridors form. The
               model builder defines the transmission lines that carry the power in the
               corridor by inserting Tie-Line (TYLN) records on the same form. The
               TYLN records must replicate lines that exist in the AC Transmission Line
               tree.

Proprietary – See Copyright Page            247               e-terrageneration Modeling Tasks
                                                                  EMS Schema Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

               Tie-lines model the lines that physically connect AGC operating areas. A
               tie corridor represents a collection of tie-lines that are monitored together.


                                   Figure 86: TYLN Definition

11.9.1 OPA and AREA Record Synchronization
               Before invoking the generation network mapping facility, GENMAP,
               confirm that the AREA records in the utility’s Netmodel clone are ordered
               in the same sequence as the OPA records in the Genmodel clone.
               Synchronization of tie-line details in the real-time Generation and Network
               databases requires that these alignments match.
               The generation network mapping facility creates TLN records and inserts
               them in Netmodel under their assigned AREA record, based upon the tie
               corridor and tie-line designations it discovers in the Genmodel database.

11.9.2 Defining the Connecting Area Utilities
               Before any tie corridor relationships can be modeled, the model builder
               must define paired utility (UTIL) records under the energy exchanging
               operating areas.
               The connecting utility (UTIL) names must be unique within each operating
               area of the Connecting Area Tie Corridors tree. Once the Connecting
               Utility records are in place, the tie corridor can be modeled by inserting
               TIE records and defining the transmission lines that reside in the corridor.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page            249               e-terrageneration Modeling Tasks
                                                                  EMS Schema Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

11.9.3 Defining the Tie Corridors
                Tie corridors are modeled by defining two mirror-image TIE records: one
                as a child of the “Near” Connecting Utility parent and one as a child of the
                “Far” Connecting Utility parent. These TIE records represent opposite
                ends of the same tie corridor, one end in each of the participating
                operating areas.
                Note: TIE records that define the same corridor must have the same
                name.

               To model a tie-line on the Transmission Lines view, complete these steps:

                   as a SCADA DEVICE record.

                   the data point “add” structures. Specify AC Line End measurements
                   and controls.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page            251              e-terrageneration Modeling Tasks
                                                                 EMS Schema Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

               12. Validate the transmission line model by selecting the Expert User
                   mode provided in the Validation window and by selecting the
                   NETVALID option from the list of validation functions.
               13. Correct any errors, and save your work again.
                   Note: Modeled transmission lines are captured as AC Transmission
                   Line, AC Line Segment, and AC Line End records in the PowerModel
                   database, and are propagated to the Netmodel database as LINE, LN,
                   and LN2 records when the definition is saved.
               To model the same transmission line as a member of a tie corridor (TIE)
               definition, complete these steps:
               1. Select the Connecting Area Tie Corridors option on the View menu.
               2. Navigate to the connecting operating area of interest, and expand it.
               3. Model the connecting electric utilities as follows:
                   a. Identify the operating areas that are connected by tie corridors and
                      tie-lines.
                   b. Add a utility (UTIL) record under these operating areas, one UTIL
                      for each operating area connection that will be modeled.
                   c. Identify each utility on a Connecting Electric Utility form using the
                      dropdown menu.
                       Note: The modeler can specify that the utility delivers power to
                       itself over a tie-line (internal tie-line).
               4. Model tie corridors under the Connecting Electric Utility record by
                  inserting TIE records. Click the right mouse button and select the Add
                  TIE option on the pop-up menu.
               5. Model tie corridor details on the Connecting Area Tie Corridor form by
                  specifying the TIE record ID, the connecting company, and the
                  operating parameters for bulk power exchange. Connecting company
                  is optional.
                   Note 1: This is one of a mirrored pair of TIE records that the model
                   builder must create. The tie-lines in these paired TIE records have the
                   same names and tie-line (TYLN) specification. The other member in
                   the mirrored pair must reside under the other utility that is party to the
                   bulk power exchange.
                   The model builder must match the identifiers in these AC Line entries
                   with those used to specify tie-lines in the tie corridors (Connecting Area
                   Tie Corridor form).
                   Note 2: Internal ties do not require a mirrored pair.

Proprietary – See Copyright Page             252                e-terrageneration Modeling Tasks
                                                                    EMS Schema Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

                   Note 3: Dynamic load ties do not require tie-lines (TYLN records).
               6. Model a dynamic load tie by setting the Dynamic Load Tie check box
                  ON. Dynamic load ties do not have Tie-Line (TYLN) children.
               7. If the tie corridor is for both dynamic load monitoring and Joint-AGC
                  operations, select the Dynamic Load Tie tab, and add requester- or
                  supplier-specific Joint AGC information.
               8. Model tie-line details on the Lines in Corridor tab of the Connecting
                  Area Tie Corridor form as follows (does not apply to dynamic load tie
                  corridor modeling):
                   a. Specify the Tie-Line ID in the Name box. This value must be
                      duplicated in the mirrored-pair specification.
                   b. Specify the line ID in the AC Transmission Line box. This value
                      must match the ID of the corresponding tie-line on the
                      Transmission Line view.
                   c. Specify the line segment ID in the Segment box.
                   d. If the tie-line is a transformer, set the Is a Line? check box OFF.
                   e. If the tie corridor measurement is taken in the parent operating
                      area, set the In This OPA? check box ON. Switch the mirrored-pair
                      flag of this type OFF.
                   f. Specify the EMS operating area station that delivers or receives the
                      bulk power exchange. This value must be duplicated in the
                      mirrored-pair specification.
                   g. Specify the Equipment group (kV level) of the branch that carries
                      the bulk power exchange to the station specified above. This value
                      must be duplicated in the mirrored-pair specification.
                   h. Specify the node name of the station specified above. This value is
                      duplicated in the mirrored-pair specification.
                   i.   Save the entry.
               9. Map tie-lines and tie corridors to SCADA measurements and controls
                  using the Generation Telemetry View templates.
               10. Save your work.

11.10 Jointly Owned Units
               “Jointly owned units” (JOUs) are units owned by more than one operating
               area, with each operating area having its own share of the unit. Share
               records must be set up for all non-physical, internally operated JOUs.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page             253               e-terrageneration Modeling Tasks
                                                                   EMS Schema Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

               This section contains background information about modeling JOUs.


                                   Figure 89: JOU Definition
11.10.1 JOU Topology
               Three types of PLC-unit combinations are used to represent a single JOU
               site:
               •   Physical Internally Operated JOU: This type has a physical internally
                   operated JOU PLC and one physical internally operated JOU unit. This
                   is modeled in the operating area (OPA) that is in control of the JOU
                   and represents the actual unit.
               •   Non-Physical Internally Operated JOU: This type is always paired
                   one-to-one with a physical internally operated JOU. This type is
                   characterized by a non-physical internally operated JOU PLC and a
                   non-physical internally operated JOU unit for each share owner. There
                   must be at least two share units under each non-physical PLC, with
                   one of these units representing a share belonging to the OPA that is
                   operating the JOU.
               •   Externally Operated JOU: This type is represented by a physical
                   externally operated JOU PLC and one non-physical externally

Proprietary – See Copyright Page             254               e-terrageneration Modeling Tasks
                                                                   EMS Schema Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

                   operated JOU unit. This type is modeled in an OPA’s topology when
                   the OPA owns a share of a JOU that is operated by another company.
               The topology of internally and externally operated JOUs is illustrated in
               Figure 90 below.

                     Externally operated                        Internally operated
       Operating         PLC                                      PLC                                 Operating
        Area A             JOU Physical, Internally
                                 Operated
                                                                        JOU Physical, Internally
                                                                              Operated
                                                                                                       Area B
                               UNIT A                                     UNIT
                               JOU Physical, Internally                   JOU Physical, Internally
                                     Operated                                   Operated


                                                                  PLC
                                                                         JOU Non-physical,
                                                                         Internally Operated

                                                                            Virtual UNIT A
                                                                               JOU Non-physical,
                                                                               Internally Operated


                                                                                SHARE


                                                                            Virtual UNIT B
                                                                                JOU Non-physical,
                                                                                Internally Operated


                                                                                SHARE


                                    Figure 90: Topology of JOUs
               Jointly owned units and their PLCs are inserted into the system topology
               just like other units and PLCs. To specify that a PLC and its units are for a
               jointly owned unit, the PLC’s “JOU?” flag is set ON. The Non-Physical flag
               also must be toggled to the correct value for the PLC and its units,
               depending on which one of the three types of JOUs is being modeled.
               Some requirements to follow about JOU topology are:
               •   A physical internally operated JOU must always be followed by its
                   corresponding non-physical internally operated JOU.
               •   A physical internally operated JOU PLC has one and only one unit,
                   and the unit must be a physical internally operated JOU.
               •   An externally operated JOU PLC has one and only one unit, and the
                   unit must be a non-physical externally operated JOU.
               •   For e-terrasimulator operation, every non-physical internally operated
                   JOU share unit belonging to an OPA other than the operating OPA has


Proprietary – See Copyright Page                          255                           e-terrageneration Modeling Tasks
                                                                                            EMS Schema Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

                   to have a matching externally operated JOU modeled in the OPA of
                   the share owner.
               •   For e-terrasimulator operation, if an internally operated JOU resides in
                   a non-EMS OPA, no matter how many share owners there are, only
                   two shares have to be modeled. There should be one share for the
                   EMS OPAs share, and one for the JOU operating OPA and the rest of
                   the shares.
               •   Externally operated JOU PLCs should be toggled so they cannot
                   accept AGC setpoints or pulses. This allows a basepoint to be
                   calculated with the PLC status set to “AUT”.

11.10.2 JOU Measurement Topology
               Measurement processing and modeling for JOUs is the same as it is for
               normal units, except that the non-physical internally operated JOU
               representing the operating owner’s share has no measurement records.

11.12 Generating Unit Parameters Checklist
               The following parameters are required when modeling generating units:


Proprietary – See Copyright Page             259                e-terrageneration Modeling Tasks
                                                                    EMS Schema Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

               •   Schedules and Regulations: Parameters that affect the schedules
                   defined for the unit, and the unit’s voltage regulation parameters.
               •   State Estimation: Parameters describing how the unit participates in
                   state estimation.
               •   Network Limits: Parameters describing the basic network parameters
                   such as rated MVA, participation factors, and minimum and maximum
                   MW output.
               •   Network Flags: Parameters describing the other basic network
                   parameters, such as whether the unit is removed from service and has
                   AGC simulation.
               •   Generation Limits: Parameters describing the basic generation
                   parameters, such as capacity, frequency deviation, and economic and
                   LFC minimum and maximum values.
               •   Unit Commitment Parameters: Parameters describing the unit’s
                   participation in unit commitment.
               •   Jointly Owned Unit Parameters: Parameters specifying if and how
                   this unit is jointly owned.
               •   Reserve Parameters: Parameters describing how and how much the
                   unit is committed to reserves.
               •   ED/Costing Parameters: Parameters describing how the unit
                   participates in economic dispatch and its startup and running costs.
               •   Unit Response Parameters: Parameters describing the unit’s ability
                   to ramp up and down.
               •   Special Operating Modes: Parameters describing any special
                   operating modes in which the unit can be, such as a pumped storage
                   unit or a synchronous condenser.
               •   Dynamic Parameters: Parameters describing the dynamic aspects of
                   the unit, such as the AVR lead/lag and delay, the damping coefficient,
                   and whether the unit is part of a combined cycle group of units.
               For modeling purposes, these parameters can be classified into two
               general groups:
               •   Steady-State Parameters are used to model the steady-state (all
                   transients have died out) behavior of the unit.
               •   Dynamic Parameters are used to model some of the long-term
                   dynamic behavior of the unit, primarily for the Dispatcher Training
                   Simulator (DTS).


Proprietary – See Copyright Page            260               e-terrageneration Modeling Tasks
                                                                  EMS Schema Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

11.13 Specifying e-terrageneration Subsystem Parameters
               The system administrator or integrator defines global settings for the
               e-terrageneration model using the Generation Parameters form of
               ModelerUI. Generation parameters are grouped on the form as follows:
               Generation Interfaces, Variable Frequency Bias, System Settings, Alarm
               Parameters, and Telemetry.
               The data entry fields provided on each tab, and their implications for
               generation subsystem modeling, are explained in the sections below.


                   Figure 92: e-terrageneration Subsystem Parameters

               Generation Interfaces tab:
               •   Use Unit Commitment or Hydro-Thermal Coordination: When
                   selected, this check box specifies that your system uses either HTC or
                   UC:
                   − HTC: When selected, this radio button specifies that your system

Proprietary – See Copyright Page            261               e-terrageneration Modeling Tasks
                                                                  EMS Schema Modeling Guide

                   − UC: When selected, this radio button specifies that your system
                     uses Unit Commitment.
               •   Used in e-terrasimulator Environment? When selected, this check
                   box specifies that the e-terrageneration model will be used in an
                   e-terrasimulator environment.
               •   Uses Network Applications? When selected, this check box specifies
                   that your EMS includes applications from the Network subsystem.
               •   Calculate CPS Reports? A check mark specifies that
                   NERC-compliant CPS reports will be produced.

11.13.2 Variable Frequency Bias
               To define how frequency bias will affect the calculation of area ACE,
               specify the desired values in the fields provided on the Variable Frequency
               Bias tab:
               •   Droop Scalar Constant: Used to model how an area’s unit governors
                   will respond to frequency deviation and to adjust the droop
                   characteristic of all area generators.
               •   Transition Scalar: Specifies the change in governor response as area
                   frequency deviation continues to reside within the Variable Frequency
                   Bias deadband region.
               •   VFBIAS Deadband Minimum: The Variable Frequency Bias
                   deadband minimum.
               •   VFBIAS Deadband Maximum: The Variable Frequency Bias
                   deadband maximum.

11.14 Generation Telemetry Model
               The generation analyst defines the generation telemetry model by
               specifying e-terrageneration/SCADA measurement record mapping in the
               Generation Telemetry tree of the ModelerUI application.
               The target records for specifying output to SCADA and the input records
               for specifying input from SCADA to the e-terrageneration subsystem
               database appear in windows on the screen. One window presents
               e-terrageneration equipment topology, and the other window presents
               SCADA measurement structures.

11.14.1 Specifying Telemetry Objects
               The e-terrageneration engineer uses the Input Object form to specify how
               the telemetered input data for AGC will be mapped from the real-time
               SCADA clone to the real-time Generation clone.
               The e-terrageneration engineer uses the Output Object form to specify
               how AGC output data will be telemetered from the real-time Generation
               clone to the real-time SCADA clone.

Proprietary – See Copyright Page            265              e-terrageneration Modeling Tasks
                                                                 EMS Schema Modeling Guide
