2.3 Schedules and Curves

2.3.1 Schedules
Schedules describe the relationship between time (X axis) and one or two dependent
variables (Y1 axis and Y2 axis).


2.3.1.1 Schedule Execution
The TimeSet (NETMOM TYMSET), WeekSeg (NETMOM WKSEG), DayType (NETMOM DAYSEG),
Season, and AbnormalDate (NETMOM ABDATE) tables are used to define the time points
pattern referenced by schedules. All the schedule points are defined in the
IntervalSchedPoint class. ETS/EMS only supports a weekly schedule starting from the
middle of the night of Sunday.
Timeset records represent the time models that are built underneath them. Each record has
a name, as well as a field specifying the type of model represented. ETS only supports a
weekly cycle, not the linear time trend.
Cycle schedules repeat each week: that is, TimeSet time models contain a set of time points
(times when component values change) that repeat week after week, except for defined
abnormal dates that interrupt the weekly cycle.
WeekSeg records are children of TimeSet. They break the week up into groups of consistent
daily schedules. WeekSegs are used to specify when a new daily schedule becomes
effective. You add another WeekSeg to a TimeSet only when the times at which you want
the component’s value to change are different from those of the previous day.
A “day schedule” refers to a time period from 00:00 hours to 23:59 hours. It is a fixed day,
unrelated to when a WeekSeg becomes effective.
The daily schedule defined by the DayType repeats each day until the WeekSeg that called
it is superseded by a new WeekSeg.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page                         94                       Network Modeling
                                                                   e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

DayType records belong to TimeSet records rather than to WeekSeg records. This is
important when defining abnormal dates, because it enables the TimeSet to contain
DayTypes that are not called by a WeekSeg. Only TimeSets that contain the name of the
DAYSEG called by an AbnormalDate are affected by that. This flexibility lets you control
which TimeSets are affected by the AbnormalDate. For example, if the AbnormalDate
FOURTHOFJULY refers to a DayType named “JULY4”, then only those TimeSets with a
DayType called “JULY4” are affected by the AbnormalDate.
The requirement that DayType names need only be unique within a particular TimeSet lets
you set up a standard naming convention for the DayType. For example, you might have a
DayType named “FRIDAY” because it begins on Friday in each of 10 different TimeSets.


2.3.1.2 Regulation Schedules
Regulation schedules are developed for use by modeled generators, load tap changing
transformers, system voltage, etc.
    Value1: Voltage Target in p.u.
    Value2: Voltage Deviation in p.u.
For phase shifter regulation schedules:
    Value 1: MW Target
    Value 2: MW Deviation


2.3.1.3 Area Load Schedules
Area load schedules are used by several different subsystems. They are used by
e-terrasimulator to simulate system load for realistic training scenarios. They are also used
when performing system studies and running contingency analysis.
As system loads are affected and vary depending on the time of day, weekday to weekend,
different load curves are typically developed to simulate load patterns for each day of the
week, weekends, and holidays. Likewise, load curves can be developed to account for the
different seasons.
    Value1: Total MW (for top load area)/Base MW (for non-top load area)
    Value2: Loss Factor (for top load area)/Fraction (for non-top load area)


2.3.1.4 Switch Schedules
Switch schedules are used by several different subsystems. They can be used by
e-terrasimulator to simulate auto voltage control by insertion or removal of static voltage
control devices such as shunt capacitors or reactors.
    Value1: Open/Close


Proprietary – See Copyright Page              95                                 Network Modeling
                                                                  e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

2.3.1.5 Load Reactive Schedules
Load reactive schedules are assigned to individual loads. They contain time-variable base
MVAr loads (minimum MVAr loads), as well as the power factor of the load. The power factor
is used to determine the MVAr load, in addition to the base, from the MW load. The sum of
the two components yields the total MVAR load.
    Value1: Load MVAR
    Value2: Power Factor


2.3.2 Curves
Curves describe the relationship between an independent variable (X axis) and one or two
dependent variables (Y1 axis and Y2 axis). They are not time-dependent.


2.3.2.1 MVAR Capability Curve
SynchronousMachine input to the network is modeled as a direct contribution of power (W
and R) at the node the unit is connected to, where W and R are the unit’s MW and MVAR
outputs, respectively.
Quantities for both W and R are often variables and have limits. The sign convention for
both is positive for real and reactive power entering the network.
Each unit VAR capability curve is defined in a table, which shows a unit’s MVAR maximum
and minimum limits for a given MW output.
    X: MW output
    Y1: Maximum MVAR
    Y2: Minimum MVAR


2.3.2.2 Load-Based Regulation Curve
A regulation schedule can also be defined based on the load.
    X: Load
    Y1: Voltage Target
    Y2: Voltage Deviation


2.3.2.3 Station Supply WR Curves
The station supply WR curves describe the relationship between the station supply (Y) with
load and the station generator output (X).
    X: Station Generator Output
    Y1: AuxiliaryLoad MW

Proprietary – See Copyright Page             96                                Network Modeling
                                                                e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

    Y2: AuxiliaryLoad MVAR


2.3.2.4 Tap Ratio Curves
In certain situations, such as for three-winding transformers, an unusual relationship
between tap setting and voltage tap ratio may exist. For these cases, tap ratio tables are
assigned to transformers indirectly by assigning them to tap types.
If a tap type is assigned to a tap ratio table, transformers assigned to that tap type have
their voltage tap ratios calculated using the table. If no table is assigned to a tap type,
transformers assigned to that tap type have their voltage tap ratios calculated in the usual
linear manner.
    X: Tap Positions
    Y1: Per-unit Voltage Tap Ratio Correction Scaling Factor


2.3.2.5 Transformer Impedance Curves
A transformer impedance curve defines the impedance correction table.
    X: Tap Positions
    Y1: Resistance Correction Scaling Factor
    Y2: Reactance Correction Scaling Factor


2.3.2.6 Phase Shifter Impedance Curves
The phase shifter impedance can be modeled as a function of the phase shifter’s angle, in
degrees. The correction table for phase-shifter impedance is referenced in the phase
shifter’s tap type. The correction table gives X and corresponding Y values, where X is the
phase shift in degrees, and Y is multiplied by a phase shifter’s nominal impedance to get the
corrected impedance. If an impedance correction table is not referenced, the phase shifter’s
impedance is assumed to be constant.
    X: Phase Shift in Degrees
    Y1: Impedance Correction Scaling Factor


2.3.2.7 Auxiliary Load Voltage Limit Curves
This curve defines voltage limits for Auxiliary Loads as a function of its MW demand.
    X: MW Output of the Auxiliary Load
    Y1: High Normal Voltage
    Y2: Low Normal Voltage
    Y3: High Emergency Voltage


Proprietary – See Copyright Page               97                              Network Modeling
                                                                e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

    Y4: Low Emergency Voltage


2.4 Monitoring
The monitoring definition is used in various network applications to compare the state of
network components against user-defined limits.
• Monitored group: A MonitoredGroup defines a set of tolerances and processing controls
  that are used by the state monitor process when checking the components that are
  assigned to that monitored group. The monitored group also provides the means for
  activating and deactivating sets of components from the monitoring process.
• Voltage limit set: A VoltageLimitSet describes a set of voltage ratings, described in per
  unit voltage. Two sets of rating values can be supplied, Normal and Emergency,
  corresponding to two levels of severity. High, low, and drop limits (exchange) are
  supplied for each severity level. The high limit corresponds to the maximum voltage, the
  low limit corresponds to the minimum voltage, and the drop limit specifies the
  maximum amount a component’s voltage can decrease from its previous value. The
  effect of voltage reduction on the limits is also supplied for the voltage group.
    The following VoltageLimitSet properties must be populated:
     – The EMSName property determines ID_VLIM (four characters)
     – Each VoltageLimitSet record has six child VoltageLimit records corresponding to the
       limit fields on the VLIM record in NETMOM.
    For VoltageLimit records, the properties that must be populated for exporting to
    NETMOM are:
     – The LimitType must be selected from the enumeration group EMSLimitType:
         ∗ Emergency EXCHANGE
         ∗ Emergency HIGH
         ∗ Emergency LOW
         ∗ Normal EXCHANGE
         ∗ Normal HIGH
         ∗ Normal LOW
     – The Value property is not mandatory for netvalid.
• Angle difference limit set: Each AngleDifferenceLimitSet has three angle separation
  limits, corresponding to three severity levels. The limit values are supplied in units of
  degrees. It is referenced by AngleDifference.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page              98                                 Network Modeling
                                                                  e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

2.4.1 Monitored Element Definition
There are two methods to assign components to groups: default and non-default. The
default method requires less data entry, but the non-default method allows more control
over individual limits. The default method assigns all components within a
GeographicalRegion by voltage level or SubGeographicalRegion by voltage level.
The non-default method individually assigns components. If specified, non-default
monitoring overrides default monitoring for a particular component. AC lines, transformers,
zero impedance branches, node limits, and buses can be assigned to a particular monitored
group using either method. Buses can be assigned to a voltage limit group using either
method. Interfaces, node pairs, and nodes must be assigned through the non-default
method.
To monitor components by the default method, the user marks the voltage level within each
GeographicalRegion or SubGeographicalRegion to be included in the monitored group and
voltage level group. Whether the default assignment is within a GeographicalRegion or
SubGeographicalRegion is controlled by an option supplied for each GeographicalRegion in
the network model definition.
To assign non-default components, the user marks the individual components to be
included in the monitor group.
For monitored nodes that have individual node voltage limits assigned, the node voltage
limits are used for monitoring. For nodes that do not, voltage limit groups assigned to the
node (non-default monitoring) or to its voltage level or station (default monitoring) in the
monitored element definition supply the voltage limits for the node.


2.4.1.1 Angle Difference
A node pair identifies a pair of nodes that can be checked for angle separation. Each node
pair is supplied by an AngleDifferenceLimitSet with three angle separation limits,
corresponding to three severity levels. The limit values are supplied in units of degrees.


2.4.1.2 Branch Group
A BranchGroup identifies a set of branch elements to be monitored for their total net flow.
The direction of the flow to be included in the net flow calculation is specified for each
branch included in the interface. A high limit (corresponding to the maximum net flow in the
interface) and a low limit (corresponding to the minimum net flow in the interface) are
specified. Each BranchGroup is identified as monitored for MW or MVAR. The individual
branch elements in a BranchGroup are defined in the BranchGroupTerminal class.


2.4.1.3 Reserve Monitor Groups/Units
A Unit Reserve Group is used in Optimal Power Flow (OPF) to monitor the MW reserve of the
defined group. A Unit Reserve Group consists of multiple units specified by the user.

Proprietary – See Copyright Page              99                                 Network Modeling
                                                                  e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

2.4.1.4 Reactive Monitored Groups/Stations
Various network applications monitor reactive reserve defined by the
ReactiveMonitoredGroup. All the ShuntCompensator and GeneratingUnits defined in the
ReacMonGroup_Station are summed to compute the reactive reserve.


2.4.1.5 ReserveMonitoringGroup/ReserveMonitoringGroup_Mem
A ReserveMonitoringGroup identifies a user-defined collection of reactive power
components. The total MVAR reserve of this dynamic reserve group can be monitored and
reported for any MVAR reserve violations based on the user-specified high and low limits.
The element components in a ReserveMonitoringGroup, such as ShuntCompensator,
SynchronousMachine, and StaticVarCompensator, are defined in the
ReserveMonitoringGroup_Mem class.
The new dynamic reserve monitoring function is only available for e-terraplatform 3.0.
Unlike the existing ReactiveMonitoredGroup, where member components based on station
selection on the fly are static, the user can decide whether to enable member reactive
components in the calculation of different dynamic reserve monitoring groups by using
MVAR type Protective Actions and Triggering Conditions defined in RASMOM.


2.4.1.6 Operational Limit Sets
There are two types of operational limit sets: branch limits and voltage limits. Limits are
used to provide alarm points to alert system operators when a piece of equipment or
transmission line is approaching or exceeding an operational limit.
Alternate limit sets are modeled as an OperationalLimitSet with a “branch limit priority”
specified. System components are rated based on factors such as ambient temperature.
Typically, alternate limit sets are developed for use during different seasons or temperature
thresholds.
• Branch Limits: A branch limit is defined for each AC line, transformer, or zero impedance
  branch that can be monitored for violating its flow rating. Three rating values can be
  supplied for the branch limit, corresponding to three levels of severity. The limit can
  apply to one or both ends of the branch, in one or both directions of flow. If the branch
  limit is directional or applies only to one end of the branch, another branch limit can be
  assigned to the same AC line, transformer, or zero impedance branch applying to the
  other end or direction of flow. The branch limits also define the possible alternate limit
  sets. If a branch limit record is defined to be manually entered, it is not overwritten with
  SCADA values.
• Branch Limit Type: For each type of branch (ACLineSegment, TransformerWinding, and
  SeriesCompensator), you can specify whether the monitoring checks ampere or MVA
  values. This specification applies to all branches of that type, and it defines the units
  (MVA or amps) assumed for the supplied branch limit values. Three sets of analog limits


Proprietary – See Copyright Page              100                                Network Modeling
                                                                  e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

    are shown: normal, emergency, and load shedding. These limits are mapped to
    NETMOM LNLIM/ZBLIM/XFLIM classes.
• Voltage Limits: These are defined for each ConnectivityNode that is monitored. The
  terminal association should refer to the BusBarSection terminal if it exists at that node;
  otherwise, the terminal of other devices at that node. Voltage limits have similar rating
  information as branch limits. Voltage limits are copied from SCADA whenever mapping
  between the network and SCADA databases is rebuilt. Voltage limits can also be
  manually entered in the network applications. If a voltage limit record is defined to be
  manually entered, it is not overwritten with SCADA values; it is mapped to the
  NETMOM NDLIM class. There are no alternate limit sets for voltage limits.
NDLIM records appear in e-terrasource as one OperationalLimitSet record with six child
OperationalLimit records. To export a NDLIM record to NETMOM, the following fields are
required.
The following OperationalLimitSet properties must be populated:
• The EMSName property appears in the tree and determines ID_NDLIM (one character)
  The Terminal must be populated. The associated connectivity node determines the ND
  parent of the NDLIM in NETMOM.
• Each OperationalLimitSet record has six child OperationalLimit records corresponding
  to the limit fields on the NDLIM record in NETMOM.
For OperationalLimit records, the properties that must be populated for export to NETMOM
are:
• The LimitType must be selected from the enumeration group EMSLimitType:
     – EmergencyChange
     – NormalChange
     – EmergencyHigh
     – NormalHigh
     – EmergencyLow
     – NormalLow
• The OpLimitType must be set to VoltageLimit.
• The Value must be populated except for change limits.
Both LNLIM and LNLIMA records appear in e-terrasource as one OperationalLimitSet record
with three child OperationalLimit records. However, which properties are populated is
different for each.
To export a LNLIM record to NETMOM, the following OperationalLimitSet properties must be
populated:
• The EMSName property appears in the tree and should be populated. This also
  determines ID_LNLIM in NETMOM.
• The Branch Priority property should be blank.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page            101                                Network Modeling
                                                                e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

• The rest of the properties in the General property group apply.
• Each OperationalLimitSet record has three child OperationalLimit records
  corresponding to the fields LIMIT1, LIMIT2, and LIMIT3 in NETMOM.
For all child OperationalLimit records, the properties that must be populated for export to
NETMOM are:
• The EMSName property appears in the tree and should be populated, but it is not
  exported.
• OpLimitType labeled "OperationalLimit Type" must be "Apparent Power" or "Current".
• The Value property must be populated.
To export an LNLIMA record to NETMOM, the following OperationalLimitSet properties must
be populated:
• The EMSName property appears in the tree and should be populated. This also
  determines ID_LNLIM in NETMOM.
• The Branch Priority property must be populated. This determines ID_LNLIMA in
  NETMOM.
• The rest of the properties in the General property group are not used.
• Each OperationalLimitSet record has three child OperationalLimit records
  corresponding to the fields LIMIT1, LIMIT2, and LIMIT3 in NETMOM.
For OperationalLimit records the properties that must be populated for export to NETMOM
are:
• The EMSName property appears in the tree and should be populated, but it is not
  exported.
• OpLimitType labeled "OperationalLimit Type" must be "Apparent Power" or "Current".
• The Value property must be populated.
Similar rules apply to the remaining branch limit record types in NETMOM: ZBLIM, ZBLIMA,
XFLIM, XFLIMA, CBLIM, and CBLIMA.


2.4.2 Network Other Tables

2.4.2.1 Network Configuration Parameters
These parameters are used for network application settings. They are mapped to the
NETMOM ITEMS record and grouped under the following categories: Functions Installed,
Contingency Redefinition, General Options, Equipment Type Disposition, VAR Violation
Monitoring, Season Definition, SCADAMAP, and Simulation.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page             102                                Network Modeling
                                                                 e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

2.4.2.2 Network Transaction/Transaction Direction
This table represents a transaction between two operating areas used in network
applications.


2.4.2.3 Mutual Coupling
Mutual coupling defines the zero sequence impedance between the two lines with mutual
coupling effects. The first terminal is the starting terminal for calculating the distance along
the first branch of the mutual coupling. The second terminal is the starting terminal for
calculating the distance along the second branch of the mutual coupling. Normally, mutual
coupling is only used for AC line segment terminals. The first and second terminals of a
mutual coupling should point to different ACLineSegments. A mutual coupling group is used
to identify all the line mutual impedances that are processed at the same time. A line
cannot appear in two different groups. It is used only by the short circuit application.


2.4.2.4 Network Alarm
This table defines the alarm category used by the network applications.


2.4.2.5 SpecialMeasurement
Unlike analogs or points mapped to the network model, the special measurement does not
correspond to any component types in the network model such as temperature dependent
ratings, system voltage reduction, load area power, and substation temperature. The
measurement can only be analog or discrete.


2.4.2.6 SumMeasurement/SumMeasurement_Member
SumMeasurement defines the summed analog measurements used by state estimation.
The participated member can be an ACLineSegment, TransformerWinding,
SeriesCompensator, SynchronousMachine, or EquivalentLoad.


2.4.2.7 ConductorLength
This table defines the conductor length and the conductor type parameters.


2.5 Contingency Modeling
One of the functions used by power system operators and planners is contingency analysis.
This is a process that simulates the loss of one or more elements of the grid to allow
operators and planners to observe how the grid reacts. An example is the loss of a
transmission line or a generator. This loss triggers the contingency analysis subsystem to
run a power flow study. The results indicate if any other elements can become overloaded

Proprietary – See Copyright Page              103                                Network Modeling
                                                                  e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

in such a situation. Power markets also use contingency definitions to run simultaneous
feasibility tests.
To allow this to function properly, the modeler must define the specific elements within the
system that are monitored for contingencies. There are six classes used to model
contingency definitions:
•   Contingency Groups (Ctg_Group)
•   Contingency Group Members (Ctg_CtgGroup)
•   Contingency
•   Contingency Element (Ctg_Equipment)
•   Conditional Contingency (ConditionalCtg)
•   Contingency Configuration
Contingencies are usually grouped together to be selected as active or inactive by the
users. Each contingency group can include multiple contingencies and each contingency
can belong to different groups. The relationship is described in the Contingency Group
Member class.
Each contingency can include multiple network elements. e-terrasource supports
contingencies defined at:
•   ACLineSegment
•   SeriesCompensator
•   ShuntCompensator
•   SynchronousMachine
•   EquivalentLoad
•   DCConverter
•   VoltageSourceConverter
•   DCPole
•   TransformerWinding
•   ConnectivityNode (all the devices connected to this node are outaged)
•   Substation (all the devices within this substation are outaged)
DCController and DCPole can also have a contingency defined for reduced power transfer
setpoints. A corresponding ACLineSegment/SeriesCompensator association is then
required.
Each contingency is mapped to the CTGS CTGL class.
Contingencies can also happen when certain network components are over the operational
limit. This is called a “conditional contingency”. The monitored element should be defined in
this class, and Contingency has a reference (optional) to this class. It is mapped to the
CTGS CNDME class.
Note that the conditional contingencies definition can be replaced by remedial action
scheme modeling, which supports more complex contingency scenarios.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page            104                                Network Modeling
                                                                e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

2.6 Dynamic Ratings
Dynamic Ratings (also known as Equipment Dependent Limits or EDL) is a new application
added to e-terraplatform 3.0. It computes dynamic branch ratings, taking into account
variables such as ambient temperature and topology. For the purposes of computing
dynamic branch ratings, a branch and its associated terminal equipment, such as isolating
circuit breakers (CBs) and disconnectors, current transformers (CTs), and wave trap (WTs),
are used to collectively determine the effective ratings on the branch. The modeling can be
defined in the e-terrasource Dynamic Rating related tree view and tables with references to
Network Model.
The Dynamic Rating hierarchy in e-terrasource mainly includes Dynamic Rating Branch,
Switch, WeatherStation, and GeographicalRegion.
The Dynamic Rating model in e-terrasource can also be exported to e-terraplatform 2.6 for
users with the application added to their EMS. The Dynamic Rating application in
e-terraplatform 3.0 supports long names for branches and the GeographicalRegion.


2.6.1 Dynamic Rating Branch
Dynamic Rating Branch lists all the branches and associated terminal equipment
participating in the Dynamic Ratings application, as well as the limit dependency models,
weather station, and ownership definitions. Participating branches have the dynamic rating
flag set to True. The hierarchical structure is defined as:
 Dynamic Rating Branch (ACLineSegment, SeriesCompensator,
 TransformerWinding)
    |-- Series Equipment Dependent Limit
    |      |-- Equipment Limit Series Components
    |-- Temperature Dependent Limit Table
    |      |-- Temperature Limit Table Point
    |-- Temperature Polynomial Limit
    |-- Scheduled Limit Dependency
    |      |-- ScheduledLimitValue
    |-- Limit Scaling Limit
    |-- WeatherStation_Equipment
    |-- GeographicalRegion_Resource
    |-- Terminal
           |-- Current Transformer
                  |-- WeatherStation_Equipment
                  |-- GeographicalRegion_Resource
           |-- High Frequency Filter
                  |-- WeatherStation_Equipment
                  |-- GeographicalRegion_Resource


Proprietary – See Copyright Page           105                                Network Modeling
                                                               e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

Note that the static OperationalLimitSet/OperationalLimits associated with different limit
defintions, current transformers, wave traps, and switches are defined in the Network
Model tree view.
In e-terraplatform 3.0 SP4 and later, an ACLineSegment can have different limit definitions
applied to each end. The SeriesCompensator and TransformerWinding still have only one
definition.


2.6.1.1 Limit Dependency
A limit dependency describes the limit calculation model used to compute an operational
limit based on external inputs. Five kinds of limit dependency models can be defined for
branches:
• Series Equipment Dependency Limit
• Temperature Dependent Limit Table
• Temperature Polynomial Limit
• Scheduled Limit Dependency
• Limit Scaling Limit
All limit dependency types have an association to an operational limit for which the limit
dependency model applies.


2.6.1.1.1 Series Equipment Dependency Limit
Series Equipment Dependency Limit is a specification of equipment that determines the
calculated operational limit values based upon other equipment and their ratings. The most
restrictive limit connected in series within the group is used. The physical connection based
on switch status, for example, may also impact which elements in the group are
considered. Any equipment in the group that is presently connected in series with the
equipment of the directly associated operational limit is used. This provides a means to
indicate which series equipment limits are considered for a computed operational limit. The
operational limit of the same operational limit type is assumed to be used from the grouped
equipment. It is also possible to make assumptions or calculations regarding how flow
might split if the equipment is not simply in series.
The series components for a branch include one conducting network equipment to be
monitored and its connected equipment up to the bus bar. The components under a series
equipment dependency limit can be automatically populated or manually defined. More
details can be found in chapter 5 Simulation Modeling.


2.6.1.1.2 Environmental Limits
The limit for power equipment can depend on environmental factors such as temperature.
The environmental model can be a polynomial function of temperature (Temperature


Proprietary – See Copyright Page             106                                Network Modeling
                                                                 e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

Polynomial Limit in ETS), or a static look up table (Temperature Dependent Limit Table and
the child record Temperature Limit Table Point in ETS).
The temperature used to calculate the Dynamic Rating of the components comes from its
associated weather station.
Environmental limits for Normal, Emergency, and LoadShed conditions need to be modeled
separately in e-terrasource. If the temperature or the polynomial parameters are the same
among the three conditions, EMSName needs to be the same for the normalization when
DYNRTG is exported to the EMS side. In the EMS DYNRTG database, the environmental limits
are defined as a combination of the referenced table, TMPMDL, and the SEG child record,
RATING.


2.6.1.1.3 Scheduled Limit Dependency
Limit may vary when the season changes. Seasonally dependent limits can be defined in
ScheduleLimitDependency and the child record ScheduledLimitValue with the association
to season.


2.6.1.1.4 Limit Scaling Limit
Users may define just one branch rating, such as for normal conditions, which the other
types of ratings (such as Emergency and Load Shed) can be derived from. This can be
modeled as LimitScalingLimit in ETS, which specifies an operational limit calculated by
scaling another operational limit with a scaling percentage factor.


2.6.2 Weather Station
Weather stations are entities that group together equipment that have the same or similar
weather. Weather stations are the source of ambient temperature data. The temperature
data can be in the form of multiple redundant measurements for real-time or forecasted
temperatures for offline studies.
The weather station hierarchy in ETS is shown below.
 WeatherStation
    |-- WeatherStation_Equipment
    |-- Analog

A WeatherStation_Equipment class is used to model the possible association of an
equipment to multiple WeatherStations. It also specifies the equipment terminal for the
ACLineSegment to indicate whether the WeatherStation should be used for one end or both
ends. The Analog associated with the WeatherStation is used for temperature
measurements.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page            107                                Network Modeling
                                                                e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

2.6.3 GeographicalRegion
Every equipment participating in Dynamic Ratings is required to have one or more owning
geographical regions.
The hierarchy related to GeographicalRegion data used in Dynamic Ratings is shown below.
 GeographicalRegion
    |-- GeographicalRegion_Resource
    |-- Analog
    |-- Season Start Table

The GeographicalRegion_Resource class is used to model the possible association of a
piece of equipment to multiple GeographicalRegions. It also specifies the equipment
terminal of an ACLineSegment for the ownership.
GeographicalRegion may have a different season start time, which is modeled in
SeasonStartTable. The Analog associated with GeographicalRegion is used for mapping
temperature telemetry to a specific GeographicalRegion/WeatherStation pair.
In e-terraplatform 3.0 SP4 and later, each GeographicalRegion can have its own limit unit
definitions for the ACLineSegment/SeriesCompensator (NonZeroImpedance and
ZeroImpedance), TransformerWinding, and Switches.


2.6.4 DynamicRatingConfiguration
This is the single-instance record where users can specify the dynamic rating application
configurations as well as a flag to control the automatic generation of the dynamic rating
component in e-terrasource.


2.6.5 Automatic Generation of Dynamic Rating Components
For network branches using Dynamic Ratings, e-terrasource provides a function to do a
topology search and find other serial components connected to those branches until the
bus bar and automatically populate the Dynamic Rating database with branches and their
connected components.
The automatic generation of dynamic rating components is implemented as part of the
e-terrasource workspace validation sequence. Any branch (currently limited to
ACLineSegment, SeriesCompensator, and TransformerWinding) that must be represented in
Dynamic Ratings has the Boolean attribute DynamicRating set to True in the Network
Model tree view. Current Transformer and Wave Trap are defined as Auxiliary Equipment
attached to the owning equipment terminal.
The logic will first check the participated branch’s OperationalLimitSet terminal association.
For branches, except ACLineSegment, it will start outwards from each terminal of the
branch and search for other station equipment that are connected to the branch’s terminal
through a connectivity node (for Switches) or are associated with the branch’s terminal (for

Proprietary – See Copyright Page             108                                Network Modeling
                                                                 e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

WaveTraps and CurrentTransformers). If multiple Switches are connected to the branch
terminals, the search processes those Switches and continues outwards from the far end
terminals of each Switch already processed. For ACLineSegment, if the two ends have
different OperationalLimitSets, the logic will search each end separately. WaveTraps and
CurrentTransformers associated with ACLineSegment should only be included if the
attached terminal has an OperationalLimitSet defined or the ACLineSegment has an
OperationalLimitSet applied to both ends. The stopping point for the search is one of the
following, whichever comes first:
• If the terminal of any Switch already processed by the search is connected to a
  connectivity node with a terminal of a BusBarSection.
• If the terminal of any Switch already processed by the search is connected to a
  connectivity node with the terminal of any other equipment (either another branch such
  as an ACLineSegment, TransformerWinding or a shunt device such as a
  SynchronousMachine, EquivalentLoad, etc.) other than the reference branch from
  whose terminals the search was initiated.

  Note: For the purpose of the auto generation logic, it is assumed that all
  SeriesCompensators are modeled as individual branches. This implies that a stopping
  point is reached when a search beginning at a branch reaches the near/far end terminal
  of a SeriesCompensator.

The auto generation populates the Series Equipment Dependent record for the branch as a
collection of EquipmentLimitComponents which reference all equipment included in the
connectivity search described above. This includes the branch from whose terminals the
search begins and all Switches, CTs, and WTs connected to one another through their
terminals.
All of the auto generated EquipmentLimitSeriesComponent will have the TOPONLY flag set
to be true. The user has the option to examine the Series Equipment Dependent and the
objects within that collection and use manual means to optionally exclude (or insert)
EquipmentLimitSeriesComponents that are not desired (or were not included) through auto
generation before it is transformed to the Dynamic Rating database in EMS. The
EquipmentLimitComponent class has a Boolean attribute Exclude that allows the user to
exclude an Equipment from one or more groupings. If an EquipmentLimitComponent has
this TOPONLY Boolean set manually by the user, the next incremental auto generation will
not result in that EquipmentLimitComponent auto generated as part of that grouping.
Before running the auto generation logic, users must set the Boolean attribute
AutoGeneration in the DynamicRatingConfiguration table to True. The auto generation logic
resets the attribute at the end of its execution. The auto generation logic uses an
incremental approach that does not destroy the existing auto generated objects prior to
execution.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page            109                               Network Modeling
                                                               e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

2.6.6 Dynamic Rating Modeling Workflow
The dynamic rating modeling should be done after the power system equipment, including
current transformer and wate traps, are already modeled in e-terrasource. The following
steps are suggested for dynamic rating modeling:
1. Select the branches to participate in DynamicRatings. (Currently, only ACLineSegment
   including those with the ZeroImpedanceLine attribute set, SeriesCompensator, and
   TransformerWinding qualify.)
2. Run Dynamic Rating in workspace validation.
3. Manually exclude an instance of an equipment from one or more groupings.
4. Add more Dynamic Ratings specific data, such as modeling of WeatherStations and
   TemperatureDependencyModels.
5. Add Dynamic Ratings specific alarm and measurements definitions.
6. Run general workspace validation (based on the metadata property and association
   definition; there is currently no dedicated dynamic rating module in e-terrasource).
7. Export to the e-terraplatform DYNRTG model.


2.6.7 Dynamic Rating Model Restrictions
The dynamic rating validation is not complete in the current e-terrasource release. Be
aware of the following restrictions:
• A branch can either have Temperature Limit tables (up to six for the three conditions
  and two ends) or Polynomial models (up to six for the three conditions and two ends),
  but not both.
• For Temperature Limit table/Polynomial table/Scheduled Limit Dependency, usually
  model three records/sets for normal, emergency, and loadshedding conditions. If not all
  of them are available, the normal condition data should be modeled. The limits
  corresponding to the same temperature or the same season should be:
  NormalLimit <= EmergencyLimit <= LoadSheddingLimit
• Temperature points must be the same under the Temperature Limit table with the same
  EMSNames for normalization.
• All participating EquipmentLimitSeriesComponents (branches, switches, CTs, and WTs)
  must have the WeatherStation and GeographicalRegion association defined.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page            110                                Network Modeling
                                                                e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

2.7 Remedial Action Schemes
Remedial action schemes (RASs) are automatic actions taken in the field in an effort to
prevent overloads or the loss of equipment in the event that a predefined event or events
occur, such as the loss of multiple transmission lines. RASs are implemented in stages, with
each stage associated with a set of triggers, and each trigger tied with a triggering
condition as well as its associated protective actions. The elements being monitored are
referred to as the “triggering conditions”, which cause the RAS to be implemented. Each
stage has a priority that defines the sequence under the parent remedial action scheme.
The same definition is applied to StageTrigger under the parent stage.
For each stage, a set of actions is defined to reduce or alleviate the overload. These actions
are referred to as “protective actions”. Similarly, remedial action plans (RAPs) are preventive
actions executed manually.
An RAP is modeled as a special case of an RAS.
The RAS definitions are then evaluated and implemented by network analysis applications,
such as STNET, PWRFLOW, STCA, and RTCA, in an effort to reduce the violations caused by
the current system (base case) or contingency-based topology.
The modeling structure for a remedial action scheme is shown below.
 Remedial Actions Schemes
    |-- Trigger Condition
    |   |-- Gate
    |       |-- Pin
    |-- Stage
        |-- StageTrigger
            |-- ProtectiveActions
                |-- PrivateProtectiveAction
                |-- ProtectiveActionShared


2.7.1 Remedial Action Schemes
An RAS is modeled to represent an automatically executed remedial action scheme, or a
manually executed remedial action plan. It can be defined with one or more stages (to
simulate the cascading effects of RASs).


2.7.2 Trigger Condition
An RAS triggering condition can have a lot of logic gates defined and connected to each
other by certain rules. This means that a gate output can connect to another gate’s input. A
triggering condition’s output can also connect to a gate’s input. Due to the complexity of
the gate logic and reusability of the triggering condition, the triggering condition is defined
separately from the RAS stage so the same triggering condition can be used by multiple

Proprietary – See Copyright Page              111                                Network Modeling
                                                                  e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

stages (or multiple triggers under the same stage) in the same RAS. This avoids defining the
same triggering condition again just because it is used by a different stage. (In
e-terraplatform 2.5, the same triggering condition must have different names.) So, an RAS
defines triggers, each of which is associated with a triggering condition and a set of
protective actions.
Each triggering condition can have one or more protective actions of varying types. If
multiple protective actions are defined for a triggering condition, they are applied together.
The TriggerCondition can also be defined as a CommunicationTrigger or as an Independent
Trigger.


2.7.3 Gate
A gate is similar to a logical gate used in the digital electronics field. Each gate has one or
more input pins and an output pin.
A simple “AND” gate is shown in the diagram below. It performs the Boolean “AND”
operation on all the inputs and the result is the output.


  Inputs              AND          Output


The RAS model supports combinations of testing gates (EQ, NE, LT, GT, LE, GE), Boolean
gates (AND, OR, NAND, EQV, NOT), and other arithmetic gates (SUM, MUL, DIV, SQR, EXP) of
the following gate input models (GateInputPins):
• Opening of a switching device is modeled as a PinSwitch.
• Branch/transformer de-energization (either end of the branch opens or both ends open)
  is modeled as a PinFlow with an association with the equipment and terminal. Flow on a
  DC Line is modeled as a PinFlow with an association with a DCLineSegment. Directional
  branch flow (which can be telemetered) is modeled as a PinFlow with an association
  with the equipment and terminal.
• Path flow is modeled as a PinBranchGroup with an association with a BranchGroup.
• Node voltage is modeled as PinVoltage with an association with a ConnectivityNode.
• Some SCADA points defined and mapped to NETMOM as “special measurements” are
  modeled as PinSpecialMeasurement with an association with a SpecialMeasurement.
• Output from another gate under the same triggering condition is modeled as a PinGate.
• Output from a triggering condition is modeled by inserting a gate input modeled as
  PinTriggerCondition.
• DC Converter Bypass/Block status is modeled as PinConverterStatus with an association
  to DCConverter. This feature is only available for e-terraplatform 3.0.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page               112                                 Network Modeling
                                                                    e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

An RAS also has functionality to make the protective action conditional to an arming status,
if available and already mapped to the SpecialMeasurement record.


2.7.4 Stage/Stage Trigger
A remedial action scheme can have multiple stages. An RAS stage trigger is associated with
a triggering condition. Each triggering condition is defined as a set of interconnected gates
with inputs and outputs. One of the gates’ outputs is designated as the triggering
condition’s output. The triggering condition is usually a logical combination of the system
conditions using the logical gates.


2.7.5 Protective Action
A protective action can be one of the following:
• Breaker open/close action modeled as ProtActSwitch with an association to Switch.
• ShuntCompensator open/close action modeled as ProtActShuntCompensator with an
  association to ShuntCompensator.
• StaticVarCompensator open/close action modeled as ProtAct StaticVarCompensator
  with an association to ShuntCompensator.
• DCPole open/close action modeled as ProtActDCPole with an association to DCPole.
• DCPole current/real power regulation modeled as ProtActDCPoleRegulation with an
  association to DCPole.
• DCController current/real power regulation modeled as ProtActDCController with an
  association to DCController.
• Network branch equipment remove/restore action modeled as ProtActACLineSegment
  with an association to ACLineSegment, ProtActSeriesCompensator with an association
  to SeriesCompensator, or ProtActTransformerWinding with an association to
  TransformerWinding.
• SynchronousMachine generation reduction modeled as a ProtActSynchronousMachine
  with an association to SynchronousMachine.
    The “Reduce To” and “Reduce By” values can come from either a SpecialMeasurement
    value or a fixed value entered by the user.
• EquivalentLoad load reduction modeled as a ProtActEnergyConsumer with an
  association to EquivalentLoad.
    The “Reduce To” and “Reduce By” values can come from either a SpecialMeasurement
    value or a fixed value entered by the user.
• SynchronousMachine remove/restore operation modeled as a
  ProtActSynchronousMachineMove with an association to SynchronousMachine.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page             113                               Network Modeling
                                                                e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

• Equivalent Load remove/restore modeled as a ProtActEnergyConsumerMove with an
  association to EquivalentLoad.
• Substation generation reduction modeled as a ProtActSubStation with an association to
  Substation.
    This is accomplished by putting units off line within the station so that the total
    generation is reduced by at least XX MW.
• SharedProtectiveAction modeled as a ProtActShared with an association to
  SharedActions.
The following items are only available for e-terraplatform 3.0:
• ShuntCompensator voltage regulation modeled as ProtActShuntCompensatorReg to set
  the target voltage with an association to ShuntCompensator. “Reduce To/By” and
  “Reduce By Percentage” are not supported.
• StaticVarCompensator voltage regulation modeled as ProtActSVCReg to set the target
  voltage with an association to ShuntCompensator. “Reduce To/By” and “Reduce By
  Percentage” are not supported.
• Transformer tap changer voltage regulation modeled as ProtActVoltTapchanger with an
  association to voltage type TapChanger. “Reduce To/By” and “Reduce By Percentage”
  are not supported.
• Transformer tap changer real power regulation modeled as ProtActPhaseShifter with an
  association to phase shifter type TapChanger. “Reduce To/By” is supported, but “Reduce
  By Percentage” is not supported.
• Transformer tap changer AVR set on/off modeled as ProtActTapchangerSet with an
  association to voltage type TapChanger.
• SynchronousMachine voltage regulation modeled as ProtActSynMachineReg with an
  association to SynchronousMachine.
• SynchronousMachine remove/restore action modeled as ProtActSynMachineMove with
  an association to SynchronousMachine.
• SynchronousMachine AGC suspension modeled as ProtActSynMachineAGC with an
  association to SynchronousMachine.
• StationReduction modeled as ProtActStationReduction with an association to
  Substation.
• Substation AGC suspension modeled as ProtActStationAGC with an association to
  Substation.
• DCConverter bypass/block status modeled as ProtActDCConverter with an association
  to DCConverter.
Note that all the protective actions defined under StageTrigger (except
SharedProtectiveAction) are private actions to the parent remedial action scheme.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page              114                                 Network Modeling
                                                                   e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

2.7.6 Shared Protective Action
All of the protective actions specific to different devices mentioned in the previous sections
can also be modeled as shared actions. Using a shared protective action definition avoids a
duplicated private protection action definition for different remedial action schemes.


2.7.7 Remedial Action Schemes in DCP
Remedial Action Schemes (RAS) are currently supported in DCP. However, it should be noted
that the following RAS-specific features are not supported:
• Arming at all levels (RAS, Stage, and all the protective actions) is not supported.
• Communication Trigger Condition is not supported.
• Only the following gate types are supported: AND, OR, NOT, GT, GE, LT, LE, EQ, and NE.
• Only the following Gate Inputs are supported: PinFlow, PinVoltage, PinBranchGroup, and
  PinGate. The absolute value for PinFlow is not supported.
• Only the following Protective Action Types are supported:
     – ACLineSegment/SeriesCompensator/TransformerWinding (Remove/Restore)
     – EquivalentLoad/SynchronousMachine (Reduce/remove)
     – Substation: AGCsuspension
     – ShuntCapacitor/StaticVarCompensator: Remove


2.8 Operator Guide Modeling
In e-terraplatform 3.0, operator guide modeling has been merged into the RASMOM
database. Operator guide modeling in e-terrasource uses the same data structures
described in section 2.7 Remedial Action Schemes, except that only the operator guide text
can be the protective action, instead of device actions. Also, only one stage is allowed for
each operator guide RemedialActionScheme.


2.9 Dynamic Reactive Reserve Modeling
In e-terraplatform 3.0, Dynamic Reactive Reserve Modeling has been merged into the
RASMOM database. Dynamic Reactive Reserve Modeling in e-terrasource has not been
implemented completely.


2.10 Network Parameter in Per Unit Support
The CIM standard defines many network parameters in engineering units, such as Ohms
and Siemens, which e-terrasource follows in the metadata definition. However, many

Proprietary – See Copyright Page             115                                Network Modeling
                                                                 e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

companies model these parameters in per unit (p.u.). These parameters then have to be
transformed from per unit to engineering units during an EMS to e-terrasource import, and
then back the other way during an e-terrasource to EMS export. For those who are familiar
with parameters in the per unit system, it is very hard to view them in engineering units.
They could also be confused with e-terrasource parameters in engineering units while the
same parameters, in per unit, appear in overview displays. Because of this, a parameter
conversion function is added to e-terrasource that users can enter and view parameters in
both engineering unit and per unit. The conversion is automatically performed by the
corresponding workspace trigger function.
The following devices have parameters in per unit added side-by-side with the existing
parameters.
• ACLineSegment/SeriesCompensator/Conductor: BCHPU, B0CHPU, G0CHPU,GCHPU,
  RPU, R0PU,XPU,X0PU, BaseMVAPU, BaseKVPU, CalculateEngineeringFromPU
• EquivalentBranch: RPU, R0PU,XPU,X0PU, BaseMVAPU, BaseKVPU,
  CalculateEngineeringFromPU
• EquivalentShunt: BPU, B0PU,GPU,G0PU, BaseMVAPU, BaseKVPU,
  CalculateEngineeringFromPU
• SynchronousMachine: RPU, R0PU,XPU, X0PU, XQuadSubtransPU, XQuadSyncPU,
  XQuadTransPU, BaseMVAPU, BaseKVPU, CalculateEngineeringFromPU
• TransformerWinding: BPU, B0PU, B0ShuntPU, BMagSatPU,BMagPU, GPU,
  G0PU,G0ShuntPU,GMagPU, RPU, R0PU,RGroundPU, XPU, X0PU,XGroundPU, BaseMVAPU,
  BaseKVPU, CalculateEngineeringFromPU
Note that DCLineSegment can only have parameters in engineering unit.
In addition, two base values, BaseMVAPU and BaseKVPU, are added for the parameter
conversion. The default value for BaseMVAPU is 100 MVA and the baseKV for the BaseKVPU.
The CalculateEngineeringFromPU flag indicates the original data source, from engineering
unit or per unit. It also triggers the proper parameter conversion based on the data source.
The user interface will also grey out the parameters converted from the source. For
example, if the data is from per unit, the engineering unit parameter will be greyed out
since it is converted from per unit.
During an e-terrasource to e-terraplatform export to NETMOM, the engineering unit
parameter is converted to per unit based on 100MVA, which is the only baseMVA allowed in
the NETMOM database for GE’s EMS system.


2.11 Network Data Export Order
Four flags in the NetworkConfiguration table control the export order of
GeographicalRegion (CO), SubGeographicalRegion (DV), LoadArea (LDAREA), and other
records. For the first three record types, the export instance is in alphanumeric order if the
corresponding flag (alphasortco, alphasortfv, and alphasortldarea) is set to True. The last
flag (alphasortothers) applies to other records, including:

Proprietary – See Copyright Page              116                                Network Modeling
                                                                  e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

•   ShuntCompensator (CP)
•   EquivalentLoad (LD)
•   Switch (CB)
•   SynchronousMachine (UN)
•   ACLineSegment/SeriesCompensator (LN/ZBR)
•   PowerTransformer (XFMR)
•   TransformerWinding (XF)
•   Substation (ST)
•   StaticVarCompensator (SVS)
•   AuxiliaryLoad (AUX)
•   Line (LINE)
•   HostControlArea (AREA)
•   MonitoredGroup (MONGRP)
•   ConnectivityNode (ND)
•   DCPole (POLE)
•   DCConverter (DCCNV)
•   DCLineSegment (DCLN)
The following records are exported based on their sort order:
• BranchLimitPriority (BRLIM)
• Different operational limit set
  (LNLIM/LNLIMA/ZBLIM/ZBLIMA/XFLIM/XFLIMA/NDLIM/NDLIMA)
For exported records that do not have a SortOrder flag, the default sort order is
alphanumeric for the following records:
•   AccuracyClass (ACURCY)
•   NetworkAlarm (CAT)
•   LoadType (LDTY)
•   VoltageLimitSet (VLIM)
•   Different curves (TAB)
•   Different schedules (SKED)
•   DCController (DCCTL)
•   SpecialMeasurement (SPMEAS)
•   SumMeasurement (SUMM)
•   AbnormalDate (ABDATE)
BaseVoltage (VL) is exported based on the voltage nominal value. If the SortOther flag is set
to True, VoltageLevel (KV) is exported based on the sort order; otherwise the base voltage
nominal value is used. Curve/schedule data points and related records are sorted based on
EMS network model requirements.
The export order of ContingencyGroup (CONGRP), Ctg_CtgGroup (CTGRP), and Contingency
(CTG) is decided by the alphasortctgs flag in the ContingencyConfiguration table. If the flag
is set to true, the CTGS records are exported alphanumerically. Otherwise, they are sorted
by SortOrder.

Proprietary – See Copyright Page             117                                Network Modeling
                                                                 e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

For RAS records, RemedialActionScheme and TriggerCondition are exported based on the
SortOrder. Stage and StageTrigger are exported based on the Priority attribute.
Most of the Dynamic Rating records are exported based on the order of EMSName. Season
is exported based on the start time.


2.12 Network Model Validation Rules
Many of the network model validation rules are implemented in the attribute and
association definitions of the metadata entity such as data range, string length, and
association cardinality. Those network model rules are enforced during data entry. In
addition to those, the following rules are defined in the network validation modules, which
are only triggered as part of full validation and network model validation.
• ACLineSegment_TwoTerminals: ACLineSegment can only have two terminals.
• ACLine_NearAndFarTerminal: ACLineSegment only has one near and one far terminal.
• AreaLoadCurve_Unique: AreaLoadCurve EMSName should be globally unique.
• AuxLoadVoltLimitCurve_Unique: AuxLoadVoltLimitCurve EMSName should be globally
  unique.
• AuxiliaryLoad_OneTerminal: AuxiliaryLoad can only have one terminal.
• BaseVoltage_Unique: BaseVoltage EMSName should be globally unique.
• BusBarSection_OneTerminal: BusBarSection can only have one terminal.
• Company_Unique: EMSName should be globally unique.
• ConnectivityNode_EMSNameLength: AC Node EMSName can only have four characters
  while DC can have eight characters.
• ContingencyConfig_OneRow: There is one instance of ContingencyConfiguration.
• DCConverter_MinExtinctionAngleLessThanMaxExtinctionAngle: DCConverter minimum
  extinction angle should be less than the maximum extinction angle.
• DCConverter_MinFiringAngleLessThanMaxFiringAngle: DCConverter minimum firing
  angle should be less than the maximum firing angle.
• DCConverter_PositiveBridgeNominalVolt: DCConverter bridge nominal voltage should
  be positive.
• DCConverter_PositiveCurrentRating: DCConverter current rating should be positive.
• DCConverter_ThreeTerminals: DCConverter should have three terminals.
• DCLineSegment_PositiveR: DC LineSegment should have positive reactance.
• EquivalentBranch_TwoTerminals: EquivalentBranch can only have two terminals.
• EquivalentLoad_OneTerminal: EquivalentLoad can only have one terminal.

Remedial Action Scheme Validation rules
• RASConfig_OneRow: RASmom Configuration should have only one row.

  but is referenced as a communication trigger condition.

• RASAnalogGate2AnalogPinError: The analog gate should not have more than two

3.2.12 HostControlArea
A host control area is defined in the EMS as an Automatic Generation Control (AGC) area.
Host control areas are at the top of a hierarchical tree that is usually associated with the
central business unit, the utility. At least one host control area must be designated as the
EMS host control area. All other host control areas must be designated as non-EMS
(external) areas. The HostControlArea class is mapped to the OPA record in GENMOM.

  Note: While not required, it is recommended that internal host control areas be ordered
  using the GenOrder property prior to external host control areas.

Whenever you define a host control area, you need to define at least one generating unit so
power exchanges can be represented and calculated properly by the e-terrageneration
and e-terratransmission applications, which account for power transactions by adjusting
unit output. In addition, you must define an area frequency measurement for the EMS host
control area.
Figure 43 illustrates the geographic alignment of the host control areas and operating
divisions of a fictitious power and light company represented in the sample EMP60 model.
The EAST host control area (with gray shading) contains one operating division, EAST. The
WEST host control area (with dotted shading) contains two operating divisions, NORTH and
SOUTH. The ECAR host control area belongs to another company.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page             142                               Generation Modeling
                                                                  e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

Figure 43. Geographic Alignment of Host Control Areas and Operating Divisions


3.2.12.1 ACE Deadband and Control Regions
Figure 44 shows how the Area Control Error (ACE) deadband and the various AGC control
regions are defined. The deadband and control regions (regulation region indicator: RRI) are
a function of the relative values of ACE and the integral of ACE. In addition, the ACE
deadband is dynamic, being a function of time.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page               143                               Generation Modeling
                                                                    e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

Figure 44. ACE Deadband and AGC Control Regions

The dynamic attribute of the ACE deadband is used to adjust the effective deadband for
AGC controls. As soon as ACE comes within the static deadband range, the dynamic
deadband is increased to its maximum value, known as the “ACE emergency assist limit”. As
long as ACE stays within the static deadband range, the dynamic deadband equals the
emergency assist level. If ACE comes out of the static deadband range and stays out, the
dynamic deadband gradually decays from the emergency assist level to the static
deadband level. The rate of decay is a function of the analyst-entered dynamic deadband
time constant, as Figure 45 illustrates.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page             144                          Generation Modeling
                                                             e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

Figure 45. ACE Deadbands and ACE Region Limits

The dynamic ACE deadband is defined as follows:
    DACEDB = ACEDB + (DT/DTMAX) * (ACEEMN - ACEDB)
where:
• DACEDB is the dynamic ACE deadband.
• ACEDB is the static ACE deadband defined in the database.
• DT is DTMAX minus the time (in seconds) for which ACE has remained outside DACEDB
  (limited between zero and DTMAX).
• DTMAX is the maximum time limit (in seconds) defined in the database.
• ACEEMN is the emergency-assist ACE level defined in the database.
Also:
    If the magnitude of ACE < ACEDB
then:
    Set DT = DTMAX, or DACEDB = ACEEMN
The integral of ACE is internally limited to a maximum value, whereas ACE itself is not.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page                 145                          Generation Modeling
                                                                 e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

3.2.12.2 Variable Frequency Bias Calculation
Variable frequency bias (VFBIAS) predicts how much the MW output of a host control area
changes for every 0.1 Hz of frequency variation that occurs in one AGC cycle. Valid values of
VFBIAS reside between the variable frequency bias low limit (VFBMIN) and the high limit
(VFBMAX).
Variable frequency bias is calculated as follows:
    VFBIAS = FBLOAD + FBGEN
where:
• FBLOAD represents the Load Contribution and is calculated as follows:
         FBLOAD = LDBIAS /1000 * SLOAD
    where LDBIAS represents the Area Load Bias, and SLOAD represents the System Load.
• FBGEN represents the Generation Contribution and is calculated as follows:
         FBGEN = DBV * DSK * SGVRES
    where DBV represents the Deadband Variable. DBV represents how the unit governors
    respond to the frequency deviation exceeding a threshold.
    DBV values reside between the unit contribution minimum (DBVMIN) and maximum
    (DBVMAX).
    The DSK term represents the Droop Scalar constant. This constant specifies how much
    of the generation frequency bias is applied to the area frequency bias.
    DSK is used to globally adjust the droop characteristics of all generators. DSK also
    models how the area’s unit governors respond to frequency deviations.
    SGVRES represents the sum of all responses from generators that are online and can
    respond in the direction of the frequency error without violating the unit regulation limit.
In the FBGEN calculation, the value of DBV changes with transitions of the absolute Actual
Frequency Deviation value (AFD) into the VFBIAS deadband region. The change in the DBV
value is determined by the transition scalar, PINC. This scalar specifies the change in
governor response as the frequency deviation continues to be greater than the threshold.
PINC affects DBV values as follows:
When absolute AFD is less than the VFBIAS deadband minimum (VFBDB1), then:
    DBV = min (DBVMIN, (DBV - PINC))
When absolute AFD exceeds the VFBIAS deadband maximum (VFBDB2), then:
    DBV = max (DBVMAX, (DBV + PINC))


Proprietary – See Copyright Page              146                               Generation Modeling
                                                                   e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

3.2.18 TransactingArea
Transacting areas are companies that can purchase or sell power among themselves.
Essentially, transacting areas are entities within a host control area that can conduct
transactions of power. Additional transacting areas can be set up for transactions with
other host control areas that have not yet been defined. The TransactingArea table is used
to model a transacting area under a host control area. The ID of a transacting area does
not need to match the ID of any other component. Each transacting area ID must be unique
within a host control area. A transacting area does not need to have physical ties with the
host control area. It is mapped to the TRA record in GENMOM.


3.2.18.1 Modeling Transaction Areas
To model transaction areas:
1. Click Generation on the toolbar and select the Transaction Contracts tree view.
2. Expand the Host control areas folder to expose its contents.
     – To add a new transaction area record, right-click the Host control area, and select
       the Insert TransactingArea option.
     – To update an existing transaction area record, click its icon.
3. Model transaction area information in the TransactingArea property sheet.


3.2.18.2 External Contract Unit Transactions
The dispatcher can use Unit Commitment (UC) or Hydro-Thermal Coordination (HTC) to
determine the desired output of external contract units for each hour of the UC study.
These outputs may then be used to automatically create transaction schedules with the
external contract units’ host control areas that represent the EMS host control area’s
portion of the generation, and have not been formally modeled as jointly owned units. This
capability is primarily used for creating schedules for the Real-Time Generation function.
External contract units have contracts that limit the level of interchange to multiples of
blocks or quantitization levels. One or many units may use the same contract. The sum of
the outputs of the units in a contract must be a multiple of the quantitization amount. For
each hour of a unit commitment study, the unit outputs are modified to correspond to the
quantitization levels of the contracts.
The dispatcher needs to specify the hours of the unit commitment study for which
schedules are to be created (the specified time must be in the future). At that time, the
dispatcher invokes the transfer from UC or HTC to the online database. This transfer
converts the contract unit outputs from UC or HTC into equivalent transaction schedules
with the contract unit’s host control area. Once the schedules are in the online scheduling
database, they are treated as any other schedule entered by the dispatcher.
Transaction type records must be defined for each external contract unit.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page              148                              Generation Modeling
                                                                  e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

3.2.18.3 Transaction Modeling Considerations
When modeling transactions, consider the following:
• Keep the number of transaction types to a minimum in the external host control areas.
• A slave transaction between an external host control area and the EMS OPA can serve
  as the slave to any number of transaction types. The same slave transaction type ID can
  serve all of the transaction types.
• Normally, in the external system, only one transaction type between host control areas
  is necessary.
• Costing information is not used for transactions in the external host control areas.
• Slave transactions are never modeled for the EMS host control area (the area being
  controlled).


3.2.19 Substation
The substation is a collection of many components and measurements, such as a
generator and its MW flow analogs.
A substation is defined within a host control area, and its name must be globally unique.
Information about substations is used by all e-terraplatform subsystems:
e-terratransmission, e-terrascada, e-terrageneration, and e-terrasimulator. It is mapped to
the PL record in GENMOM.

Startup groups specify the number of units at a plant that can be synchronized

3.2.21 ResourceController
Each substation has one or more resource controllers, which are signaled by AGC to control
the output of one or more generating units. It is mapped to the PLC record in GENMOM.


3.2.21.1 PulseCalibration
AGC uses the Pulse Calibration values to convert the desired PLC error into a control
command raise/lower pulse. A one-second pulse is equal to a “calibration” MW change
signal. The PulseCalibration table is used to specify the calibration values used in different
MW ranges.
The PulseCalibration table is constructed by entering a series of generation breakpoints
(MW) that give the Pulse Calibration (MW/sec) at the MW level specified. For MW values
between breakpoints, the calibration associated with the lower breakpoint is used.
The Pulse Calibration Raise value must be within the Raise Low Limit and Raise High Limit,
and the Pulse Calibration Lower value must be within the Lower Low Limit and Lower High
Limit. The first point of the table must have zero MWs. It is mapped to the CALTBL record in
GENMOM.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page              150                              Generation Modeling
                                                                  e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

To model resource controllers for a substation:

2. Navigate to the Substation icon for the appropriate substation and expand it.
3. Expand the Resource controllers folder (in the Station Equipment folder) to expose its
   contents.
     – To add a new resource controller record, right-click the Substation icon under which
       new resource controller is to be added and select the Insert ResourceController
       option.
     – To add multiple resource controller records, right-click the Resource controllers
       folder and select the Add Multiple Resource controller option.
4. Model resource controller information in the Resource controller property sheet.
5. Map the resource controller to the appropriate SCADA measurements and controls.


3.2.22 GeneratingUnit
Generators are components that supply power to the transmission (or distribution) network
system. A generating unit is a device defined in a substation. When a generating unit is
defined, its terminal node must be specified. The name of the device must be unique within
a substation. It is mapped to the UNIT record in GENMOM.


3.2.22.1 Fuel
This table is used to define Generation fuel types. It is mapped to the FUEL record in
GENMOM.


3.2.22.2 ForbiddenZone
Generating units with certain physical characteristics have a region of their MW output that
is not desirable for operation. For hydroelectric units, it can be a region of excessive
vibration due to cavitation. For thermal units, it can be a region of uneconomical operation
due to steam turbine valve point loading. These regions are known as forbidden zones,
prohibited operating zones, gray zones, or disallowed operating ranges. All of these are
referred to as “forbidden zones” in this document.
Forbidden zones are defined by their upper and lower bounds. These limits are given in
gross or net MW, consistent with the other MW values for the unit.
Each Forbidden Zone record represents a separate forbidden zone. Units without
telemetered forbidden zone limits can contain multiple Forbidden Zone records. Units with
telemetered forbidden zone limits can only contain one Forbidden Zone record, a restriction
enforced during validation.

Proprietary – See Copyright Page             151                              Generation Modeling
                                                                 e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

When multiple Forbidden Zone records exist, their limits must be in ascending order. The
limits do not need to be confined by the unit economic or LFC limits, but are confined by the
unit capacity limit.
Two values can be checked against the forbidden zone limits: unit basepoints and unit
desired generation. If flags have been set to enforce the forbidden zone limits in the
Economic Dispatch (ED), unit basepoints are calculated normally and then compared to the
zone limits. If unit basepoints are found within the forbidden zone, they are adjusted to one
of the zone limits based on the current generation, the calculated unrestricted limit, and the
basepoint zone crossing percentage. The basepoint zone crossing percentage is the
amount of the zone that must be crossed by the basepoint before the adjusted basepoint is
set to the zone limit, which is opposite the current generation.
The desired generation for each ResourceController (PLC) is the PLC’s basepoint plus the
PLC’s regulation component. The desired generation for a PLC with the forbidden zone
enforcement flag set is checked against the forbidden zones. If the desired generation is not
in or across a forbidden zone, the PLC is allowed to control the unit normally. If the desired
generation crosses the forbidden zone, it does not violate the LFC limit, and the time
between crossings is greater than the minimum time setting, the PLC is allowed to control
the unit across the zone. If the desired generation is in the forbidden zone, if the desired
generation is across the zone without the minimum time between the crossing being
expired, or if the current generation is too far away from the forbidden zone limit, the PLC
control is limited to the forbidden zone limit closest to the current generation.
The processing for desired generation related to forbidden zones is effective only for those
PLCs that have the flag set to enforce forbidden zone restrictions in unit controls.
An alarm is issued if the PLC is controlling a unit across a forbidden zone, and the AGC or
the PLC is suspended. An alarm is also issued when the PLC is controlling a unit across a
forbidden zone, the AGC or PLC is paused, and the time delay for the AGC or PLC to wait
before entering the suspend state is set to prevent the suspend state.
The ForbiddenZone class is mapped to the FZONE record in GENMOM.


3.2.22.3 GrossToNetActivePowerCurve
This table defines curves that are used to perform gross to net or net to gross conversions
for measurements for resource controllers, units, and records that are children of units. This
allows gross and net measurements to be used as alternates for each other. This table is
mapped to the GRSNET record in GENMOM.


3.2.22.4 IncrementalHeatRateCurve
Incremental heat rate curves are modeled for each unit whose generation type defines it as
economically dispatchable. You construct the curve by entering a series of points that give
the incremental fuel units (Mega BTU) per MWH at the MW level specified. AGC interpolates
the points linearly to determine the incremental heat rate at intermediate points.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page             152                              Generation Modeling
                                                                 e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

Incremental heat rate curves must increase monotonically between the minimum
economic dispatch point and the unit capability. An incremental heat rate curve is never
extrapolated, and must be defined over the complete range of generation. The first point of
the curve must occur at zero MWs.
Each incremental heat rate curve corresponds to a SUBSTATION and UNIT identifier. The
unit’s incremental heat rate curve is constructed as a series of points, each of which
specifies the incremental heat in MBTU per MWH that is required to maintain generation at
a specified MW level.
It is mapped to the HRATE record in GENMOM.


3.2.22.4.1 AutoSelectionCriteria
For units having multiple Incremental Heat Rate Curves (IHRCs), the IHRC in use can be
selected by the operator or criteria can be defined to support automatic selection. The
automatic selection is based on any combination of:
• Time of year
• Temperature
• Telemetered status
• Fuel in use
This table is used to hold the selection criteria. It is mapped to the HRCRIT record in
GENMOM.


3.2.22.5 OperatingShare
This table is used to define share details for a Jointly Owned Unit (JOU). It is mapped to the
SHARE record in GENMOM.


3.2.22.6 WindSpeedCurve
This table is used to model wind curves. It is mapped to the WCURVE record in GENMOM.
