4.4.6.4 Multiple Breaker Operation
In the multiple control function, a control command sequence is executed on a single
“dummy” point by the operator. The software then issues control command sequences to
multiple points.
The structure illustrated in Figure 75 is an example of a multiple breaker operation. The
Calculation record must be set to model a Multiple Control calculation.
In a multiple control sequence, the following occurs:
1. The first Command Reference record is a placeholder, and the master Command is
   never issued.
2. The Commands pointed to by subsequent Command Reference records are issued in
   sequence. Each control has an expected value set.
3. The Discrete parent of each Command reflects the change resulting from issuing the
   control.

 SUBSTN = PIRI
  DEVTYP = CB
   DEVICE = BREAKER_1
    MEAS = CTRL
     POINT = STAT
      CTRL(1) = TRIP
      CTRL(2) = CLOS
   DEVICE = BREAKER_2
    MEAS = CTRL
     POINT = STAT
      CTRL(3) = TRIP
      CTRL(4) = CLOS
   DEVICE = MASTER     DUMMY
    MEAS = CTRL      DUMMY
     POINT = STAT     DUMMY
      CTRL(5) = TRIP   DUMMY
      CTRL(6) = CLOS   DUMMY
   DEVICE = MASTER_TRIP
    MEAS = MBO2
     CTLREF = 5      (MASTER TRIP   NOT REALLY CONTROLLED)
     CTLREF = 1      (BREAKER_1 TRIP)
     CTLREF = 3      (BREAKER_2 TRIP)
   DEVICE = MASTER_CLOSE
    MEAS = MBO2
     CTLREF = 6      (MASTER CLOSE    NOT REALLY CONTROLLED)
     CTLREF = 2      (BREAKER_1 CLOSE)
     CTLREF = 4      (BREAKER_2 CLOSE)

Figure 75. Multiple Breaker Processing

If any breaker (or breakers) within a group has control inhibited by a tag or by other means,
group control is still allowed; however, the control of any individual breaker inhibited due to
tagging or some other reason is not activated. If the Area of Responsibility of a device in a

Proprietary – See Copyright Page              272                                  SCADA Modeling
                                                                  e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

multiple breaker control group is not assigned to the console attempting control of the
group, control of such breakers is inhibited. It is possible to individually control any breaker
that belongs to one or more groups.


4.4.6.5 Modeling a Simultaneous Control Sequence
To model a simultaneous control sequence:
1. Insert a Calculation record, and name it for easy identification.
    “SIMUL1” might be a good name.
2. Set the Calculation Type field to “Simultaneous Control Sequence”.

      Note: Selecting the Simultaneous Control option establishes that the record structure
      being modeled supports the operation of controls from one control relay. The Discrete,
      Command, and Data Item records must already be in place.

3. Add a Calculation Argument, and select the type as a Command reference.
4. Insert one Calculation Argument record for each Command record that has been
   modeled.
     – Assign the first Command Reference Calculation Argument record to the master
       Command record.
        The master Command record is the one that has an assignment to a telemetered
        CARD data item.
     – Assign the other Command Reference Calculation Argument records to their dummy
       Command record.


4.4.6.6 Modeling a Multiple Control Sequence
To model a multiple control sequence:
1. Insert a Calculation record, and name it for easy identification.
    “Multiple1” might be a good name.
2. Set the Calculation Type field to “Multiple Control Sequence”.

      Note: Selecting the Control Sequence option establishes that the record structure
      being modeled supports the operation of controls from multiple control relays. The
      Discrete, Command, and Data Item records must already be in place.

3. Add a Calculation Argument, and select the type as a Command reference.
4. Insert one Calculation Argument record for each Command record that has been
   modeled.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page              273                                   SCADA Modeling
                                                                   e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

     – Assign the first Command Reference Calculation Argument record to the dummy
       master Command record.
        The master Command of a multiple sequence cannot be a member of any other
        control sequence. However, the master of a simultaneous sequence is allowed to be
        a member of a multiple sequence.
     – Assign the other Command Reference Calculation Argument records to Command
       records that model control of real devices in the field.
        Each of the referenced Command records has a data item telemetered card
        assignment that supports a control operation.


4.4.7 Modeling SCADA Stale Data
Stale data is an e-terrascada 3.0 feature. It detects when an analog’s value is not changing
more than a Stale deadband within a timeframe.
To model stale data:
1. In SCADA Global Parameters, in the SCADA Parameters grouping:
     – Turn on Enable Stale Detection Processing.
     – Provide the Stale Detection Heartbeat value. It is recommended to have a value of at
       least 10.
     – Provide the maximum number of analogs for which stale detection will generate an
       event/alarm. It is recommended not to exceed 500.
     – Set how a remote site will see a stale data (suspect or remote replaced).
2. For all analogs for which this feature should be enabled:
     – In scada/scada Parameters/scada Processing parameter:
         ∗ Enable the stale data detection.
         ∗ Provide the timeframe for the stale data detection.
         ∗ Provide the deadband and the zero definition.
     – In scada/scada Alarming
         ∗ Enable/disable the alarming for the stale data detection. Note that the total
           number of analogs for which this setting is yes should be less than or equal to
           the value provided in the SCADA global parameters.
3. For all substations in which analog stale data detection is enabled, in the scada
   grouping, scada alarming:
     – The exception when at least one analog is stale.
     – The exception when no more analogs are stale (return to normal).


Proprietary – See Copyright Page              274                                 SCADA Modeling
                                                                 e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

     – The exception when one analog source is stale (an analog is not necessarily stale if a
       second source is available and not stale).
     – The exception when no analog source is stale (return to normal).
     – The category for the exceptions.


4.4.8 Modeling SCADA Bays

4.4.8.1 How to Model a Bay
To model a bay:
• Make sure that a Baytype exists in the baytype table.
• Create an Equipment Group under the Substation and link it to any existing bayType
  rather than the standard equipmentGroupType.
• Under SCADA > SCADA Bay, add the specific Bay information (optional).
• Set Bay Equipment Group in General to Yes.


4.4.8.2 Device Topology Settings
In SCADA > SCADA Bay:
• Included in Bay Topology: The device is included in the bay topology. It needs to be
  assigned to a Connectivity node (at the level of the device and analog for energy
  devices; at the level of the discrete for connectivity devices).
• Use OR for Bay Topology Connectivity: When using the standard bay topology
  processing, the connectivity status of this device is contributing in the general bay
  connectivity status using the OR Boolean operator.


4.4.8.3 Bay Settings per Bay
Specific Bay settings for a given bay (EquipmentGroup) are topologic settings.
• Bay Topology Formula #: This provides the Boolean expression of the devices’
  connectivity status to compute the bay connectivity. The result of the bay connectivity is
  the logical OR of every formula result (1 means closed/connected, 0 means opened). The
  device in the formula is specified using the device ID. The device needs to be included in
  the bay topology (‘Included In Bay Topology’ set to Yes) and needs to be a connectivity
  device (containing one discrete with SCADA Near and Far Connectivity Nodes not
  empty).


Proprietary – See Copyright Page             275                                  SCADA Modeling
                                                                 e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

4.4.8.4 Bay Settings General (BayType)
The settings on the BayType are common to all bays that use this type.
Only BayTypes are imported from/exported to SCADAMOM.
• Hierarchical Actions Enabled: Specifies if the children of the Equipment Group inherit
  from the Not in Service, Alarm Inhibit, and/or Test Mode. When settings are inherited,
  the children behave as if they were set to this state (e.g., Not in Service) but they do not
  appear in the appropriate e-terrascada lists. This is different from the mass actions.
• Hierarchical Tagging: Specifies if all the children of the Equipment Group inherit from
  the blocking control/setpoint tags applied on the Equipment Group. As with the
  Hierarchical Actions, the tags are not applied on the children but e-terrascada will
  check the restrictions on both measurement and parent equipment group.
• Hierarchical Selection Enabled: If enabled, e-terrascada prevents any control/setpoint
  sequence from being initiated if one is still ongoing.
• Topology Processing: Select one of the following:
     – No Topology: Topology processing is disabled.
     – Standard Topology Processing: Basic processing for topology connectivity and
       energization computation. This setting works for simple bay architecture.
         ∗ Connectivity: AND of all the topological devices’ connectivity statuses in the bay.
           If Use OR for Bay Topology Connectivity is set, e-terrascada will use the OR
           operator rather than AND.
         ∗ Energization:
           - GROUNDED if one of the device is grounded
           - DEAD if all devices are dead
           - LIVE if one device is live
           - UNKNOWN if one device is unknown.
     – Standard Formula Topology Processing: This setting has the same energization
       process as Standard Topology Processing but it uses the formulas defined in the
       Equipment Group rather than the basic connectivity computation (see section 4.4.8.3
       Bay Settings per Bay).
     – Custom Topology Processing: Uses the processing defined in the scada custom
       calculation.

4.4.9.1 Block Load Shed Modeling on Terminals and Power System Resources
The following properties may be included on any modeled terminal or power system
resource. The properties identify the terminal or power system resource as containing a
load measurement to be populated within the LOADSHED database.
The following Block Load Shed related properties are located under the “Block Load Shed”
property group:
• Block Load Shed Load: Set to Yes if this record is associated with a Load within Load
  Shed.
• Block Load Shed Voltage Reduction: Set to Yes if this record is associated with a Voltage
  Reduction Load within Load Shed.
• Block Load Shed External Point: Set to Yes if this record is used to model a Load with an
  externally associated discrete. If this flag is enabled, a child Block Load Shed Point
  record is expected to be modeled.
• Block Load Shed Local: Set to Yes if this record has a locally defined Load Shed discrete.
• Block Load Shed Duplicate: Set to Yes if the block load shed information is to be
  duplicated into a special Block Load Shed level.
• Block Load Shed Test: Set to Yes if this record is to be copied into the Block Load Shed
  Test application.
• Block Load Shed Percent: The percentage of load estimated to be shed by the
  associated load.
• Block Load Shed Area: The name of the Area Of Responsibility to be used for Block Load
  Shed operations.
• Block Load Shed Customers: The number of customers affected by shedding this load.
• Block Load Shed Group: The Block Load Shed group to which this record is associated.
• Block Load Shed Level: The Block Load Shed level to which this record is associated.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page            277                                  SCADA Modeling
                                                                e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

• Block Load Shed Timeout: The supervisory control timeout for associated Block Load
  Shed controls.
• Block Load Shed Peak MW: The Load Shed Peak MW value associated with this load.


4.4.9.2 Block Load Shed Point (BLSPT)
This record may be modeled under a power system resource or under a child terminal of
the power system resource. If the Block Load Shed Point is associated with an AC Line
Segment or Series Compensator, the Block Load Shed Point record must be modeled under
the near or far terminal.
This record provides a reference to an externally located discrete status point (the discrete
is not modeled under this power system resource).
The following associations are defined on this record:
• Discrete: The externally located discrete status point.
• Terminal: A reference to the parent terminal under which this record is modeled.
• Power System Resource: A reference to the parent power system resource under which
  this record is modeled.
The following properties are defined on this record:
• Percentage: The estimated percentage of load affected by the trip of the external status
  point.
• Customers Affected: The number of customers affected when the external load is shed.
• Command Timeout: The control timeout period in seconds when a shed is issued for the
  external status point.


4.4.9.3 Block Load Shed Duplicate (BLSDUP)
This record indicates the level and group to which the load information is duplicated into a
second level within the area specified in Block Load Shed Area of the parent terminal or
power system resource.
The following associations are defined on this record:
• Terminal: A reference to the parent terminal under which this record is modeled.
• Power System Resource: A reference to the parent power system resource under which
  this record is modeled.
The following properties are defined on this record:
• Load Shed Group: The Block Load Shed group (within the level) to which this device
  belongs.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page             278                                  SCADA Modeling
                                                                 e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

• Load Shed Level: The number of the Block Load Shed level to which this device is to be
  duplicated (i.e., if this is the fourth level modeled under the Block Load Shed Area,
  specify 4).

5. Simulation Modeling
The e-terrasource model is based upon the industry standard IEC-61970 CIM model. The
CIM model has been extended to support data modeling for e-terrasimulator (DTS). It
supports DTSMOM, which includes the modeling of relays and prime movers, and DYDEF
(default data to be used when the actual values are not available) models in
e-terraplatform.

Simulation modeling can be performed from several different types of displays, depending
on the task at hand.

  Note: The screenshots this chapter are based on a User Domain selection of DTSMOM,
  DYDEF, and related Domain Sets. For more details, see section 1.4.5 Initialize Domain Sets
  for e-terraplatform Version.

5.2 Simulation Model
This section describes how to model components that are used by the e-terrasimulator
subsystem of e-terraplatform.
Background information, technical topics, and modeling procedures are discussed for each

5.2.1 Simulation Reference Tables
The Simulation Reference tables are:
• Detailed Steam Turbine Default Values: A set of default values used for the modeling of
  a detailed steam turbine.
• Feed-Water Gain and Fuel-Air Gain tables: Two 8 x 8 tables, used by the boiler of a
  detailed steam turbine.
• Simulation Configuration: One set of general parameters used by the simulator.
• Simulation Configuration Modeling Title: Entity used to enter the Modeler notes.
• Simulation Configuration Title: Entity used to enter the Model description.
• Synchrocheck Type: Entity representing a type of Synchrocheck for the Synchro-Check
  Relays.


5.2.1.1 Detailed Steam Turbine Default Values
Most of the default values are defined directly in the Metamodel. However, for the detailed
steam turbine modeling, there are two default sets of values depending on the nature of
the control of the turbine. As explained in section 5.2.2.5.4 Modeling a New Detailed Steam

Turbine, a boiler can have a coordinated control with its turbine; the coordination is then

5.2.1.2 Feed-Water Gain

  Note: The feed-water gain is mapped to the DTSMOM FWX and DTSMOM FWY classes.

The principal components that affect boiler steaming response are the fuel dynamics, the
boiler firing air driven by the fans, and the feed water pumps and their controls. These are
approximately represented by two parallel paths: one path has a slower lag dynamic, while
the other has a faster oscillatory response characteristic. Each simulation path has a
function that represents change of steaming capability due to changes of auxiliary device
capability with unit voltage and frequency.
The slower path represents the Fuel-Air Gain components, and the faster path represents
the Feed-Water components. These paths do not correspond directly to the fuel or
feed-water components or their controls, but they have been chosen to obtain response
characteristics of more-detailed boiler and equipment response analyses.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page              289                               Simulation Modeling
                                                                  e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

5.2.1.2.1 Modeling a New Feed-Water Gain
There are 64 (8 x 8) sets of Feed-Water Gain values. These can be inserted directly from the
Grid Displays.

  Note: The feed-water gain entity has some FeedWaterGain Validation Rules defined.


5.2.1.3 Fuel-Air Gain

  Note: The fuel-air gain is mapped to the DTSMOM FAX and DTSMOM FAY classes.

As explained earlier, the principal components that affect boiler steaming response are the
fuel dynamics, the boiler firing air driven by the fans, and the feed water pumps and their
controls. These are approximately represented by two parallel paths: one path has a slower
lag dynamic, while the other has a faster oscillatory response characteristic.
The slower path represents the fuel-air components.


5.2.1.3.1 Modeling a New Fuel-Air Gain
There are 64 (8 x 8) sets of Fuel-Air Gain values. These can be inserted directly from the Grid
Displays.

  Note: The fuel-air gain entity has some FuelAirGain Validation Rules defined.

The generation dynamics used by the simulator consist of the following types of turbines:

5.2.2.1 Combustion Turbine

  Note: The combustion turbine is mapped to the DTSMOM GAST class.

The combustion turbine model simulates the dynamic response of a single-shaft
combustion turbine-generator.

                                                                                                  voltage


Figure 87. Combustion Turbine Model

The combustion turbine model has the following components:
• Load reference motor (speed changer)
• Frequency regulator
• Governor deadband
• Deration due to temperature: When you define your model, you specify the reference
  temperature at which the combustion turbine was designed to operate and the ambient
  temperature.
• Output deration due to off-nominal frequency and voltage: You must specify output
  sensitivities to variations from the nominal frequency and voltage, and the voltage and
  frequency above which there is no deration.
These components are used to adjust the maximum power output from the combustion
turbine model based on a high or low ambient temperature. The maximum power output
for each combustion turbine is calculated on the basis of the maximum output, the
difference between the ambient temperature and the reference temperature, and the
turbine’s sensitivity to changes in temperature. If the ambient temperature entered is
greater than the reference temperature, the maximum power output is derated. On the

Proprietary – See Copyright Page                                          292                                      Simulation Modeling
                                                                                                     e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

other hand, if the ambient temperature is less than the reference temperature, the
maximum power output is increased.

  Note: The maximum power output (taking into account the effects of temperature) is
  calculated once when the combustion turbine is initialized, and it remains static until the
  combustion turbine is manually marked as uninitialized or a new copy of the DTSMOM
  database is brought online.

By setting a different ambient temperature for a particular combustion turbine, the
e-terrasimulator (DTS) instructor can simulate different geographical and weather
conditions for training scenarios.


5.2.2.1.1 Modeling a New Combustion Turbine
To model a new combustion turbine:
1. Ensure that synchronous machines are already associated with their Voltage Levels.
2. From the Network Model tree, browse to an existing synchronous machine and insert a
   new CombustionTurbine record.

  Note: A combustion turbine can be part of a Combined Cycle Plant. In addition, the
  combustion turbine entity has some CombustionTurbine Validation Rules defined.


5.2.2.2 Drum Boiler

  Note: The drum boiler is mapped to the DTSMOM BOIL class.

The boiler controls subsystem, shown in Figure 88, contains controls for boiler pressure,
fuel/air mixture, and feedwater. Inputs to this subsystem are throttle pressure from the
boiler (or MW demand from coordinated control), MW error from coordinated control (see
section 5.3.9.1.1 DST Coordinated Control Subsystem), and terminal voltage and frequency

The boiler controls subsystem includes the following components:
• Pressure Controller: The pressure controller block simulates a proportional-integral
  derivative (PID) controller whose input is the difference between the throttle pressure
  error and the MW error. Gain constants are setpoints on the controller at the plant.
• Fuel/Air Controls: The fuel/air control block simulates the delay in delivering fuel to the
  boiler and the deration of the fuel supply system’s output caused by off-nominal voltage
  and frequency.
• Feedwater Auxiliary Controls: The feedwater auxiliary control block represents controls
  on the boiler water supply. A model of a proportional-integral derivative (PID) controller
  includes output deration due to off-nominal voltage and frequency. The proportional
  and integral gain constants for the feedwater controller and the time constant for the
  feedwater pump are setpoints defined for the equipment at the plant.
The sum of the fuel/air and feedwater outputs is the total boiler charging, which is input to
the boiler subsystem.
A parameter named “DrumBoilerController” is used to indicate the type of control system in
use. For drum-type boilers, DrumBoilerController is set equal to one, and feedwater controls
are not a part of the system. Once-through boiler arrangements are modeled by setting
DrumBoilerController equal to zero. Depending on the individual plant, you may be justified
in assigning DrumBoilerController a value between zero and one, but the general rule is one
for drum-type boilers and zero for once-through arrangements.
The gain constant of the turbine steam flow is usually equal to the gain constant for MW
demand from coordinated control. When the two are equal, either MW demand from


Proprietary – See Copyright Page                                                   294                                                      Simulation Modeling
                                                                                                                              e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

coordinated control or steam flow from the turbine (but not both) is used as input to the
boiler controls. If, for instance, the steam flow gain constant is one, the steam flow from the
turbine is not used as a feedback value to the boiler controls.


5.2.2.2.1 Modeling a New Drum Boiler
To model a new drum boiler:
1. From the Detailed Steam Turbines tree view, insert a new DrumBoiler record.
2. Link this new drum boiler to the detailed steam turbine record.
    For more information, see section 5.2.2.5.4 Modeling a New Detailed Steam Turbine.

  Note: The drum boiler entity has some DrumBoiler Validation Rules defined.

The heat recovery boiler is a type of boiler used in a combined cycle plant.

  Note: None of the arguments of the heat recovery boiler is used by the simulator, except

Figure 89. Hydroelectric Turbine Model

The hydroelectric turbine model has five main components:
• Load reference motor (speed changer)
• Frequency regulator
• Governor backlash: Deadband is not used because of the large inertia of the gates.
• Gate positioning equipment: A change in gate position causes a transient oscillation
  response in turbine output. In a hydroelectric plant, this response is partially damped by
  a transient regulation adjustment, a fine-tuning parameter that is unique for each site.
  In the model, the transient regulation constant is used in conjunction with the frequency
  regulation constant to determine the gate’s servomotor position and limits. The
  oscillations are simulated with the user-defined transient time constant. Once the new
  gate position is determined, it is checked against user-specified rate and position limits.
• Non-instantaneous response of the water in the penstock after the gate position has
  changed. You must specify the water time constant.


5.2.2.4.1 Modeling a New Hydro Turbine
To model a new hydro turbine:
1. Ensure that synchronous machines are already associated with their Voltage Levels.
2. From the Network Model tree, browse to an existing synchronous machine and insert a
   new HydroTurbine record.

  Note: The Hydro Turbine entity has some HydroTurbine Validation Rules defined.

5.2.2.5 Steam Turbine

  Note: The steam turbine is mapped to the DTSMOM GST or DTSMOM DST class, depending
  on the model of the steam turbine.

Boiler-turbine steam plants can be modeled using the “generic” steam turbine (GST) model,
or the “detailed” steam turbine (DST) model:
• The GST model assumes a constant throttle pressure, typically 1.0 per unit megawatts.
  For further information, see section 5.2.2.5.1 Overview of a Generic Steam Turbine.
• The DST model makes no assumption about throttle pressure. It contains submodels of
  boiler dynamics and throttle pressure variations. For further information, see section
  5.2.2.5.3 Overview of a Detailed Steam Turbine.
In a typical system, between four and eight of the largest fossil-fired units should be
modeled using the DST model. The remaining units should be modeled using the GST model.
Nuclear plants can be modeled only with the generic steam model. Both models support
dual-shaft.


5.2.2.5.1 Overview of a Generic Steam Turbine
The generic steam turbine (GST) model is used to simulate fossil-fired and nuclear steam
plants. The model does not include steam supply system dynamics, and it assumes that
throttle pressure is constant.
The generic steam turbine model is composed of two subsystems, described in the
following sections:
• 5.3.10.1 GST Governor Subsystem
• 5.3.10.2 GST Turbine Subsystem


5.2.2.5.2 Modeling a New Generic Steam Turbine
To model a new generic steam turbine:
1. Ensure that synchronous machines are already associated with their Voltage Levels.
2. From the Network Model tree, browse to an existing synchronous machine and insert a
   new Steam Turbine record.
3. Update the “IsDetailedSteamTurbine” flag of the newly created steam turbine to False.

  Note: A generic steam turbine can be part of a Combined Cycle Plant. In addition, the
  Steam Turbine entity has some SteamTurbine Validation Rules defined.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page            297                               Simulation Modeling
                                                                e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

5.2.2.5.3 Overview of a Detailed Steam Turbine
The detailed steam plant model is used to simulate the dynamic response of a fossil-fired
steam plant, including details of its steam supply and control systems.
The Detailed Steam Turbine Model is composed of five subsystems, described in the
following sections:
• 5.3.9.1.1 DST Coordinated Control Subsystem
• 5.3.9.1.2 DST Boiler Controls Subsystem
• 5.3.9.1.3 DST Turbine Controls Subsystem
• 5.3.9.1.4 DST Boiler Subsystem
• 5.3.9.1.5 DST Governor Subsystem


5.2.2.5.4 Modeling a New Detailed Steam Turbine
To model a new detailed steam turbine:
1. Ensure that synchronous machines are already associated with their Voltage Levels.
2. From the Network Model tree, browse to an existing synchronous machine and insert a
   new Steam Turbine record.
3. Update the “IsDetailedSteamTurbine” flag of the newly created steam turbine to True.
4. From the Detailed Steam Turbines tree view, link the newly created Steam Turbine
   record to a new drum boiler.
    To do so, insert a new Drum Boiler record, if it was not created before. From the steam
    turbine, insert a new Steam Turbine – Boiler Association record.
5. Finally, from the SteamSup_SteamTurb record, add the association with the new drum
   boiler.

  Note: The detailed steam turbine entity has some SteamTurbine Validation Rules defined.


5.2.2.6 Steam Turbine – Boiler Association
The SteamSup_SteamTurb record represents the link between a steam turbine and its
boiler (see section 5.2.2.5.4 Modeling a New Detailed Steam Turbine or section 5.2.2.7.1
Modeling a New Combined Cycle Plant).

  Note: The SteamSup_SteamTurb entity has some SteamSup_SteamTurb Validation Rule
  defined.

5.2.2.7 Combined Cycle Plant

  Note: The combined cycle plant is mapped to the DTSMOM CCYC class.

The basic design of a combined cycle mode in the simulator is a mathematical link between
multiple Combustion Turbines and a single fossil unit (Steam Turbine). The total output of
the combustion turbines is used to modify an input to the steam turbine unit prime mover
(throttle pressure setpoint, TPSP). The mathematical linkage between the total output MW
of the combustion turbines and the throttle pressure setpoint of the steam turbine is shown
in Figure 90.


Figure 90. Combustion Turbine(s) Output vs. Throttle Pressure Setpoint of the Steam Turbine

Define two points:
     – (gtMin, gstTpspiMin)
     – (gtMax, gstTpspiMax)
Where:
     – gtMin: This is the total minimum combustion turbine(s) output, which has an effect
       on the steam turbine.
     – gtMax: This is the total maximum combustion turbine(s) output, after which total
       combustion turbine(s) output has no more effect on the steam turbine.
     – gstTpspiMin: This is the throttle pressure setpoint of the steam turbine with the total
       combustion turbine(s) output less than “gtMin” MWs.
     – gstTpspiMax: This is the throttle pressure setpoint constant.

                                                                      e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide

turbine(s) output of “X” p.u. MWs is:

5.2.2.7.1 Modeling a New Combined Cycle Plant
To model a new combined cycle plant:
1. Ensure that the GeneratingUnit is already associated with a synchronous machine,
   which is also already associated with its turbine (Combustion Turbine or Steam Turbine).
2. From the Combined Cycle Plants and Boilers tree view, insert a new
   CombinedCyclePlant record and a new Heat Recovery Boiler record.
3. From the Network Model tree, browse to existing generating units and add to them the
   association with the newly created CombinedCyclePlant record.
4. Go back to the Combined Cycle Plants and Boilers tree view. From the associated steam
   turbine, insert a new Steam Turbine – Boiler Association record associated with the
   newly inserted Heat Recovery Boiler record.
5. From the combustion turbine(s) associated with the new combined cycle plant, add the
   association with the same Heat Recovery Boiler record.

  Note: A combined cycle plant is associated with only a set of steam or combustion
  turbines. It can also just be associated with one steam turbine. In addition, the combined
  cycle plant entity has some CombinedCyclePlant Validation Rules defined.

5.2.4.1 Current Relay

  Note: The current relay is mapped to the DTSMOM OCRY class.

The current relay model is the most complex relay model in e-terrasource. It includes
considerations for time-until-trip as a function of current, a method of accumulating
incremental shifts in the relay disk device, automatic reclosure processing, and breaker
action schedules.
Electro-mechanical relay devices protect transmission lines. When the current in a line
exceeds a minimum pickup current, a disk begins to turn. As long as the current in the line
exceeds the pickup current, the disk advances incrementally until either the relay trips or
the current drops below the pickup current. When the current in the line drops below the
pickup current (with or without the aid of a circuit breaker trip), the disk unwinds at a linear
rate until it reaches the zero position or until the current in the line once again exceeds the
pickup current.
Changes in disk position are computed on the basis of present disk position and current.
When the current exceeds the pickup current, the disk position changes incrementally,
according to the inverse time curve. For this reason, only the current relay with the
“InverseTimeFlag” flag set to True is processed.


Figure 91. Current Relay Inverse Time Curve Model

Proprietary – See Copyright Page               303                               Simulation Modeling
                                                                   e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

The rate at which the relay disk advances is defined mathematically by what is known as
the “inverse-time characteristic”. The curve representing the inverse-time characteristic is
called an “inverse-time curve”. This curve is defined as follows:

                                       1=
                                            (              1−           )
Where:
     – “TimeDelay1” is the trip point that corresponds to the sustained current.
     – “K” is the inverse-time characteristic constant.
     – “CurrentLimit1” is the sustained current being sensed.
     – “Pickup” is the current relay’s user-defined minimum pickup current.
The user models each current relay’s sustained current-to-trip point correspondence and
minimum pickup current value. These user-specified values determine “K”, the constant in
the inverse-time characteristic for that relay, as follows:
                              =          1×(                  1−            )
Figure 91 illustrates how a user-defined sustained current “CurrentLimit1” and a minimum
pickup current “Pickup” define a trip point “TimeDelay1”. The figure also shows the current
“InstantTrip” that causes an instantaneous trip.
How long does it take the relay to trip? That depends on the current in the line and the
current relay’s modeled values. If the line current exceeds the current relay’s pickup value
by only a little, the circuit breaker might not trip for an hour or more. On the other hand, if
the current is at the relay’s “InstantTrip” level, the breaker can trip instantaneously.
The reset time specified for a current relay is the time it takes the relay to unwind from the
trip position to the zero disk position. The reset time is used to calculate the linear rate at
which the relay disk resets whenever the current falls below the pickup value.
Directional current relays only increment the disk position when the sensed current flows in
the specified direction. When current is flowing in the opposite direction, the disk rewinds
regardless of the magnitude of the reverse current.


5.2.4.1.1 Modeling a New Current Relay

  Caution: Only the current relays with the “InverseTimeFlag” flag set to True are processed.

To model a new current relay:
1. Ensure that the ACLineSegments, SeriesCompensators, and Switches are already
   associated with some Voltage Levels. Also, ensure that the transformer windings are
   already associated with Power Transformers.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page                304                              Simulation Modeling
                                                                   e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

2. From the Network Model tree, browse to the existing Substations:
     – If the current relay is protecting a line, browse to an ACLineSegments or
       SeriesCompensators under Voltage Levels.
     – If the current relay is protecting a transformer, browse to a transformer winding
       under a power transformer.
3. From the equipment, insert the new “CurrentRelay” flag and associate it with an existing
   terminal.
To associate the newly created current relay with its breakers:
1. From the current relay, insert a new Relay – Switch Association record for each breaker.
2. From the new ProtectionEq_Switch record, add the association with an existing switch.
The following functionalities apply for modeling a current relay:
• Model a current relay that senses current in or around a transformer that is tapped on a
  bus or line.
• Link this current relay to a logical set of switching devices, with at least one of them.
• If the current relay is protecting a line, the line isolation scheme applies (for more
  details, see section 5.3.3 Current Relay: Line Isolation Scheme).
• If the current relay is protecting a transformer, the transformer isolation applies (for
  more details, see section 5.3.5 Current Relay: Transformer Isolation).
• Define a three-timepoint Reclose Schedule for this current relay’s set of switching
  devices (for more details, see section 5.3.6 Current Relay: Reclose Schedule).
• In addition, the current relay can have the following functionalities:
     – A current relay can be directional (for more details, see section 5.3.2 Current Relay:
       Directional).
     – A current relay and/or its breakers can be associated with a Reclose Schedule (for
       more details, see section 5.3.6 Current Relay: Reclose Schedule).

  Note: The current relay entity has some CurrentRelay Validation Rules defined.


5.2.4.2 Frequency Relay

  Note: The frequency relay is mapped to the DTSMOM FRY class.

The frequency relay model checks for under- and over-frequency in the system. When the
frequency at a node violates the user-specified minimum or maximum trip frequency for a
period longer than the user-specified delay time, any breakers controlled by that relay are
brought to one of three user-specified states: open, closed, or no change.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page              305                                 Simulation Modeling
                                                                    e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

There is an option to lock out the relay after it trips. When a relay is locked out, the
simulator cannot take any action on the relay or any of the breakers it controls until the
user-specified lockout time has elapsed.


5.2.4.2.1 Modeling a New Frequency Relay
To model a new frequency relay:
1. Ensure that the Switches are already associated with some Voltage Levels.
2. From the Network Model tree, browse to the existing Substations, and insert the new
   FrequencyRelay record. Associate the new relay with an existing terminal.
To associate the newly created frequency relay with its breakers:
1. From the frequency relay, insert a new Relay – Switch Association record for each
   breaker.
2. From the new ProtectionEq_Switch record, add the association with an existing switch.
The following functionalities apply for modeling a frequency relay:
• A frequency relay can be locked out (for more details, see section 5.3.8 Relay: Lockout).
• A frequency relay can have load restoration logic (see section 5.3.7 Frequency Relay:
  Load Restoration).

  Note: The frequency relay entity has some FrequencyRelay Validation Rules defined.


5.2.4.3 Generic Under-Frequency Relay

  Note: The generic under-frequency relay is mapped to the DTSMOM GENUFR class.

The generic under-frequency relay model can be defined at a company level or at a
substation level. The material in this section describes the generic under-frequency relay
model at a company level, but it can also be applied to the substation level.

  Caution: The Generic Under-Frequency Relay model can only be defined to be either at
  company levels or substation levels. It cannot be defined to be at both levels at the same
  time.

It is used to simulate LOADSHED by scaling a company’s load as a function of frequency.
This relay model does not replace, but augments, the existing over-/under-frequency relay
model. Through these two models, the modeler can specify the under-frequency protection
strategy of the company.
Each relay has three frequency breakpoints and three corresponding load-scaling factors.
When the frequency at a company drops below a frequency breakpoint, the loads defined
for that company are scaled by the corresponding load-scaling factor.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page             306                               Simulation Modeling
                                                                 e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

Load-scaling factors take effect independently as the frequency drops past the breakpoints.
For example:
• To scale a parent company load by 10% at Frequency1, LoadScale1 is set to 0.9000.
• To scale the same unadjusted parent load another 10% at Frequency2, LoadScale2 is
  set to 0.8100 (0.90*0.90).
• To scale parent load another 10% at Frequency3, LoadScale3 is set to 0.7210
  (0.81*0.90).
In this way, the scaling factors independently scale the parent load.
In e-terrasimulator, the frequency at each load point is evaluated prior to power flow
processing. e-terrasimulator finds which island the load point is in, and uses the island
frequency to determine the correct load-scaling multiplier. This load scalar is obtained from
the generic under-frequency relay model for the load point’s parent company.
If the per-unit frequency is above the Frequency1 value, the multiplier is set to 1.0. If the
per-unit frequency is below the Frequency1 value, a load scalar (LoadScale1, LoadScale2, or
LoadScale3) is used to reduce the load. The resultant load is then used in the power flow
calculation.

  Caution: In e-terrasimulator, frequency is constant within an electrical island,
  independent of company boundaries. If a company spans more than one electrical island,
  only the company’s loads that are in the low-frequency island are scaled.


5.2.4.3.1 Modeling a New Generic Under-Frequency Relay
To model a new generic under-frequency relay:
1. Ensure that the Geographical Region and Substations have been previously modeled.
2. From the Generic Under-Frequency Relay tree, insert a new
   GenericUnderfrequencyRelay record.
     – If the generic under-frequency relay is modeled at the company level, add the
       association with an existing geographical region.
     – If the generic under-frequency relay is modeled at the substation level, add the
       association with an existing substation (“Equipment Container”).

  Note: The generic under-frequency relay entity has some GenericUnderfrequencyRelay
  Validation Rules defined.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page             307                               Simulation Modeling
                                                                 e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

5.2.4.4 Generic Unit Frequency Relay

  Note: The Generic Unit Frequency relay is mapped to the DTSMOM GENUNFR class and is
  only available for e-terraplatform 3.0 and later.

When e-terrasimulator (DTS) is running, the Generic Unit Frequency relay will monitor the
frequency sensed node. When a particular setting is violated, the relay will pick up and the
associated timer will be started. When the timer elapses beyond the delay setting, the relay
will trip. Once the relay is tripped, it will be locked out until it is manually reset. If, during the
delay period, the violation is removed, the corresponding timer will be reset.
To satisfy these requirements, each frequency setting has its own associated timer. Each
timer works independently and can start and reset itself when a violation for that frequency
is detected or removed. For example, If a Generic Unit Frequency Relay is modeled to have
three over frequency settings with reversed delay time (i.e., the higher the frequency, the
faster the relay trips.), a very high frequency may start three timers at the same time. Then,
if the frequency decreases while the simulation continues, one or all timers could be reset
at different times.
For those units located in a different island than relay frequency sensed nodes, the UI will
reflect that the trip becomes disabled.


5.2.4.4.1 Modeling a New Generic Unit Frequency Relay
To model a new generic under-frequency relay:
1. Ensure that the Synchronous Machines have been previously modeled.
2. From the Generic Unit Frequency Relay Tree View, insert a new
   GenericUnitfrequencyRelay record.
3. From the Network Model tree, browse to an existing Synchronous Machine that has Unit
   Isolation Breakers defined, and associate this Synchronous Machine to the new Generic
   Unit Frequency Relay.
4. Select whether you want to enable or disable the trip for this Synchronous Machine.

  Note: The generic unit frequency relay entity has some GenericUnitFrequencyRelay
  Validation Rules defined.


5.2.4.5 Impedance Relay

  Note: The impedance relay is mapped to the DTSMOM IMPRY class.

A transmission line protection scheme includes the use of impedance relays (distance
relay). Impedance relays, as part of a permissive overreaching transferred tripping scheme,
are used to trip transmission lines in the event of fault. A severe line overload condition


Proprietary – See Copyright Page                 308                                 Simulation Modeling
                                                                       e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

happens when the line voltage is significantly low and line current is dramatically high.
Under this condition, it is viewed by the impedance relays at both ends as a fault condition.
Impedance relays are used whenever overcurrent relays do not provide adequate
protection. They function even if the short circuit current is relatively low. The speed of
operation is independent of the current magnitude.
The impedance relays usually compare the impedance between the relay and the fault.
Impedance at the fault is derived by the vector product of the voltage and current at that
relay.
In simulating impedance relays in the simulator, the classical impedance characteristic
provided by a true impedance relay is used. An impedance relay compares the magnitude
of voltage at the relaying point with the magnitude of the product of the fault current and a
replica impedance inside it. The voltage at the fault point is assumed to be zero, while the
voltage at the relaying point is less than the voltage across the replica impedance . The
fault is said to be inside the reach of the relay if the voltage is detected to be less than the
voltage across the replica impedance .
The equation is:
                                             |   |<|   ×     |
Or:
                                         |             |<|       |
The replica impedance is usually user-definable for each line and is usually set as a
multiple of the impedance of the line.
During simulation, in each power flow cycle, the voltage at the sensed node of the
protected equipment and the current through the protected equipment are used to
evaluate the magnitude of           . If the measured impedance is less than the product of
the user-defined replica impedance multiplier and the actual impedance of the line, the
relay and the associated breakers are tripped.

  Note: The impedance relay is considered to be non-directional. It detects a fault in any
  direction.


5.2.4.5.1 Modeling a New Impedance Relay
To model a new impedance relay:
1. Ensure that the ACLineSegments, SeriesCompensators, and Switches are already
   associated with some Voltage Levels. Also, ensure that the transformer windings are
   already associated with Power Transformers.
2. From the Network Model tree, browse to an existing substation:
      – If the impedance relay is protecting a line, browse to an ACLineSegments or
        SeriesCompensators under Voltage Levels.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page                 309                               Simulation Modeling
                                                                     e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

     – If the impedance relay is protecting a transformer, browse to a transformer winding
       under a power transformer.
3. From the equipment, insert the new ImpedanceRelay record and associate it with an
   existing terminal.

  Caution: An Impedance Relay cannot be associated with an ACLineSegment which has its
  ZeroImpedanceLine flag set.

To associate the newly created impedance relay with its breakers:
1. From the impedance relay, insert a new Relay – Switch Association record for each
   breaker.
2. From the new ProtectionEq_Switch record, add the association with an existing switch.

  Note: The impedance relay entity has some ImpedanceRelay Validation Rules defined.


5.2.4.6 Reclose Schedule

  Note: The reclose schedule is mapped to the DTSMOM RECSK class.

A reclose schedule is a group of Reclose Sequence records that a breaker or relay follows.
The material in this section describes line reclose sequences, but it can also be applied to
other reclose schemes.
If a relay monitoring a transmission line trips, a multi-attempt reclose sequence is typical.
The first reclose attempt is almost instantaneous, the next occurs after 10 or 15 seconds,
and another occurs approximately 45 seconds after the relay trips.
You can model many different reclose schemes. Specifying reclose actions for several time
points is entirely optional. Multiple time points are typically used to model complicated
reclose schemes.
For complex bus arrangements, such as a breaker-and-a-half or a double-breaker, the first
breaker to be reclosed can be designated; this designated breaker is always processed first.
In reclose sequences, only the designated breaker is processed. The designated breaker is
processed until it successfully closes. The non-designated breakers are then closed
simultaneously, two seconds after the designated breaker closes.


5.2.4.6.1 Modeling a New Reclose Schedule
To model a new reclose schedule:
1. From the Reference Tables tree, insert a new RecloseSchedule record.
2. From this reclose schedule, insert Reclose Sequence records by defining a different
   incremental and unique RecloseStep.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page              310                               Simulation Modeling
                                                                  e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

  Note: The reclose schedule entity has some RecloseSchedule Validation Rules defined.


5.2.4.7 Reclose Sequence

  Note: The reclose sequence is mapped to the DTSMOM RECPT class.

A Reclose Schedule is defined as a combination of incremental reclose sequences. The
reclose sequence then defines the time point when the associated breaker can reclose,
based on the previous ones.


5.2.4.7.1 Modeling a New Reclose Sequence
To model a new reclose sequence:
1. From the Reference Tables tree, browse to an existing Reclose Schedule.
2. From this reclose schedule, insert a new RecloseSequence record.

  Note: The reclose sequence entity has some RecloseSequence Validation Rules defined.

5.2.4.10 Voltage Relay

  Note: The voltage relay is mapped to the DTSMOM VRY class.

Voltage relays monitor voltage at a specified node. If the voltage violates the user-specified
maximum or minimum for a period longer than the user-specified delay time, any breakers
controlled by that relay are brought to one of three designated states: open, closed, or no
change.
You can specify that the relay be locked out after it trips. If the relay is locked out, the
simulator cannot take any action on the relay or any of the breakers it controls, and the
relay is inoperative for the user-specified lockout time.


5.2.4.10.1 Modeling a New Voltage Relay
To model a new voltage relay:
1. Ensure that the Switches are already associated with some Voltage Levels.
2. From the Network Model tree, browse to an existing substation and insert the new
   VoltageRelay record.
3. Associate the new relay with an existing terminal.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page              312                                Simulation Modeling
                                                                   e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

To associate the newly created Voltage Relay with its breakers:
1. From the voltage relay, insert a new Relay – Switch Association record for each breaker.
2. From the new ProtectionEq_Switch record, add the association with an existing switch.
In addition, the voltage relay can have the following functionality:
• A voltage relay can be locked out (for more details, see section 5.3.8 Relay: Lockout).

  Note: The voltage relay entity has some VoltageRelay Validation Rules defined.


5.2.4.11 Relay – Switch Association
The ProtectionEq_Switch record represents the many-to-many association between a relay
and its breakers.
A relay can indeed be associated with more than one breaker, and a breaker can be
associated with more than one relay.
For more details, see sections 5.2.4.1.1 Modeling a New Current Relay, 5.2.4.2.1 Modeling a
New Frequency Relay, 5.2.4.5.1 Modeling a New Impedance Relay, and 5.2.4.10.1 Modeling a
New Voltage Relay.

  Note: The ProtectionEq_Switch entity has some ProtectionEq_Switch Validation Rules
  defined.


5.3 Functionality Model
This section groups some functionality that can be modeled for the simulator.


5.3.1 EMSName vs. Name
Unlike the CIM record names, e-terraplatform databases have record IDs with a specified
string length.
To use both functionalities, for some CIM records, an “EMSName” has been added to be
used by the e-terraplatform databases. If that EMS name is not defined, the e-terraplatform
record IDs are equal to a truncated Name field, based on their string length.


5.3.2 Current Relay: Directional
When the current in a line exceeds a minimum pickup current, a disk in the Current Relay
begins to turn. As long as the current in the line exceeds the pickup current, the disk
advances incrementally until either the relay trips or the current drops below the pickup
current.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page              313                               Simulation Modeling
                                                                  e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

Directional current relays only increment the disk position when the sensed current flows in
the specified direction. When current is flowing in the opposite direction, the disk rewinds
regardless of the magnitude of the reverse current.
To define a current relay to be directional, the “IsDirectional” flag should be set to True, and
the “PowerDirectionFlag” flag should be set as well.


5.3.3 Current Relay: Line Isolation Scheme
If the Current Relay is protecting a line, one of two methods can be used:
• Method 1: Link the Reclose Schedule to the current relay.
    In this scheme, certain circuit breakers can be specified as designated breakers. When
    the relay trips, all the breakers trip first. The Reclose Schedule is first activated for the
    designated breakers. Once the designated breakers close successfully, the reclose
    scheme is activated for the other breakers. There is a two-second delay between
    activations.
• Method 2: Link a unique Reclose Schedule to each of the breakers under current relay
  control.
    This allows for master and slave breakers to be specified, where a slave begins its
    Reclose Sequence only after its master has successfully reclosed. There is also a
    user-specified delay between the end of the master’s schedule and the activation of the
    slave’s schedule.


5.3.4 Current Relay: Master and Slave Breakers
If the Current Relay is protecting a line, and a Reclose Schedule has been defined for each
of its breakers, a master breaker should then be specified.
A breaker is marked as “Master” if its associated Relay – Switch Association record has its
“IsRelayMasterBreaker” flag set to True.
The following rules apply for modeling this functionality:
• Only the ProtectionEq_switch records associated with a current relay can have their
  “IsRelayMasterBreaker” flag defined.
• A current relay can only have one master breaker.
• The master breaker should have a reclose schedule with fewer Reclose Sequence points
  than the reclose schedules for the slave breakers.


5.3.5 Current Relay: Transformer Isolation
A transformer isolation scheme can be defined by linking the protecting switching devices
to a Current Relay that has a Reclose Schedule.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page               314                                Simulation Modeling
                                                                    e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

Take the example of a transformer isolation/reclosure scheme shown in Figure 92.


Figure 92. Hypothetical Transformer Isolation Scheme

Three high-voltage transmission lines lead off to other substations. These lines are
connected to the high side bus (117) by three circuit breakers:
• The preferred breaker (114117)
• The alternate breaker (115117)
• A third high-voltage circuit breaker (116117)
The high-voltage side of the transformer (T2) is connected to the high side bus by a
disconnect (117119). Similarly, the low-voltage side of the transformer is connected to the
low side bus (719) by a second disconnect (719728). Two feeders lead off of the low side bus,
connected by circuit breakers (719720 and 719721).
One possible sequence of events resulting in a hypothetical isolation scheme is as follows.
The relay trips and all the breakers around the transformer, except for the high side and low
side disconnects, open (114117, 115117, 116117, 719720, and 719721 open). These actions
correspond to the action specified at the “IsolationReclosureAction1” of each breaker.
At the first reclosure time point (specified by the first reclosure point record for this breaker
Reclose Schedule), the high side and low side disconnects open (117119 and 719728 open).
These actions correspond to the action specified at the “IsolationReclosureAction2” of each
breaker.
At the second reclosure time point, the preferred breaker (114117) closes if its source (line)
side is energized. If the preferred breaker cannot close, the alternate breaker (115117)
closes if its source side is energized. These actions correspond to the action specified at the
“IsolationReclosureAction3” of each breaker.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page               315                                Simulation Modeling
                                                                    e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

  Note: For this scheme to work as described, 114117 and 115117 must be defined as
  “Live-Line Dead-Bus”. This ensures that the transmission line is energized before the
  simulator can close in the high side bus.

If the transformer is tapped on a line, 114117 and 115117 must be defined as “Live-Bus
Dead-Line”, and the breaker node order definition must be correct with respect to bus and
line.
When making the assignments, refer to the preferred and alternate breakers’
corresponding circuit breaker records.
At the third reclosure time point (and only if either 114117 or 115117 has been successfully
closed), all other breakers close. 117119 and 719728 remain open. These actions
correspond to the action specified at the “IsolationReclosureAction4” of each breaker.
This is an example of a transformer isolation/reclosure scheme. Many different scenarios
can be modeled.


5.3.5.1 Modeling a Transformer Isolation
To model a transformer isolation:
1. Ensure that the Current Relay protecting a transformer has a Reclose Schedule and is
   associated with some Switches.
2. From the Network Model tree, browse to a Current Relay protecting a transformer.
3. For each Relay – Switch Association record associated with this relay, update the four
   isolation reclosure actions under the section “Relay Transformer Isolation Sequence” by
   selecting the following options:
     – Close
     – None
     – Open
Any Reclose Schedule used by a current relay to isolate a transformer must have at least
three reclosure points in the schedule to allow:
• High side disconnect opening
• Reclosure of preferred or alternate breaker
• Reclosure of all other breakers except low side disconnect


5.3.6 Current Relay: Reclose Schedule
A Current Relay can be associated with a Reclose Schedule. If the current relay has a
reclose schedule defined, even if its associated breakers have a different reclose schedule,
it follows the reclose schedule defined at the current relay level.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page             316                               Simulation Modeling
                                                                 e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

5.3.7 Frequency Relay: Load Restoration
After a frequency excursion causes load shedding in the form of closing/opening individual
or multiple breakers for individual loads, the load restoration relay checks the island
frequency and restore loads on an individual load basis when the frequency returns to a
value higher than a predefined threshold for longer than a specified time delay.
The following requirements are identified for implementing frequency time-based
automatic load restoration:
• All load restoration relays are Frequency Relays whose load shedding and load
  restoration functions can be switched on/off locally.
• The frequency relay trips whenever it detects that the frequency at the sensed node is
  outside the threshold (i.e., higher than the frequency setting for over-frequency, or lower
  than the frequency setting for under-frequency).
• For shedding, as soon as the frequency is detected to be beyond the threshold, the relay
  operates a shedding action, which is configured to be OPEN or CLOSE. In this way,
  various schemas of switching in devices and switching out other devices are possible.
  One or more devices can be triggered whose actions can be independent of other
  devices that are triggered together.
• For restoration, as soon as the frequency is detected to be beyond the threshold for
  over a configurable period and if the relay has been operated in the previous minutes,
  the relay operates the restoration action. The restoration action can be configured to be
  OPEN or CLOSE. One or more devices can be triggered whose actions can be
  independent of other devices that are triggered together.


5.3.7.1 Modeling a Load Restoration
From the Relay – Switch Association record associated with a Frequency Relay, update the
following fields:
• ProtectLoadOverAction
• ProtectLoadUnderAction

  Note: This is only possible for a ProtectionEq_Switch associated with a frequency relay.


5.3.8 Relay: Lockout
A relay can be locked out for a certain amount of time. By doing so, the instructor cannot
change the state of the relay.


Proprietary – See Copyright Page             317                               Simulation Modeling
                                                                 e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

For the frequency and voltage relays, the relay can be locked depending on the nature of
the fault. It can be locked after the relay trips for an “Under” condition, as well as for an
“Over” condition. The following two properties should be defined to model those two lockout
times:
• LockoutTimeLow
• LockoutTimeHigh
For the other relays, it is sufficient to define the LockoutTime field.


5.3.9 Steam Turbine: Detailed Steam Turbines (DST)
The detailed steam plant model is used to simulate the dynamic response of a fossil-fired
steam plant, including details of its steam supply and control systems.


5.3.9.1 Detailed Steam Turbine Model
The Detailed Steam Turbine (DST) model simulates the following types of generating units:
• Drum Boiler systems
• Once-through boiler systems (represented as well in e-terrasource by a Drum Boiler
  record)
• Oil-, gas-, or coal-fired units
• Conventional boiler following operation
• Coordinated control operation
• Single- (tandem) or dual-shaft (cross-compound) operation
The same basic model is used for each plant type. The type of plant being modeled is
determined by the values and definitions of individual parameters. For example, drum and
once-through boiler systems differ in response times and storage capacity. A drum boiler
system has a large boiler drum storage time, on the order of 200 seconds, while a
once-through boiler system has a faster response, on the order of 5 seconds, but a much
smaller storage capacity.
Figure 93 shows the major feedback and component interaction paths for the DST model.

Inputs to the subsystem are raise/lower pulses, frequency, unit electrical power, and
throttle pressure error from the boiler controls. Output signals are power (MW) demand and
MW error to the boiler controls, and the load reference motor (LRM) drive signal to turbine
control.
The coordinated control model consists of a demand accumulator and a proportional
integral (P-I) controller for the LRM. The demand accumulator stores raise/lower pulses
from AGC. The output is present demand power from AGC. The sum of AGC demand and the
frequency regulation component is total MW demand. This value is fed forward to the boiler
controls.
Gain parameters for the P-I controller are related to setpoints on the real controller.
If boiler steam flow is used as feedback to the boiler controls, MW demand is not typically
used as input to the boiler controls. In this case, the gain constant on the MW demand


Proprietary – See Copyright Page                                        320                                             Simulation Modeling
                                                                                                          e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

signal fed forward to the boiler controls is zero. If the steam flow is not a feedback signal,
the gain constant is one.
The power error bias gain, pressure error bias gain, and unit power signal gain are assigned
values of one or zero. These variables are used to indicate whether the data paths exist or
are being used.

signal. Output from the turbine controls is the steam flow into the turbine.

Figure 95. DST Turbine Controls Model

The turbine controls subsystem includes the following components:
• Speed Changer: The speed changer block includes user-specified rate and position
  limits. A feedback loop around the speed changer is established during initialization of
  the DTS, if the model includes coordinated control.
• Governor Frequency Regulator
• Backlash


Proprietary – See Copyright Page                                                         321                                                     Simulation Modeling
                                                                                                                                   e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

• Governor Hydro Controls: The governor Hydro control block includes a P-I controller for
  the control valve positioning equipment. First-stage pressure feedback is included by
  setting the gain constant of the feedback loop equal to one. The output of this block is
  input to the least value gate.
• Initial Pressure Limiter (IPL): The IPL block models the controls that prevent water from
  entering the turbine. The user-defined IPL setpoint is subtracted from the throttle
  pressure value to yield the IPL error signal, which is then multiplied by the IPL error gain
  constant. The result is input to the least value gate.
• Least Value Gate: The least value gate compares the governor P-I signal, the IPL signal,
  and the operator-defined load limit. The smallest of the three, which represents the
  most restrictive limit on the steam flow, is checked against rate and position limits, and
  the control valve is moved.
• Steam Flow: Steam flow is a product of the control valve position and throttle pressure.


5.3.9.1.4 DST Boiler Subsystem
The boiler subsystem, shown in Figure 96, is modeled as a storage element of defined
capacity and a pressure drop caused by superheater losses. Superheater losses are
proportional to the square of the steam flow; the proportionality constant is the
superheater pressure drop coefficient.

5.3.9.1.5 DST Governor Subsystem
The Detailed Steam Turbine (DST) governor subsystem is essentially identical to the Generic
Steam Turbine governor subsystem. For more information, see section 5.3.10.1 GST
Governor Subsystem.


5.3.10 Steam Turbine: Generic Steam Turbines (GST)
The Generic Steam Turbine (GST) model is used to simulate fossil-fired and nuclear steam
plants. The model does not include steam supply system dynamics, and it assumes that
throttle pressure is constant.
The generic steam turbine model is composed of two subsystems, described in the
following sections.


5.3.10.1 GST Governor Subsystem
A block diagram of the GST governor model is shown in Figure 97.

The GST governor subsystem includes the following components:
• Load reference motor (speed changer)
• Frequency regulator
• Governor deadband
• Control valve rate and position limits
• Multiplier: The control valve position is multiplied by the throttle pressure setpoint (the
  throttle pressure setpoint is assumed to be 1.0 p.u. for the GST model).

The output of the GST governor subsystem is power delivered by the steam flow to the
turbine.


5.3.10.2 GST Turbine Subsystem
The turbine model can be used to represent an arrangement with up to two shafts, three
stages, and two reheaters. Simpler arrangements are represented by setting some
parameters to zero.
The Steam Turbine subsystem is used with both the generic and detailed steam models. A
block diagram of the steam turbine subsystem is shown in Figure 98. The additions of two
possible steam flow feedback loops (one to the boiler controls and the other to the governor
Hydros controller) are shown in the diagram as dashed lines.

                                                                                                                     SHAFT 1
          (For Boiler-Turbine Model)                                                                               (High Pressure Shaft)
                To Boiler                                                                                      +

 (For Boiler-Turbine Model)                                                                                             SHAFT 2

Figure 98. GST Turbine Model

The turbine model can be used to represent an arrangement with up to two shafts, three
stages, and two reheaters. Simpler arrangements are represented by setting some
parameters to zero.
The model of the steam turbine subsystem consists of turbine stage power fractions and
reheaters. The power fractions and reheater time constants selected determine the overall
response of the generic steam model.
The steam power available is divided among the three stages on each shaft. The fraction of
the total power that each stage receives is its power fraction. The sum of the power
fractions on each shaft must equal one or zero.

Proprietary – See Copyright Page                                   324                                      Simulation Modeling
                                                                                              e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide


<!-- salto de página -->

Between one turbine stage and the next is a reheater. The reheater is shared by both
shafts, if two shafts are used. Each reheater is associated with a user-defined time
constant, which simulates the delay between a change in input steam flow and the
resultant change at the output of the reheater.
The output at each shaft is in per unit, and is based on the sum of the two units’ nameplate
base MVA ratings.

5.5 Simulation Workspace Validation
This section describes in detail the “Simulation Validation” and “Simulation Model Auto-
Generation” workspace validation sequences specific to the Simulation subsystem, in
addition to the other workspace validation sequences.
The “Simulation Validation” workspace validation sequence has the following modules:
• Simulation Generation Dynamic Model: This module checks if the prime-movers and
  other related dynamic model entities are well defined for the simulation model.
• Simulation Model: This module checks if the simulation model is well defined for some
  basic rules.
• Simulation Protection Model: This module checks if the relays and other related
  protection model entities are well defined for the simulation model.
The “Simulation Model Auto-Generation” workspace validation sequence has the following
module:
• Simulation Model AutoGeneration: This module performs the auto-generation of the
  Simulation model. For more details about this topic, refer to section 5.6 Simulation Auto-
  Generation.
Notes:
• Unlike the “Simulation Model AutoGeneration” workspace validation module, the
  “Simulation Generation Dynamic Model”, “Simulation Model”, and “Simulation Protection
  Model” workspace validation modules are part of the “Full Validation” workspace
  validation sequence.
• The “validation_message_max” global parameter can be defined to limit the number of
  Error, Warning, and Info messages, per validation rule:
    If the Validation Rule count hits the maximum defined, it will display the
    SIM_Validation_HitMax_Column message, which will show the number of messages
    that are not displayed for this rule. You can then decide to augment or reduce that
    parameter value for better usability.


Figure 101. validation_message_max Parameter


Proprietary – See Copyright Page               330                               Simulation Modeling
                                                                   e-terrasource EMS Modeling Guide
